title: Resolve a changed-strength barcode alert
stem: A client's tablet strength was changed this morning. Scanning the evening tablet produces a wrong-strength alert, although the drug name matches. What should the nurse do next?
options: Give it and ask pharmacy to update the barcode
Compare the current order with the supplied product
Split the tablet to match yesterday's dose
Use the barcode from the morning package
why: The discrepancy must be resolved before an uncertain dose is given.
The alert may reflect an outdated supply after the dose change.
Yesterday's dose does not establish the current prescription or tablet suitability.
A different package's barcode cannot verify the tablet being administered.
takeaway: The alert may reflect an outdated supply after the dose change.
learningObjective: Verify current strength and supply when scanning detects a medication discrepancy.

title: Replace a contaminated controlled medication
stem: While preparing a prescribed controlled analgesic, a tablet falls onto the floor. The client reports severe pain. What is the best action?
options: Place the dropped tablet in the client's drawer for later disposal
Discard it now and request replacement at the next scheduled dose
Arrange documented disposal and a replacement dose promptly
Document the dropped tablet as administered and obtain another
why: Unsecured storage leaves an unidentified controlled medication accessible.
Waiting until the next dose unnecessarily leaves the current pain untreated.
This maintains safe medication handling while addressing pain without unnecessary delay.
Incorrect administration documentation can create a false cumulative dose record.
takeaway: This maintains safe medication handling while addressing pain without unnecessary delay.
learningObjective: Replace a contaminated controlled analgesic while preserving accountability and timely pain relief.

title: Investigate uncertain prior administration
stem: An antihypertensive is due. The client says another nurse already gave it, but the administration record is blank. Blood pressure is stable. What should happen first?
options: Give it because the electronic record is blank
Mark it refused because the client questioned it
Wait one hour and give it if pressure is unchanged
Verify administration with the nurse and available records
why: A blank entry does not exclude an undocumented dose.
Questioning prior administration is different from declining treatment.
Blood pressure alone cannot establish whether the earlier dose occurred.
A stable client allows clarification that prevents duplicate dosing.
takeaway: A stable client allows clarification that prevents duplicate dosing.
learningObjective: Resolve possible undocumented administration before exposing the client to a duplicate dose.

title: Select an accurate oral measuring device
stem: A child is prescribed 1.8 mL of an oral liquid. The caregiver's cup has 5-mL markings. What should the nurse provide?
options: A calibrated oral syringe with suitable graduations
A second cup with the same graduations
Instructions to fill just below the cup's first mark
Instructions to round to 2.5 mL for convenience
why: Fine mL markings allow measurement of the small prescribed volume.
Another coarsely marked cup does not improve measurement accuracy.
Visual estimation below 5 mL is imprecise for 1.8 mL.
Rounding the prescribed volume this far changes the intended dose.
takeaway: Fine mL markings allow measurement of the small prescribed volume.
learningObjective: Match an oral measuring device's graduations to a small prescribed volume.

title: Review redosing after vomiting
stem: Ten minutes after an oral antibiotic, a child vomits. No intact medicine is visible and the child is now comfortable. What should the nurse do?
options: Reschedule the next dose sooner without consultation
Assess timing and obtain drug-specific redosing guidance
Repeat the full dose because vomiting was early
Give half a dose as a compromise
why: Changing the interval can unintentionally increase exposure.
Some medication may have been absorbed, so replacement needs specific guidance.
Early vomiting does not prove that none of the dose was absorbed.
An arbitrary half-dose does not resolve uncertainty about absorption.
takeaway: Some medication may have been absorbed, so replacement needs specific guidance.
learningObjective: Seek drug-specific guidance when vomiting makes absorption uncertain.

title: Address a tolerability-related refusal
stem: A client declines a scheduled antibiotic because the last dose caused nausea without rash or breathing symptoms. What is the best response?
options: Document refusal and leave the concern for discharge teaching
Recommend stopping the course until all nausea resolves
Assess the nausea and discuss an acceptable treatment plan
Record an allergy and request permanent avoidance of the class
why: Deferring discussion misses a current barrier to necessary treatment.
Unreviewed interruption may leave the infection inadequately treated.
A manageable adverse effect may be addressed while respecting the refusal.
Isolated nausea does not establish an immune-mediated allergy.
takeaway: A manageable adverse effect may be addressed while respecting the refusal.
learningObjective: Address a tolerability barrier while respecting an informed medication refusal.

title: Handle a single-dose vial remainder
stem: A nurse withdraws a dose from a vial labelled single-dose. A second dose for the same client is due that evening. What should happen to the remainder?
options: Refrigerate it because only one client will receive it
Label it with the usual multidose discard date
Withdraw the evening dose into a labelled syringe for bedside storage
Discard it according to policy after preparation
why: Same-client use does not change the container's single-dose designation.
A multidose beyond-use policy does not apply to this vial.
Future preparation and storage require an approved process, not repurposing opened single-dose supply.
Single-dose packaging is not intended for storage after opening.
takeaway: Single-dose packaging is not intended for storage after opening.
learningObjective: Distinguish single-dose vial handling from approved multidose storage.

title: Verify a client-owned product
stem: A client brings a weekly organizer after admission. One tablet does not match the current medication list. The client says it is the usual heart medicine. What is appropriate?
options: Have the medication identified and the intended order verified
Give it because it was placed in today's compartment
Use the old discharge list as the active prescription
Omit only the unfamiliar tablet for the entire admission
why: Both product identity and current treatment intent remain uncertain.
Organizer placement is not independent verification of the product.
An older list may omit subsequent changes or discontinued therapy.
An unresolved omission may interrupt necessary treatment.
takeaway: Both product identity and current treatment intent remain uncertain.
learningObjective: Verify both product identity and current authorization for client-owned medicines.

title: Prevent transdermal duplication
stem: A client using a daily medicated patch sometimes forgets where yesterday's patch was placed. Which strategies are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Apply the new patch first and search later
Use the same small skin area every day
Write a replacement schedule from memory each morning
Check for and remove the old patch before replacement
Record the application time and site
why: This permits unintended overlapping exposure while the old patch remains.
Repeated placement can irritate skin and does not ensure old-patch removal.
Reconstructing timing from memory is unreliable when forgetfulness is the problem.
An old patch may continue delivering medication after a new one is applied.
A simple record helps identify patches and prevents duplicate applications.
takeaway: An old patch may continue delivering medication after a new one is applied.
learningObjective: Use a reliable patch-removal and application record to prevent duplicate exposure.

title: Maintain eye-drop sterility
stem: During teaching, a client repeatedly steadies an eye-drop bottle by resting its tip on the lower lashes. Which correction is most useful?
options: Hold the bottle farther away and squeeze several drops
Aim at the centre of the eye to avoid the lashes
Support the hand on the face while keeping the tip clear
Wipe the tip after each contact and continue
why: A distant, forceful technique wastes medicine and reduces accuracy.
Direct corneal placement causes discomfort and does not solve contamination risk.
Hand support can improve control without contaminating the dropper tip.
Post-contact wiping does not reliably restore sterility.
takeaway: Hand support can improve control without contaminating the dropper tip.
learningObjective: Correct eye-drop technique to improve control while maintaining tip sterility.

title: Perform an independent dose check
stem: Policy requires an independent check of a high-alert infusion. Which actions preserve independence? Select all that apply.
options: The second nurse verifies only that the pump is running
The second nurse signs after reviewing yesterday's dose
Each nurse calculates from the original prescription
Both compare results before administration begins
One nurse states the answer while the other calculates
why: Pump operation does not establish that the programmed dose is correct.
Yesterday's treatment cannot verify the current preparation and order.
Separate calculations reduce the chance of carrying forward the same arithmetic error.
Differences can then be resolved before the client is exposed.
Knowing the first answer can bias the second calculation.
takeaway: Separate calculations reduce the chance of carrying forward the same arithmetic error.
learningObjective: Preserve independence when performing a required high-alert medication double check.

title: Administer verified medicines through a tube
stem: A client receives four immediate-release medicines through a gastric tube. Pharmacy has confirmed each formulation is suitable for the tube; mixing them has not been assessed. Which practices support safe administration? Select all that apply.
options: Flush between medicines using the prescribed fluid plan
Combine all preparations to reduce nursing time
Add the medicines to the full feeding container
Use the same flushing volume for every client
Give each prepared medicine separately
why: Flushing clears residual medicine while respecting the client's fluid allowance.
Compatibility for individual tube use does not establish mixture compatibility.
The client may not receive the complete dose if feeding is interrupted.
Fluid restrictions and tube characteristics require an individualized plan.
Separate administration reduces interaction and blockage risks and supports complete dosing.
takeaway: Separate administration reduces interaction and blockage risks and supports complete dosing.
learningObjective: Separate tube medications and apply an individualized flushing plan.

title: Relate renal decline to drug exposure
stem: A frail adult's creatinine rises during dehydration. A scheduled medicine is eliminated mainly by the kidneys, and the client is newly drowsy. What concern should guide review?
options: A duplicate administration during the medication round
Accumulation despite an unchanged prescribed dose
Reduced absorption caused by the creatinine rise
Tolerance requiring a higher dose
why: A duplicate dose remains a possible cause to investigate, but the stated renal decline specifically supports reduced clearance even with correct administration.
Reduced clearance can increase exposure even when administration has not changed.
The main stated change affects elimination rather than proving poor absorption.
New drowsiness during renal decline suggests increased effect, not reduced response.
takeaway: Reduced clearance can increase exposure even when administration has not changed.
learningObjective: Connect acute renal decline with possible accumulation of a renally eliminated medicine.

title: Evaluate additive sedation
stem: A client stable on an opioid becomes unusually sleepy after a sedative is added. Respirations are currently 14/min and regular. What is the best next action?
options: Check blood pressure and review whether orthostatic dizziness is present
Reassess after the client has completed a full sleep cycle
Assess sedation and breathing before further sedating doses
Give the next sedative because respirations exceed 12/min
why: Blood pressure and postural symptoms may be relevant, but they do not assess progressive sedation and ventilation after adding another central depressant.
Waiting may miss progressive sedation and ventilatory impairment.
Combined effects can progress, so current safety and the regimen need review.
A single respiratory rate does not establish safety with increasing sedation.
takeaway: Combined effects can progress, so current safety and the regimen need review.
learningObjective: Assess increasing sedation before further doses of interacting central depressants.

title: Review an elevated vancomycin level with renal change
stem: A client receives vancomycin 1 g IV every 12 hours for a susceptible infection. The level drawn immediately before the 0800 dose is 24 mg/L; creatinine rose from 80 to 135 micromol/L over 48 hours. The client-specific order says to withhold a dose when the predose level exceeds 20 mg/L and contact pharmacy or the prescriber. Fever is improving and the client is stable. What should the nurse do?
options: Give the 0800 dose and request a creatinine check tomorrow.
Withhold the 0800 dose and report the level and renal trend.
Give half the 0800 dose while asking for a revised schedule.
Repeat the level in two hours, then give 1 g if it has fallen.
why: Clinical improvement does not establish safe drug clearance when the predose concentration and creatinine have risen.
The measured level exceeds the supplied hold criterion; the changing renal function adds concern for accumulation and requires a revised dosing decision.
The nurse should not select a dose reduction; the prescriber or pharmacy dosing service must review concentration and renal function.
A falling level alone does not define a safe restart dose or interval; the current instruction requires holding and contacting the dosing team.
takeaway: Interpret medication levels with renal trends and apply the client-specific hold and reporting instructions.
learningObjective: Apply a supplied vancomycin hold parameter when a correctly timed level is elevated and renal function is changing.

title: Evaluate an antiemetic beyond sedation
stem: After a prescribed antiemetic, a client is mildly sleepy but wakes easily and remains alert during conversation. They can swallow safely and have no intake restriction but have not attempted fluids. Which assessment best determines the intended therapeutic response?
options: Ask about nausea and assess tolerance of a small permitted intake
Record sleep as proof that nausea resolved
Measure respiratory rate and compare it with the predose value
Wait for a full meal before reassessing
why: This measures the target symptom and its functional effect.
Sedation can occur without relief of nausea.
Respiratory monitoring evaluates medication safety; it does not directly establish nausea relief or tolerance of permitted intake.
A smaller permitted intake can evaluate response sooner and more tolerably.
takeaway: This measures the target symptom and its functional effect.
learningObjective: Evaluate nausea relief separately from medication-related sedation and safety findings.

title: Resolve uncertain Y-site compatibility
stem: A maintenance infusion runs through the only available lumen. A new IV medicine is due, but Y-site compatibility is not documented. The client is stable. What comes first?
options: Pause the maintenance fluid and give the medicine through the same tubing
Verify compatibility and an appropriate administration method
Run the medicine slowly through the Y-site
Look for cloudiness after starting the medicine
why: A pause does not establish compatibility with residual solution or an appropriate flushing/interruption plan; the infusion purpose and administration method still need verification.
The nurse needs a safe plan before the solutions contact each other.
A slower rate cannot establish chemical compatibility.
Some incompatibilities are not visible, and exposure has already occurred.
takeaway: The nurse needs a safe plan before the solutions contact each other.
learningObjective: Verify a safe administration method when Y-site compatibility is unknown.

title: Identify the correct infusion pathway
stem: Two similar clear infusions run through separate lumens. A replacement bag is ready, but one tubing label has detached. What should the nurse do?
options: Choose the bag whose remaining volume matches the record
Replace the label using the previous shift's diagram
Trace the relevant tubing from bag to client
Use the pump positioned nearest the correct lumen
why: Estimated volume cannot verify the tubing connection.
A diagram may not reflect connections changed since handover.
Physical tracing confirms the actual connections before the bag is changed.
Equipment position does not reliably identify the connected pathway.
takeaway: Physical tracing confirms the actual connections before the bag is changed.
learningObjective: Trace actual infusion connections rather than relying on device position or old labels.

title: Respond to resistance during flushing
stem: A peripheral catheter flushed easily earlier but now resists flushing and causes pain. What is the safest next action?
options: Use a smaller syringe to generate more pressure
Reposition the arm and begin the medicine at a slower rate
Flush until blood return appears
Stop using the catheter and assess the site and patency
why: Higher pressure can damage the catheter or surrounding tissue.
Changing position or rate does not establish patency or resolve the cause of new pain and flushing resistance.
Continuing against resistance can worsen a catheter complication.
New pain and resistance suggest a complication requiring assessment.
takeaway: New pain and resistance suggest a complication requiring assessment.
learningObjective: Stop catheter use and assess new pain with flushing resistance.

title: Differentiate phlebitis from infiltration
stem: A peripheral IV site is warm and red, with tenderness tracking along the vein. There is no cool swelling. Which problem is most consistent?
options: Phlebitis
Simple nonvesicant infiltration
A dressing-related skin reaction only
Systemic fluid overload
why: Vein-tracking warmth and tenderness favour venous inflammation.
Infiltration more often causes localized swelling and coolness.
A localized adhesive pattern would not explain tenderness along the vein.
Fluid overload does not explain this focal vein-tracking inflammation.
takeaway: Vein-tracking warmth and tenderness favour venous inflammation.
learningObjective: Differentiate vein-tracking inflammation from infiltration or adhesive irritation.

title: Teach a sublingual formulation
stem: A client prescribed a sublingual tablet says they will swallow it quickly to avoid the taste. What should the nurse explain?
options: It can be mixed into a drink if the full drink is taken
It should dissolve under the tongue as directed
Chewing is equivalent to letting it dissolve
Taking it after food gives the same onset
why: This converts the intended route to gastrointestinal administration.
The prescribed formulation relies on absorption through oral mucosa.
Chewing changes intended administration and may affect absorption.
Swallowing with food does not reproduce the sublingual route.
takeaway: The prescribed formulation relies on absorption through oral mucosa.
learningObjective: Explain how swallowing changes an intended sublingual administration route.

title: Address inhaler coordination difficulty
stem: A client presses a metered-dose inhaler before starting inhalation despite repeated coaching. Hand strength is adequate. What is the most useful next step?
options: Rehearse the written press-and-breathe sequence before the next dose
Arrange a dry-powder inhaler to remove the press-and-breathe step
Trial a compatible spacer with return demonstration
Add extra puffs to compensate for estimated loss
why: The client has already had repeated coaching; repeating the sequence does not directly address the demonstrated timing barrier.
A dry-powder device may be suitable for some clients, but inspiratory ability and device suitability must be assessed; a compatible spacer directly addresses this demonstrated barrier.
A spacer reduces the timing coordination required for delivery.
The delivered amount remains uncertain and the prescription is altered.
takeaway: A spacer reduces the timing coordination required for delivery.
learningObjective: Select a device aid for an observed inhaler-coordination barrier.

title: Prevent wrong-route liquid delivery
stem: An oral liquid must be given through a feeding tube while the client also has an IV line. Which preparation best reduces a route mix-up?
options: Label a Luer syringe for oral use and place it by the feeding pump
Use a labelled enteral syringe and select the line nearest the feeding pump
Use a labelled Luer syringe and have a second nurse confirm the drug
Use a labelled enteral syringe and trace the tube
why: Labelling and location cannot prevent a vascular connection when equipment is compatible with IV access.
Dedicated equipment and a label help, but equipment position does not verify which tube reaches the intended enteral route.
A drug check does not remove the vascular connection risk of using IV-compatible equipment for an enteral dose.
Dedicated equipment and tracing reduce wrong-route connection risk.
takeaway: Dedicated equipment and tracing reduce wrong-route connection risk.
learningObjective: Use dedicated labelled enteral equipment and line tracing to prevent route errors.

title: Manage an unavailable time-critical dose
stem: A client's prescribed time-critical medicine is due, but the dispensing cabinet is empty. The previous dose was given on time. What should the nurse do?
options: Contact pharmacy promptly and escalate any anticipated delay
Document omission immediately and wait for routine restocking
Move the dose to the next medication round independently
Use a similar medicine available in the cabinet
why: Timely supply coordination protects continuity and allows an alternate plan if needed.
The supply problem may be resolved before a clinically important delay.
Changing timing may reduce therapeutic coverage without review.
Therapeutic substitution requires an authorized plan.
takeaway: Timely supply coordination protects continuity and allows an alternate plan if needed.
learningObjective: Escalate a supply delay affecting time-critical therapy without unauthorized substitution.

title: Apply a localized topical order
stem: A topical corticosteroid is prescribed twice daily to one small elbow lesion. The client asks for it on new undiagnosed facial redness too. What is appropriate?
options: Use the facial rash response to confirm its diagnosis
Treat the ordered area and arrange review of the facial rash
Apply a thinner layer to the face using the same order
Use a weaker steroid left from a previous prescription on the face
why: An empiric steroid response does not establish a safe diagnosis.
A new site and diagnosis require assessment before extending therapy.
Less product does not authorize a new treatment site.
An old prescription does not establish the new diagnosis or current treatment authorization.
takeaway: A new site and diagnosis require assessment before extending therapy.
learningObjective: Distinguish an authorized topical treatment site from a new undiagnosed rash.

title: Respond to possible ACE inhibitor angioedema
stem: A client taking ramipril for several months develops a swollen tongue and muffled voice. There is no rash. What is the priority?
options: Observe until a rash develops to confirm allergy
Withhold tomorrow's ramipril and arrange routine follow-up
Activate emergency help and assess airway patency
Give an oral antihistamine before deciding whether to escalate
why: ACE inhibitor angioedema may occur without an itchy rash.
Stopping future exposure does not manage the current airway threat.
Tongue swelling and voice change may rapidly progress to airway obstruction.
Oral treatment can delay airway care and may be unsafe to swallow.
takeaway: Tongue swelling and voice change may rapidly progress to airway obstruction.
learningObjective: Prioritize a threatened airway in suspected ACE inhibitor angioedema without rash.

title: Evaluate a new cough during ACE therapy
stem: A client has a persistent dry cough after starting an ACE inhibitor. Temperature, oxygenation and weight are unchanged, and there is no dyspnea. What is most appropriate?
options: Begin fluid restriction for presumed pulmonary congestion
Advise stopping all antihypertensives until the cough disappears
Request antibiotics based on cough duration alone
Report the cough for medication review
why: The assessment does not demonstrate congestion warranting that intervention.
An indiscriminate interruption may destabilize blood pressure control.
A persistent dry cough alone does not establish bacterial infection.
The timing and otherwise stable assessment support considering an ACE inhibitor effect.
takeaway: The timing and otherwise stable assessment support considering an ACE inhibitor effect.
learningObjective: Consider an ACE inhibitor adverse effect after a dry cough with otherwise stable findings.

title: Assess potassium-sparing therapy safely
stem: A client taking spironolactone plans to replace table salt with a potassium-based substitute. Potassium is currently 4.8 mmol/L, reference 3.5–5.0. What is best?
options: Review the substitute with the prescriber or pharmacist first
Approve it because today's potassium is within range
Separate the salt substitute from spironolactone by two hours
Start it now and review potassium at the usual annual visit
why: Spironolactone and added potassium can together cause hyperkalemia.
A current normal value does not predict safety after potassium intake increases.
Dose separation does not remove the potassium-retaining effect of spironolactone.
A substantial new potassium source warrants review before routine use.
takeaway: Spironolactone and added potassium can together cause hyperkalemia.
learningObjective: Review concentrated potassium intake in a client using potassium-sparing therapy.

title: Assess possible digoxin accumulation
stem: A client's pulse falls from 76 to 48/min after several days of poor intake and worsening kidney function. Digoxin is due; nausea and yellow-tinged vision are new. What should happen?
options: Encourage oral fluids and reassess after the next dose
Withhold the dose and arrange urgent rhythm and toxicity assessment
Give it because the serum level was therapeutic last week
Treat nausea first and give digoxin once it settles
why: Giving another dose before review may worsen toxicity.
Renal decline, bradycardia and characteristic symptoms suggest possible digoxin accumulation.
A previous level does not reflect the current renal and clinical changes.
Suppressing one symptom does not address possible cardiac toxicity.
takeaway: Renal decline, bradycardia and characteristic symptoms suggest possible digoxin accumulation.
learningObjective: Integrate renal decline, pulse trend and new symptoms when assessing digoxin toxicity.

title: Assess severe muscle symptoms on a statin
stem: A client taking atorvastatin reports diffuse muscle pain, weakness and tea-coloured urine after no unusual exercise. What is appropriate?
options: Encourage exercise to distinguish stiffness from medication effects
Wait for the next scheduled lipid panel before reporting
Arrange prompt assessment for muscle injury and renal complications
Suggest taking the next dose with food to reduce intolerance
why: Exertion may worsen injury and delay assessment.
Lipid results do not assess an acute muscle-injury complication.
This symptom combination is concerning for serious statin-associated muscle injury.
Food does not address muscle breakdown or dark urine.
takeaway: This symptom combination is concerning for serious statin-associated muscle injury.
learningObjective: Recognize the muscle and renal warning pattern associated with statin therapy.

title: Clarify nitrate use after a PDE5 inhibitor
stem: A client with chest discomfort has a nitroglycerin order and reports sildenafil use earlier today. Blood pressure is 116/72 mmHg. What should the nurse do?
options: Give nitrate because systolic pressure is above 100 mmHg
Give half the nitrate dose before seeking advice
Wait for the sildenafil effect to wear off before assessing pain
Withhold nitrate and urgently notify the chest-pain team
why: The initial pressure does not remove the drug interaction.
An unprescribed partial dose does not establish interaction safety.
Chest discomfort still needs immediate assessment and an alternative plan.
The combination can cause severe hypotension despite an initially normal pressure.
takeaway: The combination can cause severe hypotension despite an initially normal pressure.
learningObjective: Identify nitrate interaction risk despite an initially acceptable blood pressure.

title: Distinguish diuretic benefit from adverse effects
stem: A client receives furosemide for congestion. Which follow-up findings support benefit rather than excessive diuresis? Select all that apply.
options: Ankle edema decreases while standing blood pressure remains stable
Weight falls and the client becomes faint on standing
Urine output rises but oxygen needs also rise
Serum potassium falls below the supplied reference range
Breathlessness decreases at the same activity level
why: Reduced edema without postural instability supports useful fluid removal.
Faintness suggests potentially excessive volume loss despite weight reduction.
Diuresis alone does not demonstrate improving pulmonary status.
Electrolyte depletion is an adverse effect rather than a treatment goal.
Improved exertional breathing supports reduced pulmonary congestion.
takeaway: Improved exertional breathing supports reduced pulmonary congestion.
learningObjective: Differentiate useful decongestion from diuretic-related perfusion and electrolyte adverse effects.

title: Respond to symptomatic thiazide-associated hyponatremia
stem: A client taking hydrochlorothiazide is newly confused. Sodium is 124 mmol/L, reference 135–145, and the next dose is due. What is the priority?
options: Plan repeat sodium testing at the next routine visit
Withhold the dose pending urgent assessment of symptomatic hyponatremia
Encourage additional plain water for presumed dehydration
Give the dose because blood pressure remains elevated
why: New confusion makes routine delayed reassessment inadequate.
Neurological symptoms with markedly low sodium require prompt review.
Free water can worsen a dilutional sodium problem.
Blood pressure alone does not outweigh this acute electrolyte concern.
takeaway: Neurological symptoms with markedly low sodium require prompt review.
learningObjective: Escalate neurological symptoms with marked hyponatremia before further thiazide dosing.

title: Explain safe beta-blocker continuation
stem: A client taking metoprolol for angina wants to stop because there has been no chest pain for weeks. What is the best response?
options: Stop now and restart if the pulse rises
Take it on alternating days until the supply is gone
Discuss any change with the prescriber and avoid abrupt withdrawal
Use it only when chest pain returns
why: A reactive restart does not safely manage withdrawal risk.
An improvised taper is not an individualized discontinuation plan.
Symptom control may reflect treatment, and abrupt withdrawal can provoke ischemia.
Changing maintenance therapy to symptom-triggered use may reduce protection.
takeaway: Symptom control may reflect treatment, and abrupt withdrawal can provoke ischemia.
learningObjective: Explain why controlled angina does not justify abrupt beta-blocker withdrawal.

title: Address postural symptoms after treatment
stem: After a first antihypertensive dose, a client becomes light-headed on standing. Supine pressure is 128/76 and standing pressure is 98/60 mmHg. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Help the client sit or lie safely and reassess symptoms
Report the positional readings for regimen review
Reassure because the supine pressure is normal
Give a large glass of water and repeat the standing measurement immediately
Give the next scheduled dose if the supine pressure has returned to baseline
why: Positioning limits immediate fall risk during symptomatic pressure reduction.
The measurable symptomatic change can guide treatment adjustment.
A normal supine reading does not explain away postural instability.
A fluid trial does not take priority over safe positioning in a symptomatic client; fluid suitability and reassessment timing require the clinical context.
Supine recovery does not resolve the symptomatic postural fall or replace review of the regimen.
takeaway: Positioning limits immediate fall risk during symptomatic pressure reduction.
learningObjective: Use positional readings and symptoms to guide immediate safety and regimen review.

title: Tailor once-daily diuretic timing
stem: A client takes prescribed once-daily furosemide at 22:00 and wakes repeatedly to urinate. There is no prescribed bedtime requirement. What should be discussed?
options: Move dosing earlier with the treatment team's timing guidance
Reduce the prescribed dose to reduce nighttime urine
Avoid daytime fluid intake so less is excreted at night
Take the dose only after a day of ankle swelling
why: Earlier administration can reduce nocturnal diuresis while preserving therapy.
Dose reduction may compromise congestion control.
Unnecessary restriction can cause dehydration without resolving timing.
Symptom-triggered use changes the prescribed maintenance schedule.
takeaway: Earlier administration can reduce nocturnal diuresis while preserving therapy.
learningObjective: Address nocturia through a feasible prescribed diuretic schedule.

title: Recognize heparin-associated thrombosis
stem: Six days after starting heparin, a client's platelets fall by more than half and a new painful swollen leg develops. What should the nurse do?
options: Apply compression and repeat platelets tomorrow
Stop heparin and urgently escalate under protocol
Give the next heparin dose while awaiting routine review
Request a lower heparin dose to reduce bruising risk
why: Local measures do not address a potentially serious medication reaction.
Thrombocytopenia with new thrombosis raises concern for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
Continued exposure can worsen immune-mediated thrombosis.
The concern is a prothrombotic immune reaction, not simply excessive anticoagulation.
takeaway: Thrombocytopenia with new thrombosis raises concern for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
learningObjective: Recognize thrombocytopenia with thrombosis as possible heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

title: Evaluate head injury during anticoagulation
stem: A client taking apixaban strikes the head in a fall. They deny headache and are alert with equal pupils. What should the nurse do?
options: Check INR before deciding whether assessment is needed
Hold the next apixaban dose and arrange review at tomorrow’s clinic
Arrange urgent head-injury assessment and follow the escalation pathway
Continue usual checks unless a headache develops
why: INR does not reliably measure apixaban's anticoagulant effect.
A dose decision does not evaluate possible intracranial injury, and delaying assessment is not justified by initially normal neurological findings.
Early normal findings do not exclude anticoagulant-associated intracranial bleeding.
Waiting for symptoms may delay recognition of occult bleeding.
takeaway: Early normal findings do not exclude anticoagulant-associated intracranial bleeding.
learningObjective: Arrange head-injury assessment despite initially normal findings during anticoagulation.

title: Respond to possible antiplatelet-related bleeding
stem: A client taking clopidogrel reports black sticky stools and dizziness. They have not taken iron or bismuth. What is the priority?
options: Provide constipation advice and review stool appearance tomorrow
Request a routine outpatient fecal screening test
Give the scheduled dose and report symptoms at handover
Assess circulation and urgently report suspected gastrointestinal bleeding
why: This presentation suggests bleeding rather than simple constipation.
A screening pathway is inappropriate for possible active symptomatic bleeding.
Administration and delayed reporting may worsen an unresolved bleeding event.
Melena with dizziness may indicate clinically significant blood loss.
takeaway: Melena with dizziness may indicate clinically significant blood loss.
learningObjective: Prioritize suspected active gastrointestinal bleeding during antiplatelet therapy.

title: Obtain a procedure-specific anticoagulant plan
stem: A client taking a direct oral anticoagulant has surgery in two days but no interruption instructions. Kidney function has recently declined. What is appropriate?
options: Obtain a plan incorporating the drug, renal function and procedure
Use the interruption schedule from a different anticoagulant
Continue because the latest INR is normal
Apply the standard 24-hour interruption in the clinic’s general preparation handout
why: These factors affect interruption and restart decisions.
Drug-specific elimination and bleeding risk differ.
A normal INR does not establish absent direct-anticoagulant effect.
A generic interval may not account for this drug, new renal decline and the procedure’s bleeding risk; an individualized plan is required.
takeaway: These factors affect interruption and restart decisions.
learningObjective: Obtain an individualized perioperative anticoagulant plan accounting for renal function.

title: Apply anticoagulant precautions to daily care
stem: A client starting anticoagulation describes their usual routines. Which planned changes are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Use a normal INR to decide whether a dose is needed
Take a missed dose together with the next one routinely
Use a soft toothbrush for gentle oral care
Check before adding nonprescription anti-inflammatory medicines
Stop anticoagulation for every small bruise
why: Not all anticoagulants are titrated by INR.
Missed-dose instructions are drug specific, and automatic doubling may be unsafe.
Reducing gum trauma helps limit preventable bleeding.
Many NSAIDs increase bleeding risk when combined with anticoagulation.
Unplanned interruptions can increase thrombosis risk.
takeaway: Reducing gum trauma helps limit preventable bleeding.
learningObjective: Apply bleeding precautions without creating unplanned anticoagulant interruptions.

title: Explain direct anticoagulant follow-up
stem: A client taking apixaban believes no follow-up is necessary because INR tests are not scheduled. Which response is best?
options: Keep a daily record of visible bruises to guide follow-up
Arrange a safety review when the prescribed dose is changed
Bleeding, kidney function and medication changes still need review
Ask for weekly INR tests to confirm effectiveness
why: Bruise tracking may help, but important bleeding can be internal and other exposure-related risks still need follow-up.
Dose changes matter, but renal function, bleeding and interactions can change at an unchanged dose.
Absence of routine INR titration does not eliminate safety monitoring.
INR is not used to routinely titrate apixaban.
takeaway: Absence of routine INR titration does not eliminate safety monitoring.
learningObjective: Explain ongoing safety monitoring when an anticoagulant is not titrated by INR.

title: Recognize clinically important nitrate hypotension
stem: After prescribed nitrate treatment, chest pain improves but pressure falls to 78/44 mmHg and the client feels faint. What is the priority?
options: Give another dose because some discomfort remains
Repeat the blood pressure in the other arm before calling for help
Recheck at the usual medication-effect interval
Activate urgent assessment and support circulation under protocol
why: Additional vasodilation can worsen circulatory instability.
Rapid confirmation can accompany but must not delay response to severe symptomatic hypotension.
The new instability requires immediate reassessment rather than routine timing.
Severe symptomatic hypotension threatens perfusion despite pain improvement.
takeaway: Severe symptomatic hypotension threatens perfusion despite pain improvement.
learningObjective: Prioritize severe nitrate-related hypotension despite improvement in chest discomfort.

title: Identify possible excessive diuresis
stem: A client treated for edema loses weight rapidly, develops dry mouth and becomes dizzy on standing. Lung sounds are now clear. What should guide the next review?
options: Possible intravascular depletion despite reduced edema
Persistent fluid overload because some ankle edema remains
Expected fluid mobilization with adequately preserved circulating volume
A need to increase diuretic frequency
why: Improved congestion can coexist with excessive circulating-volume loss.
Residual peripheral edema does not exclude depleted circulating volume.
Dry mouth and symptomatic postural change argue against assuming that circulating volume remains adequate merely because lung sounds cleared.
More diuresis may worsen the symptoms of depletion.
takeaway: Improved congestion can coexist with excessive circulating-volume loss.
learningObjective: Recognize intravascular depletion despite residual peripheral edema.

title: Evaluate amlodipine-associated edema
stem: A client develops bilateral ankle edema after an amlodipine increase. Weight, lung sounds and exercise tolerance are unchanged. What is most appropriate?
options: Delay reporting until breathlessness develops
Assess and report possible medication-related peripheral edema
Request an automatic diuretic increase for heart failure
Start leg elevation and compression and reassess at the next routine visit
why: A medication adverse effect can warrant review before respiratory compromise.
The timing and absence of pulmonary symptoms support reviewing amlodipine.
The assessment does not establish systemic congestion as the cause.
Local measures may be considered, but a new dose-related change should be assessed and communicated rather than managed as established benign oedema.
takeaway: The timing and absence of pulmonary symptoms support reviewing amlodipine.
learningObjective: Consider amlodipine-related edema when pulmonary congestion findings are absent.

title: Prioritize a rate-slowing drug combination
stem: A client taking diltiazem and metoprolol has new near-syncope and pulse 42/min. Both morning doses are due. What should happen?
options: Give only diltiazem because it is not a beta-blocker
Give metoprolol alone because diltiazem was added more recently
Withhold pending urgent assessment of symptomatic bradycardia
Give both because blood pressure is within range
why: Diltiazem can also slow cardiac conduction and rate.
Both slow the heart rate, and an arbitrary selection does not resolve symptomatic bradycardia.
Combined rate-slowing effects may be contributing to instability.
A normal pressure does not remove the danger of symptomatic bradycardia.
takeaway: Combined rate-slowing effects may be contributing to instability.
learningObjective: Recognize symptomatic bradycardia with concurrent rate-slowing medicines.

title: Plan ACE inhibitor safety monitoring
stem: A client has started ramipril while continuing prescribed hydrochlorothiazide. Which pairs should be included in the planned medication-safety follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Creatinine and serum potassium trends
Prothrombin time and INR trends
Hearing acuity and vestibular function
Serum amylase and lipase trends
Blood pressure and postural symptoms
why: Renal function and potassium can change after ACE inhibitor initiation, particularly when volume status is changing.
These measure coagulation and are not routine indicators of the stated ACE inhibitor effects.
These assessments target possible ototoxicity in other treatment contexts, rather than the stated ACE inhibitor effects.
Pancreatic enzymes do not monitor the stated renal, potassium or haemodynamic effects.
Combined therapy can produce clinically important hypotension, including symptomatic postural changes.
takeaway: Combined therapy can produce clinically important hypotension.
learningObjective: Select hemodynamic, renal and potassium follow-up for ACE inhibitor therapy.

title: Explain a prescribed nitrate-free interval
stem: A client removes a nitrate patch for a prescribed daily interval but worries this means treatment is failing. What explanation is most useful?
options: The interval helps preserve the response to subsequent nitrate exposure
The interval is mainly intended to let the previous application site recover
The interval makes up for slower nitrate absorption while the client is asleep
The interval compensates for the kidneys retaining nitrate between applications
why: Continuous nitrate exposure can produce tolerance, so a prescribed nitrate-free interval helps maintain responsiveness.
Skin-site rotation and skin assessment matter, but preventing tolerance is the main purpose of the prescribed nitrate-free interval.
The interval is not prescribed because normal sleep makes nitrate absorption too slow.
The standard planned interval addresses tolerance, not an assumed renal-clearance problem.
takeaway: Continuous nitrate exposure can produce tolerance and reduce effect.
learningObjective: Explain the role of a prescribed nitrate-free interval in limiting tolerance.

title: Clarify an undocumented anticoagulant transition
stem: A transfer list contains both warfarin and a direct oral anticoagulant, without a transition plan. The client cannot explain the change. What is appropriate?
options: Hold both for several days to ensure clearance
Clarify the intended transition before uncertain doses
Continue both until the next routine INR result
Choose the medicine the client used longest
why: An arbitrary interruption may create avoidable thrombosis risk.
Unplanned overlap can cause bleeding, while an incorrect omission can leave thrombosis untreated.
The list alone does not authorize overlap and INR may be insufficient.
Duration of prior use does not establish current treatment intent.
takeaway: Unplanned overlap can cause bleeding, while an incorrect omission can leave thrombosis untreated.
learningObjective: Resolve an undocumented anticoagulant transition before uncertain overlapping doses.

title: Address a timing barrier to adherence
stem: A client skips antihypertensive doses because rotating shifts make the schedule difficult. They understand the purpose and can afford the medicine. What is the most useful intervention?
options: Arrange financial assistance as the first step
Set a reminder alarm for the same clock time each day
Develop a feasible prescribed schedule with the client and team
Review how consistent therapy reduces the long-term risk of stroke
why: Cost is not the barrier reported in this scenario.
A fixed reminder may not make the prescribed schedule feasible across changing sleep and work periods; the schedule itself needs discussion.
This directly addresses the identified timing barrier.
The client already understands treatment purpose; repeating benefits does not directly resolve the reported scheduling barrier.
takeaway: This directly addresses the identified timing barrier.
learningObjective: Match adherence support to a rotating-shift scheduling barrier.

title: Apply a type 1 diabetes sick-day plan
stem: A client with type 1 diabetes has influenza and poor appetite. They plan to stop basal insulin until eating normally. Which teaching priority addresses the most urgent misconception?
options: How to choose tolerated carbohydrate-containing foods
How to match mealtime doses to the amount eaten
How to resume usual activity after the fever settles
How to continue basal insulin under the sick-day plan
why: Food planning matters, but it does not correct the dangerous plan to omit basal insulin.
Mealtime adjustment is relevant but does not replace the continuing basal requirement.
Recovery activity is less urgent than preventing current insulin deficiency.
Without basal insulin, ketoacidosis can develop despite poor food intake.
takeaway: Without basal insulin, ketoacidosis can develop despite poor food intake.
learningObjective: Maintain an individualized insulin and monitoring plan during illness with poor intake.

title: Address lipohypertrophy before dose escalation
stem: A client has erratic glucose despite prescribed insulin use. They inject into the same firm abdominal lump because it hurts less. What is the most useful next step?
options: Assess injection sites and teach rotation into healthy tissue
Request a higher insulin dose for the persistent high readings
Rotate daily between the abdomen, upper arms and thighs
Teach deeper injections into the same lump
why: Lipohypertrophy can cause unpredictable absorption and needs correction before assuming dose failure.
Increasing insulin before correcting unpredictable absorption can cause hypoglycaemia when injections move into healthy tissue.
Frequent changes between body regions may add absorption variation; a consistent site-rotation plan within suitable healthy tissue is needed.
Changing depth does not restore normal absorption in damaged tissue.
takeaway: Lipohypertrophy can cause unpredictable absorption and needs correction before assuming dose failure.
learningObjective: Address injection-site lipohypertrophy before assuming the prescribed insulin dose is ineffective.

title: Explain why insulin pens are individual devices
stem: Two spouses use the same insulin product and ask to share a pen with separate needles. What is the best explanation?
options: Cleaning the outer pen permits sharing
Blood contamination may occur inside the pen
Sharing is acceptable when neither has a known infection
Sharing is acceptable if both prescribed doses match
why: External cleaning does not disinfect its internal fluid pathway.
Changing the needle does not make a pen safe for another person.
Unrecognized bloodborne infection still makes shared use unsafe.
Matching doses does not address contamination inside the device.
takeaway: Changing the needle does not make a pen safe for another person.
learningObjective: Explain why changing needles does not make insulin pens safe to share.

title: Verify a concentrated insulin transition
stem: A client's insulin prescription changes to a concentrated pen. They want to withdraw the insulin using their old syringe because it feels familiar. What is appropriate?
options: Explain the new pen instructions and ask the client to repeat the prescribed dose
Use the old syringe markings while following the new pen label
Reteach dosing with the prescribed pen and return demonstration
Convert to the old syringe volume using the previous label
why: Repeating the dose checks recall but does not establish the ability to use the unfamiliar concentrated-insulin device correctly.
The syringe markings may not correspond to the concentrated pen product.
Observed device-specific technique helps prevent a concentration-related dosing error.
Old volume instructions may deliver the wrong amount of concentrated insulin.
takeaway: Observed device-specific technique helps prevent a concentration-related dosing error.
learningObjective: Verify device-specific administration when a concentrated insulin product is prescribed.

title: Link a sulfonylurea to skipped-meal symptoms
stem: A client taking gliclazide reports shakiness during a shift after missing lunch. They have a glucose meter available. What should the nurse advise first?
options: Eat a routine snack and check at the next scheduled time
Rest first and check glucose only if symptoms persist
Arrange a change to tomorrow's dose before assessing the symptoms
Check glucose now and follow the low-glucose plan if needed
why: A routine snack and delayed check may not adequately identify or treat a current low.
The meter is available, and rest does not determine whether glucose is dangerously low.
A future regimen adjustment does not address the possible current hypoglycemia.
Gliclazide plus a missed meal makes the current shakiness concerning for hypoglycemia.
takeaway: Gliclazide plus a missed meal makes the current shakiness concerning for hypoglycemia.
learningObjective: Assess possible sulfonylurea-associated hypoglycemia after a missed meal.

title: Review metformin during acute renal decline
stem: A client taking metformin is admitted with vomiting, dehydration and new acute kidney injury. A usual dose is due. What is appropriate?
options: Seek prompt medication review before administering the dose
Give it because the long-term prescription has not changed
Give half the dose without contacting the team
Give it with food and defer the kidney result
why: Acute renal impairment and dehydration can change metformin safety.
The acute illness changes the assessment required before administration.
An arbitrary reduction is not an authorized renal-adjustment plan.
Food does not remove the accumulation concern from acute renal impairment.
takeaway: Acute renal impairment and dehydration can change metformin safety.
learningObjective: Reassess metformin safety when dehydration and acute renal impairment develop.

title: Recognize possible euglycemic ketoacidosis
stem: A client taking empagliflozin has persistent vomiting, abdominal pain and deep breathing. Glucose is only moderately elevated. What should the nurse do?
options: Repeat capillary glucose in one hour to decide whether emergency assessment is needed
Urgently assess for ketones and acid-base disturbance
Use the glucose value to exclude a diabetic emergency
Hydrate while arranging routine sick-day telephone review later
why: Glucose may understate SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis; persistent vomiting, abdominal pain and deep breathing warrant urgent assessment now.
SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis can be serious even when glucose is only moderately elevated.
Moderate glucose does not exclude ketoacidosis with this medication and symptom pattern.
Persistent vomiting and deep breathing require more urgent assessment.
takeaway: SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis can be serious even when glucose is only moderately elevated.
learningObjective: Recognize ketoacidosis warning symptoms during SGLT2 therapy despite modest glucose elevation.

title: Evaluate severe symptoms during GLP-1 therapy
stem: A client taking semaglutide reports severe persistent upper abdominal pain and repeated vomiting. Mild nausea had occurred previously. What is best?
options: Use small frequent drinks and judge the response by whether nausea settles
Request a smaller dose at the next routine medication review
Arrange prompt clinical assessment before further dosing
Apply the previous mild-nausea plan and reassess tomorrow
why: Nausea relief does not exclude a serious cause of continuing severe upper-abdominal pain.
A routine dose discussion is too delayed for persistent severe pain with repeated vomiting.
Severe persistent pain differs from earlier mild nausea and requires evaluation.
The changed severity makes routine delayed self-management insufficient.
takeaway: Severe persistent pain differs from earlier mild nausea and requires evaluation.
learningObjective: Distinguish severe persistent abdominal symptoms from mild expected GLP-1 intolerance.

title: Assess hyperglycemia after glucocorticoids
stem: A client starts systemic prednisone and subsequently has thirst and repeatedly elevated glucose despite no prior diabetes diagnosis. What interpretation best guides care?
options: A previous normal glucose rules out a medication contribution
The results reflect undiagnosed diabetes unrelated to prednisone
Thirst is sufficient evidence to reduce prednisone independently
The steroid may have increased glucose and monitoring needs
why: Normal pretreatment values do not exclude steroid-associated hyperglycemia.
The temporal association warrants assessment of a steroid contribution without assuming a permanent diagnosis.
Treatment changes require review of the indication and glucose management plan.
Glucocorticoids can raise glucose even without previously diagnosed diabetes.
takeaway: Glucocorticoids can raise glucose even without previously diagnosed diabetes.
learningObjective: Connect new hyperglycemia with systemic glucocorticoid exposure and monitoring needs.

title: Verify practical insulin readiness
stem: An older adult is preparing to manage a new insulin pen independently at home. Which findings support readiness? Select all that apply.
options: The client accurately demonstrates selecting and delivering the prescribed dose
The client explains when and how to treat low glucose
The client agrees with every instruction but cannot show dose selection
The client identifies the pen only by cap colour
The client relies on a family member who will not be present
why: Return demonstration tests practical ability rather than verbal agreement.
Recognizing and responding to hypoglycemia supports safer independent use.
Agreement alone does not demonstrate the ability to administer insulin.
Colour cannot reliably establish the prescribed insulin product.
A plan dependent on unavailable assistance does not support independent use.
takeaway: Return demonstration tests practical ability rather than verbal agreement.
learningObjective: Evaluate demonstrated insulin administration and hypoglycemia-management competence.

title: Plan discontinuation after prolonged steroid use
stem: A client has taken systemic prednisone daily for months and wants to stop because symptoms improved. What is the best response?
options: Reuse the taper schedule provided for a previous brief course of prednisone
Arrange a prescriber-directed taper and discuss adrenal suppression
Stop when the current package is finished regardless of dose
Alternate full doses and no doses based on daily symptoms
why: A schedule for a brief course may not account for months of adrenal suppression or the current underlying disease.
Prolonged therapy can suppress endogenous cortisol, making abrupt withdrawal hazardous.
Package completion does not establish a safe discontinuation schedule.
An improvised schedule does not address adrenal recovery reliably.
takeaway: Prolonged therapy can suppress endogenous cortisol, making abrupt withdrawal hazardous.
learningObjective: Explain the need for a supervised discontinuation plan after prolonged systemic steroid use.

title: Improve levothyroxine administration consistency
stem: A client takes levothyroxine with iron on some mornings and without breakfast on others. Thyroid results have become variable. What is the best teaching focus?
options: Alternate breakfast and fasting administration according to convenience
Request a higher dose before addressing administration technique
Use consistent instructed timing and separate interacting supplements
Separate iron only on days when thyroid blood tests are scheduled
why: Variable food exposure can continue to produce variable absorption.
Correcting inconsistent administration may prevent unnecessary dose escalation.
Variable food and iron exposure can alter levothyroxine absorption.
Absorption consistency is needed between tests, not just on sampling days.
takeaway: Variable food and iron exposure can alter levothyroxine absorption.
learningObjective: Address inconsistent levothyroxine absorption from variable meals and interacting supplements.

title: Recognize possible thyroid overreplacement
stem: After a levothyroxine increase, a client develops palpitations, heat intolerance and tremor. What should the nurse do?
options: Move the levothyroxine dose to bedtime to reduce daytime symptoms
Reassure that symptoms reflect adjustment and keep routine follow-up
Provide relaxation teaching and defer thyroid review unless anxiety persists
Report symptoms for thyroid and cardiovascular assessment
why: Timing changes do not evaluate or correct possible excessive hormone exposure after a dose increase.
The adrenergic symptom cluster after a dose increase warrants earlier review.
Relaxation alone does not address possible excessive hormone replacement.
The temporal pattern suggests possible overreplacement requiring review.
takeaway: The temporal pattern suggests possible overreplacement requiring review.
learningObjective: Identify possible thyroid overreplacement from new symptoms after a dose increase.

title: Report fever during antithyroid treatment
stem: A client taking methimazole develops fever and a sore throat. They ask whether to treat it as a usual cold. What is appropriate?
options: Promptly contact the treatment team for assessment and blood-count guidance
Use cold remedies and report only if symptoms persist a week
Arrange a thyroid-function test and use its result to decide about review
Treat it as an allergy solely because fever followed treatment
why: Agranulocytosis is uncommon but serious and must be considered.
Delayed assessment may miss a serious drug-associated infection risk.
Thyroid hormone control does not assess neutrophil suppression or infection risk; these symptoms need prompt review and blood-count guidance.
Fever and sore throat require evaluation rather than an assumed mechanism.
takeaway: Agranulocytosis is uncommon but serious and must be considered.
learningObjective: Escalate fever and sore throat during methimazole therapy for marrow-toxicity assessment.

title: Evaluate oral bisphosphonate suitability
stem: A client prescribed oral alendronate cannot remain upright because of an acute back condition. What should the nurse do before administration?
options: Crush it into a small volume of food
Clarify an appropriate treatment plan or alternative
Give it with breakfast to protect the esophagus
Give it just before sleep to minimize discomfort
why: Changing formulation does not establish safety and can increase irritation.
Upright positioning is part of reducing esophageal injury with oral alendronate.
Food reduces absorption and does not replace positioning requirements.
Recumbency increases the risk of esophageal exposure.
takeaway: Upright positioning is part of reducing esophageal injury with oral alendronate.
learningObjective: Clarify oral bisphosphonate suitability when upright positioning is not possible.

title: Recognize desmopressin-associated water retention
stem: A client taking desmopressin drinks unusually large amounts of water, passes less urine and develops headache, confusion and weight gain. What is the priority concern?
options: Dehydration from inadequate antidiuretic effect
Hyperglycemia-related osmotic fluid loss
Water retention with possible hyponatremia
A medication headache without a fluid disturbance
why: Inadequate effect would favour excessive urine loss rather than retention and weight gain.
Osmotic diuresis would more typically increase urine output and cause volume loss.
Reduced water excretion plus excess intake can dilute sodium and affect neurological function.
Reduced urine output, weight gain and confusion suggest a wider water-balance problem.
takeaway: Reduced water excretion plus excess intake can dilute sodium and affect neurological function.
learningObjective: Recognize neurological warning symptoms of water retention during desmopressin therapy.

title: Escalate failed oral adrenal replacement
stem: A client with adrenal insufficiency cannot keep prescribed hydrocortisone down during gastroenteritis and feels increasingly weak. What is appropriate?
options: Wait until the next routine tablet time
Take smaller bites of food before retrying for several hours
Replace the missed medicine with extra salt and water
Urgently follow the emergency sick-day replacement plan
why: Delay can allow adrenal crisis to develop.
A prolonged trial of oral intake can delay necessary parenteral replacement.
Fluids and salt cannot replace deficient glucocorticoid activity.
Vomiting can prevent absorption when illness increases cortisol needs.
takeaway: Vomiting can prevent absorption when illness increases cortisol needs.
learningObjective: Activate emergency replacement planning when vomiting prevents oral glucocorticoid absorption.

title: Prepare for new exercise with insulin
stem: An insulin-treated client plans to start prolonged evening exercise. Which elements belong in a safe individualized plan? Select all that apply.
options: Continue exercising through shakiness until a planned break
Monitor glucose around activity and afterward as instructed
Keep rapid carbohydrate readily available
Assume an adequate pre-exercise meal prevents every low
Omit all basal insulin on exercise days
why: Symptoms require timely assessment rather than continued exertion.
Exercise can alter glucose during activity and later recovery.
Accessible treatment supports a prompt response to low glucose.
Delayed hypoglycemia can still occur despite prior food intake.
Blanket basal omission can create significant insulin deficiency.
takeaway: Exercise can alter glucose during activity and later recovery.
learningObjective: Plan glucose monitoring and hypoglycemia treatment around a new exercise pattern.

title: Plan insulin use across time zones
stem: A client using basal and mealtime insulin will cross several time zones. Which preparations are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Keep basal and mealtime doses on the home clock throughout the trip
Pack all insulin with ice directly against the cartridges
Adjust mealtime doses after arrival according to appetite at each meal
Obtain an individualized dosing and monitoring schedule
Carry accessible supplies and hypoglycemia treatment
why: Maintaining every home-clock dose may mismatch changed meal times and dose intervals; an individualized travel plan is needed.
Freezing can damage insulin and make it unreliable.
Appetite alone does not establish carbohydrate intake, glucose status or the appropriate dose intervals across time zones.
Time changes can alter intervals between doses and meals.
Lost checked luggage should not interrupt essential treatment.
takeaway: Time changes can alter intervals between doses and meals.
learningObjective: Prepare an individualized insulin schedule for travel across time zones.

title: Evaluate emergency glucagon teaching
stem: A partner receives training with the client's prescribed glucagon rescue device. Which statement shows appropriate understanding?
options: I will try to give a drink before using it even if swallowing is unsafe
I will practise by partly discharging the real rescue device
I will use the device as taught and call for emergency help
If the person wakes, no further glucose checks are needed
why: Oral intake during impaired consciousness creates aspiration risk.
A partially used single-use device may not provide the intended emergency dose.
Severe hypoglycemia needs rescue treatment plus assessment and continued monitoring.
Low glucose can recur and the cause still needs review.
takeaway: Severe hypoglycemia needs rescue treatment plus assessment and continued monitoring.
learningObjective: Evaluate a caregiver's understanding of prescribed glucagon rescue and subsequent monitoring.

title: Assess abnormal insulin appearance
stem: A clear insulin product now contains visible particles after being left near a heater. What should the nurse advise?
options: Use it if the next glucose reading is normal
Increase the dose to compensate for possible loss of potency
Refrigerate it again and assume potency is restored
Do not use it and arrange a verified replacement
why: A glucose result cannot verify the damaged product's reliability.
The degree of damage is unknown, making dose compensation unsafe.
Cooling cannot reverse damage already caused by improper storage.
Unexpected particles and heat exposure raise concern about product integrity.
takeaway: Unexpected particles and heat exposure raise concern about product integrity.
learningObjective: Respond to abnormal insulin appearance after possible heat damage.

title: Respond to interrupted pump delivery
stem: A client with type 1 diabetes finds that insulin pump delivery stopped several hours ago. They feel well but glucose is rising. What should happen?
options: Check glucose and ketones as directed and activate the backup insulin plan
Wait for symptoms before using the backup plan
Give a correction through the same unverified malfunctioning system
Reconnect and postpone all monitoring until bedtime
why: Pump interruption can quickly lead to insulin deficiency and ketoacidosis.
Feeling well does not exclude evolving insulin deficiency.
The intended dose may not be delivered until function is confirmed.
Restored connection alone does not show that glucose and ketones are safe.
takeaway: Pump interruption can quickly lead to insulin deficiency and ketoacidosis.
learningObjective: Activate a backup insulin plan when pump interruption causes rising glucose.

title: Distinguish antithyroid benefit from excessive suppression
stem: A client starts treatment for hyperthyroidism. Which change best supports the intended response?
options: The client reports a new sore throat and fever
Resting tachycardia and tremor decrease without new cold intolerance
Weight rises rapidly with profound lethargy and cold intolerance
Palpitations persist but the client is less worried
why: These can indicate an important adverse effect requiring assessment.
This suggests reduced excess hormone effect without clear hypothyroid symptoms.
These findings may suggest excessive suppression rather than balanced treatment.
Reduced anxiety does not establish a physiological treatment response.
takeaway: This suggests reduced excess hormone effect without clear hypothyroid symptoms.
learningObjective: Distinguish controlled hyperthyroidism from excessive suppression or treatment toxicity.

title: Clarify an incomplete correction scale
stem: A client's premeal glucose lies above the highest range on the prescribed insulin correction scale. The client is alert and the meal is available. What should the nurse do?
options: Use the highest listed dose as the final plan
Repeat the glucose after the meal before contacting the prescriber
Contact the authorized prescriber or follow the escalation instruction
Extend the scale by repeating its last numerical increment
why: That dose may be insufficient or inappropriate for the unlisted range.
A later value does not replace current clarification of a result outside the authorized dosing scale.
The incomplete scale does not authorize extrapolation to an unlisted range.
A pattern in listed doses is not a prescription for higher values.
takeaway: The incomplete scale does not authorize extrapolation to an unlisted range.
learningObjective: Seek an authorized dose when a correction scale omits the current glucose range.

title: Recognize complications during chronic corticosteroid therapy
stem: A client taking long-term systemic corticosteroids is reviewing when to call the clinic. Which changes need prompt same-day assessment rather than routine teaching? Select all that apply.
options: New fever with a worsening cough
Black sticky stools with new light-headedness
Joint pain improves enough to walk farther
Mild sleep difficulty after a dose taken late in the day
Mild appetite improvement without other changes
why: Immunosuppression raises concern about infection and its progression.
This pattern may indicate gastrointestinal bleeding.
Functional improvement may be an intended anti-inflammatory benefit.
This merits timing advice or routine review but is less urgent than infection or bleeding signs.
This can occur with corticosteroids and is less urgent than the listed red flags.
takeaway: Immunosuppression raises concern about infection and its progression.
learningObjective: Identify infection and bleeding warning symptoms during chronic systemic corticosteroid use.

title: Obtain cultures without an avoidable antibiotic delay
stem: A stable client with an indwelling urinary catheter has orders for a urine culture and a first antibiotic dose. The sampling port is readily accessible and collection can occur now. What is appropriate?
options: Collect the specimen promptly before the first dose
Give the dose and collect urine after symptoms improve
Wait for the culture result before giving the ordered antibiotic
Collect the sample from a previously filled drainage bag
why: Antibiotic exposure can reduce culture yield when sampling is easily obtained first.
Treatment may reduce the chance of identifying the organism.
Specimen collection does not require delaying treatment until results return.
Old bag urine may not reliably represent a fresh diagnostic specimen.
takeaway: Antibiotic exposure can reduce culture yield when sampling is easily obtained first.
learningObjective: Collect an available ordered culture before antibiotics without awaiting the result.

title: Reassess therapy when susceptibility results arrive
stem: A client improving on an empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic has a culture identifying a susceptible organism. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: Add the targeted medicine while completing the broad-spectrum course
Team review for the most targeted effective regimen
Complete the broad-spectrum course solely because the response is good
Repeat the culture before considering any regimen review
why: Unnecessary overlap adds exposure without automatically improving treatment.
The identified organism and susceptibilities can support narrower effective coverage.
Improvement does not remove the benefit of reviewing unnecessary broad coverage.
Existing clinically relevant susceptibility results can already inform the treatment review.
takeaway: The identified organism and susceptibilities can support narrower effective coverage.
learningObjective: Anticipate targeted antimicrobial review after organism susceptibility becomes available.

title: Clarify an incomplete allergy history
stem: A client reports 'a penicillin allergy' before receiving a newly prescribed antibiotic. No reaction details are recorded. What is the best next step?
options: Remove the allergy because no written proof is available
Request an antibiotic from a different class because penicillins and cephalosporins are both beta-lactams
Ask what happened, when it occurred and what treatment was needed
Assume nausea and airway swelling carry the same risk
why: An undocumented history still needs investigation before removal.
A shared broad class does not establish identical allergy risk for every product; the reaction history and proposed antibiotic need assessment.
Reaction characteristics help the team assess the allergy and antibiotic plan.
Different reaction types require different clinical interpretation.
takeaway: Reaction characteristics help the team assess the allergy and antibiotic plan.
learningObjective: Elicit reaction details before interpreting a nonspecific antibiotic allergy history.

title: Respond to severe antibiotic-associated diarrhea
stem: A client taking antibiotics has six watery stools in eighteen hours, abdominal cramping and increasing thirst. What is most appropriate?
options: Recommend loperamide before evaluating the cause
Give routine intolerance advice because no fever is reported
Arrange a stool sample for the next clinic day before deciding on further care
Assess hydration and report possible antibiotic-associated infection
why: Antimotility treatment may be inappropriate with suspected infectious colitis.
Absence of fever does not exclude important antibiotic-associated infection or dehydration.
Delaying the decision until a later sample does not address current fluid losses and possible transmissible infection.
Frequent diarrhea and thirst raise concerns about colitis and fluid depletion.
takeaway: Frequent diarrhea and thirst raise concerns about colitis and fluid depletion.
learningObjective: Assess significant antibiotic-associated diarrhea for hydration and infectious complications.

title: Interpret antibiotic response using trends
stem: After antibiotics begin for pneumonia, which findings most clearly support improvement? Select all that apply.
options: Temperature trend and respiratory symptoms improve
Usual activity becomes easier at the same oxygen requirement
One normal temperature while an antipyretic is active
Less coughing accompanied by increasing somnolence
A falling white count with worsening hypotension
why: The infection's clinical manifestations should lessen with effective treatment.
Functional improvement adds meaningful evidence of recovery.
This alone can mask fever without establishing infection control.
Reduced cough with declining alertness may indicate deterioration.
Laboratory improvement does not outweigh new circulatory compromise.
takeaway: The infection's clinical manifestations should lessen with effective treatment.
learningObjective: Judge antimicrobial response using clinical trends rather than isolated laboratory changes.

title: Recognize aminoglycoside ototoxicity
stem: A client receiving gentamicin reports new ringing in the ears and unsteadiness. The next dose is due. What is appropriate?
options: Wait until the antibiotic course is complete to arrange testing
Promptly report the symptoms and clarify the next dose
Give the dose because hearing loss has not been confirmed
Treat dizziness with a sedative before administration
why: Delay may allow potentially irreversible injury to progress.
Aminoglycosides can cause auditory and vestibular toxicity.
Early symptoms warrant review before further potentially harmful exposure.
Sedation can obscure neurological assessment without addressing ototoxicity.
takeaway: Aminoglycosides can cause auditory and vestibular toxicity.
learningObjective: Report new auditory or balance symptoms during aminoglycoside exposure.

title: Review aminoglycoside clearance during renal decline
stem: During gentamicin therapy, urine output falls and creatinine rises. The most recent drug level predates these changes. What is appropriate?
options: Increase the dose because less drug reaches the urine
Compare today’s oral intake with yesterday’s before approving the dose
Request prompt review of current levels and dosing
Use the prior drug level to approve the next several doses
why: Reduced elimination generally raises systemic accumulation concerns.
Intake comparison may inform hydration assessment but cannot establish current gentamicin clearance or safety with rising creatinine and falling urine output.
Reduced clearance can increase exposure after a previously acceptable level.
An earlier level may no longer represent the client's exposure.
takeaway: Reduced clearance can increase exposure after a previously acceptable level.
learningObjective: Reassess aminoglycoside clearance after acute renal deterioration.

title: Assess a vancomycin infusion reaction
