stem: During IV vancomycin, a client develops flushing and itching over the neck and chest. Blood pressure and breathing remain stable. What should the nurse do first?
options: Continue unchanged because blood pressure is normal
Label all future glycopeptides as confirmed anaphylactic allergies
Reduce the rate until flushing settles, then restore the prescribed rate
Pause the infusion and assess/report the reaction
why: Stable pressure does not justify ignoring a new infusion reaction.
The current findings do not establish that specific immune mechanism.
Symptom improvement after slowing does not establish a safe restart plan; the reaction first needs assessment and an authorized administration decision.
The pattern may be infusion related, but assessment is needed before a revised plan.
takeaway: The pattern may be infusion related, but assessment is needed before a revised plan.
learningObjective: Pause and assess a stable flushing reaction during vancomycin infusion.

title: Recognize a severe cutaneous drug reaction
stem: After starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, a client develops fever, a spreading painful rash and mouth sores. What is appropriate?
options: Urgently escalate and withhold further doses pending review
Give the next dose after an antihistamine reduces the itching
Treat mouth sores as thrush separate from a mild skin eruption
Request a routine dose reduction while continuing the medicine
why: Painful rash with mucosal involvement suggests a potentially severe drug reaction.
Reduced itching does not exclude severe mucocutaneous injury or make further exposure safe.
The combined mucosal and painful skin findings require consideration of a severe drug reaction.
Continuing exposure during a possible severe reaction can worsen harm.
takeaway: Painful rash with mucosal involvement suggests a potentially severe drug reaction.
learningObjective: Recognize mucosal involvement and painful rash as a serious antimicrobial reaction pattern.

title: Respond to tendon pain during fluoroquinolone use
stem: A client taking ciprofloxacin reports new Achilles tendon pain without trauma. What should the nurse advise?
options: Continue ciprofloxacin, reduce tendon loading and discuss pain at routine follow-up.
Withhold ciprofloxacin, rest the tendon and contact the prescriber promptly.
Continue ciprofloxacin, use gentle calf stretches and report pain if swelling appears.
Withhold ciprofloxacin, rest for two days and restart the course if pain resolves.
why: Reducing activity does not remove the need to stop further exposure and obtain prompt review of new tendon pain.
New tendon pain requires stopping further exposure and avoiding tendon stress while the treatment plan is promptly reviewed.
Stretching loads a potentially injured tendon, and visible swelling is not required before action is needed.
Symptom improvement does not authorize restarting ciprofloxacin; the prescriber must review the antibiotic plan.
takeaway: Fluoroquinolones can cause tendon injury that needs treatment review.
learningObjective: Respond promptly to new tendon pain during fluoroquinolone treatment.

title: Address tetracycline chelation
stem: A client takes doxycycline together with calcium supplements and an antacid each morning. What instruction is most useful?
options: Separate the antacid but continue calcium with doxycycline
Take them together only when a full meal is eaten
Check the product-specific separation interval with the pharmacist
Take an extra doxycycline tablet with the supplements
why: Both mineral sources can affect absorption and require product-specific review.
A meal does not reliably remove this interaction.
Minerals can bind doxycycline and reduce its absorption.
Additional dosing is not a safe solution to impaired absorption.
takeaway: Minerals can bind doxycycline and reduce its absorption.
learningObjective: Address reduced tetracycline absorption from concurrent mineral-containing products.

title: Differentiate expected rifampin discoloration from danger
stem: A client taking rifampin reports orange urine but no pain, jaundice or systemic symptoms. What is the best response?
options: Stop the medicine until urine becomes clear
Assume orange urine confirms dehydration
Report it as confirmed urinary bleeding
Explain expected discoloration and review symptoms requiring reporting
why: An expected effect alone does not justify interrupting essential therapy.
The medication itself can account for the colour change.
Orange discoloration without assessment is not proof of hematuria.
Rifampin can discolour body fluids without indicating organ injury.
takeaway: Rifampin can discolour body fluids without indicating organ injury.
learningObjective: Distinguish expected rifampin fluid discoloration from warning symptoms of injury.

title: Report vision changes on ethambutol
stem: A client taking ethambutol says colours look different and reading is newly blurred. What is appropriate?
options: Promptly contact the treatment team before further dosing
Wait for the next routine eye appointment in several months
Recommend stronger reading glasses first
Reassure because the client has no eye pain
why: Ethambutol-associated optic toxicity needs timely assessment.
A new change requires earlier review to limit potential injury.
A prescription change should not precede evaluation of possible drug toxicity.
Optic toxicity can occur without pain.
takeaway: Ethambutol-associated optic toxicity needs timely assessment.
learningObjective: Report new vision and colour-perception changes during ethambutol therapy.

title: Evaluate neuropathic symptoms during isoniazid
stem: A client taking isoniazid reports new tingling in both feet and has not been taking prescribed pyridoxine. What is most appropriate?
options: Try wider footwear and reassess whether tingling improves over the coming week
Assess and report the tingling and missed pyridoxine
Restart pyridoxine and wait until the routine visit to mention symptoms
Provide foot-comfort advice and request an analgesic for the discomfort
why: A mechanical explanation should not postpone review of new bilateral tingling during isoniazid treatment with missed supplementation.
Possible isoniazid-related neuropathy and the supplementation plan require review.
Resuming supplementation does not remove the need to assess newly developed neuropathy.
Symptom management alone does not evaluate possible treatment-related neuropathy or address the missed pyridoxine plan.
takeaway: Possible isoniazid-related neuropathy and the supplementation plan require review.
learningObjective: Link new peripheral tingling and missed pyridoxine to isoniazid-treatment review.

title: Support a complex tuberculosis regimen
stem: A client finds the tuberculosis regimen difficult to manage and is considering taking only the tablet that causes least nausea. Which responses are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Explore adverse effects and arrange regimen support
Explain why the prescribed combination should not be self-selected
Recommend taking only one medicine until appetite returns
Suggest saving omitted tablets to add after treatment ends
Assume missed doses are resolved once symptoms improve
why: Addressing tolerability and practical barriers supports effective combination treatment.
Unplanned partial treatment can promote failure and resistance.
Selective therapy can undermine the intended regimen.
A delayed self-designed course is not an appropriate treatment plan.
Symptom improvement does not establish completion or cure.
takeaway: Addressing tolerability and practical barriers supports effective combination treatment.
learningObjective: Address tuberculosis treatment barriers without permitting self-selected partial regimens.

title: Explain oral vancomycin for intestinal infection
stem: A client prescribed oral vancomycin for C. difficile asks why an IV route is not automatically stronger. What is the best explanation?
options: IV treatment would be preferred if venous access were easier
The routes can be exchanged at the same dose when necessary
Oral treatment is reserved only for mild intestinal disease
Oral treatment reaches the intestinal infection site
why: Access convenience does not determine vancomycin delivery to the intestinal lumen.
Their distribution and therapeutic roles are not interchangeable.
Route choice for intestinal vancomycin is not simply a marker of mild illness.
The route is chosen for drug delivery to the target site rather than general IV superiority.
takeaway: The route is chosen for drug delivery to the target site rather than general IV superiority.
learningObjective: Explain why the intestinal treatment target determines oral vancomycin's role.

title: Administer oral nystatin for local effect
stem: A client prescribed nystatin oral suspension immediately swallows it without distributing it in the mouth. What teaching is most useful?
options: Follow the prescribed directions for contact with affected oral surfaces
Mix it into a full drink to eliminate the taste
Stop treatment as soon as the first patch disappears
Use it immediately before rinsing vigorously with water
why: Local contact is important when treating oral candidiasis.
Dilution and rapid swallowing may reduce useful oral contact.
Visible improvement does not automatically establish course completion.
Immediate rinsing may remove medicine from the treatment area.
takeaway: Local contact is important when treating oral candidiasis.
learningObjective: Teach oral nystatin contact with affected mucosal surfaces.

title: Review fluconazole with anticoagulation
stem: A client stable on warfarin is newly prescribed fluconazole. What should the nurse ensure?
options: Advise extra vitamin K foods to offset the new drug
Interaction review and an appropriate anticoagulation-monitoring plan
Continue usual monitoring because both doses are standard
Take warfarin and fluconazole at different times of day to prevent the interaction
why: Unplanned dietary compensation makes anticoagulation less predictable.
Fluconazole can increase warfarin effect and bleeding risk.
Standard doses do not exclude a clinically significant interaction.
Timing separation does not prevent the metabolic effect that can increase warfarin exposure.
takeaway: Fluconazole can increase warfarin effect and bleeding risk.
learningObjective: Plan interaction monitoring when fluconazole is added to warfarin.

title: Assess a QT-risk antibiotic combination
stem: A client prescribed azithromycin takes another QT-prolonging medicine and has potassium below the supplied reference range. What is appropriate?
options: Separate the two medicines by one hour
Check pulse regularity and proceed if the pulse remains regular
Clarify the regimen and electrolyte correction/monitoring plan
Give the antibiotic because there is no current chest pain
why: Timing separation does not reliably remove their electrophysiological interaction.
A regular palpable pulse does not measure QT interval or remove hypokalaemia-related dysrhythmia risk.
Combined QT risk and hypokalemia can increase dysrhythmia risk.
Dysrhythmia risk can exist without chest pain.
takeaway: Combined QT risk and hypokalemia can increase dysrhythmia risk.
learningObjective: Integrate electrolyte and medication risks before administering a QT-prolonging antibiotic.

title: Review clarithromycin with a statin
stem: A client taking simvastatin receives a new clarithromycin prescription. While urgently clarifying this interaction, which additional symptom assessment is particularly relevant?
options: Persistent dry cough with throat irritation
Ringing in the ears with loss of balance
Constipation with dry mouth and urinary hesitancy
New muscle pain, weakness or dark urine
why: That pattern is more characteristic of another drug class than this interaction.
This is an important adverse-effect pattern but not the principal simvastatin interaction concern.
These suggest anticholinergic effects rather than the primary muscle-toxicity risk.
Clarithromycin can increase simvastatin exposure and the risk of serious muscle injury.
takeaway: Clarithromycin can increase simvastatin exposure and the risk of serious muscle injury.
learningObjective: Recognize muscle-injury symptoms as the key toxicity concern with clarithromycin and simvastatin.

title: Identify a potassium-raising antibiotic interaction
stem: A client taking ramipril develops new weakness after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Potassium rises from 4.4 to 5.8 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0), while creatinine is unchanged and the radial pulse is regular. What should the nurse do next?
options: Promptly report the potassium trend, weakness and medicines for rhythm and treatment review
Arrange a repeat potassium at tomorrow’s routine blood draw because creatinine is unchanged
Continue the current regimen while checking for an irregular pulse at routine observations
Separate ramipril and the antibiotic between morning and evening doses
why: The drug combination can raise potassium; a new elevation with weakness needs prompt clinical review despite a currently regular pulse.
Stable creatinine does not exclude a medication-related potassium rise or justify postponing assessment of new symptoms.
A regular palpable pulse does not exclude an important potassium disturbance or establish the regimen is safe to continue.
Dose spacing does not remove the potassium-retaining effects of trimethoprim and ACE inhibition.
takeaway: Assess a new symptomatic potassium rise during interacting therapy even when creatinine and pulse appear stable.
learningObjective: Integrate potassium trend, new symptoms and interacting therapy to select prompt treatment review.

title: Clarify antibiotic delivery with continuous feeds
stem: A client receives continuous enteral nutrition and a new antibiotic through the tube. Pharmacy identifies an interaction with the feed's minerals. What is appropriate?
options: Increase the antibiotic amount to compensate for reduced absorption
Obtain a product-specific timing or alternative-route plan
Apply the same two-hour feed hold used for another antibiotic
Mix the antibiotic directly into the feed to dilute minerals
why: Unprescribed dose compensation is unreliable and potentially unsafe.
The interaction and nutrition requirements need coordinated management.
The appropriate interval depends on this product, the interaction and nutrition requirements; a schedule for another antibiotic is not interchangeable.
Mixing may worsen binding and make dosing incomplete.
takeaway: The interaction and nutrition requirements need coordinated management.
learningObjective: Coordinate antibiotic administration with a mineral-containing continuous enteral feed.

title: Reassess presumed lower urinary infection
stem: A client treated with nitrofurantoin for cystitis develops fever, flank pain and vomiting. What should the nurse do?
options: Continue the lower-UTI plan if an antiemetic relieves vomiting
Arrange repeat urine testing at the next routine visit to compare with the initial sample
Promptly assess possible upper infection and review the regimen
Request a urinary analgesic to address the new flank discomfort
why: Reduced vomiting would not remove the significance of fever and flank pain.
Routine delayed sampling is insufficient for newly systemic and flank symptoms that may indicate upper-tract infection.
Fever, flank pain and vomiting suggest progression beyond bladder-focused treatment.
Pain relief alone does not assess a possible upper urinary infection.
takeaway: Fever, flank pain and vomiting suggest progression beyond bladder-focused treatment.
learningObjective: Reassess presumed cystitis when systemic and flank symptoms develop during therapy.

title: Plan antibiotic use after discharge
stem: A client leaves hospital with an antibiotic course and asks what to do if symptoms settle or adverse effects develop. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Keep remaining doses for a similar illness months later
Share unused doses with someone who has the same symptoms
Restart the entire course independently after a missed dose
Take the medicine for the prescribed course unless the team changes the plan
Report severe adverse effects promptly for treatment advice
why: Future symptoms may have a different cause requiring reassessment.
Similar symptoms do not establish the same infection or prescription.
Missed-dose management does not usually mean an unreviewed new course.
Duration should follow the individualized treatment plan rather than symptom-based guessing.
Serious reactions may require urgent review and an altered regimen.
takeaway: Duration should follow the individualized treatment plan rather than symptom-based guessing.
learningObjective: Teach prescribed antibiotic duration, missed-dose guidance and adverse-effect escalation.

title: Assess home IV antibiotic readiness
stem: A client will manage home IV antibiotic therapy with nursing support. Which demonstrations support safe discharge planning? Select all that apply.
options: The client explains how to report fever, rash or line problems
The client follows the taught aseptic connection procedure
The client plans to change infusion speed whenever running late
The client recognizes the bag by colour but cannot confirm its label
The client expects the pump alarm to identify every site complication
why: Recognizing complications supports timely contact and reassessment.
Observed technique helps establish practical ability to handle the system.
Unprescribed rate changes can cause adverse effects or delivery problems.
Appearance alone does not verify drug, dose or intended client.
Infiltration or inflammation may occur without a reliable pump alarm.
takeaway: Recognizing complications supports timely contact and reassessment.
learningObjective: Evaluate practical readiness for supported home intravenous antibiotic therapy.

title: Assess lithium during volume loss
stem: A client taking lithium has gastroenteritis, coarse tremor and unsteady walking. The usual evening dose is due. What is most appropriate?
options: Use last month's normal lithium result to guide tonight's dose
Withhold pending prompt toxicity and hydration assessment
Give the dose after an oral rehydration drink
Treat the tremor with the usual anxiety PRN medicine
why: An old result does not reflect the current illness and clearance changes.
Fluid loss can reduce lithium clearance, and the new neurological signs suggest toxicity.
One drink does not resolve possible accumulated lithium or neurological toxicity.
Symptom suppression can obscure assessment without addressing lithium exposure.
takeaway: Fluid loss can reduce lithium clearance, and the new neurological signs suggest toxicity.
learningObjective: Integrate gastrointestinal losses, neurological changes and renal clearance when assessing possible lithium toxicity.

title: Plan stable intake with lithium
stem: A client stable on lithium plans a low-sodium weight-loss diet and strenuous outdoor exercise. What is the most relevant teaching?
options: Replace sweat losses with the usual sports drink during exercise.
Track body weight each morning while starting the new routine.
Coordinate sodium and hydration changes with the prescriber.
Reduce sodium gradually while recording the amount eaten.
why: A sports drink does not by itself establish an appropriate sodium and fluid plan for lithium therapy.
Weight trends may help monitor balance but do not address the proposed sodium change or establish lithium safety.
Sweating and reduced sodium intake can alter lithium handling; the plan should preserve appropriate consistency and monitoring.
A gradual change can still change lithium concentrations; the medication plan needs coordinated review.
takeaway: Sweating and reduced sodium intake can alter lithium handling; the plan should preserve appropriate consistency and monitoring.
learningObjective: Explain why major sodium and fluid changes warrant review during lithium therapy.

title: Review a new lithium interaction
stem: A client taking lithium has a stable level from last month and a new hydrochlorothiazide prescription for hypertension. Kidney function was last checked with that level. Which follow-up plan best addresses the new medicine?
options: Separate the lithium and hydrochlorothiazide administration times.
Check for tremor at the next routine mental-health appointment.
Arrange repeat thyroid testing after the new prescription begins.
Arrange an interaction review with lithium-level and renal monitoring.
why: Dose spacing does not remove the renal interaction that can raise lithium concentrations.
Symptom review matters, but a planned monitoring response is needed before overt toxicity develops.
Lithium can affect thyroid function, but thyroid tests do not assess the new risk to lithium clearance.
Thiazides can reduce lithium clearance; a recent stable level does not predict the level after this addition.
takeaway: Thiazides can reduce lithium clearance; a recent stable level does not predict the level after this addition.
learningObjective: Identify a need for lithium monitoring when a thiazide is added.

title: Assess early antidepressant activation
stem: One week after starting an antidepressant, a client reports marked restlessness and new thoughts of self-harm. What is the priority?
options: Assess immediate safety and arrange urgent clinical review.
Explain the usual delay before full antidepressant benefit.
Recommend taking the medicine earlier in the day.
Compare appetite and sleep with the pretreatment baseline.
why: New self-harm thoughts and marked activation require prompt risk assessment and support.
That explanation may be helpful later but does not address the newly expressed safety risk.
Timing may help selected sleep effects but does not adequately address new thoughts of self-harm.
Those outcomes are relevant to efficacy, but immediate safety takes priority in this presentation.
takeaway: New self-harm thoughts and marked activation require prompt risk assessment and support.
learningObjective: Assess new agitation and self-harm risk soon after antidepressant initiation.

title: Identify serotonin toxicity
stem: A client taking sertraline consistently starts prescribed tramadol. Within a day they develop agitation, sweating, diarrhea, tremor and inducible ankle clonus. Which concern should the nurse communicate urgently?
options: Possible anxiety-related medication activation.
Possible serotonin toxicity.
Possible antidepressant discontinuation symptoms.
Possible gastroenteritis with dehydration.
why: Activation may cause restlessness, but the broader autonomic and neuromuscular pattern is more concerning for a toxic syndrome.
The added serotonergic medicine plus autonomic and neuromuscular findings, particularly clonus, supports urgent assessment for toxicity.
The client reports consistent sertraline use, and the new exposure and clonus fit toxicity better than withdrawal.
Diarrhea can occur with infection, but gastroenteritis does not adequately explain the drug timing and clonus.
takeaway: The added serotonergic medicine plus autonomic and neuromuscular findings, particularly clonus, supports urgent assessment for toxicity.
learningObjective: Recognize a concerning autonomic and neuromuscular pattern after serotonergic medicines are combined.

title: Recognize antipsychotic-related hyperthermia
stem: After an antipsychotic increase, a client develops high fever, generalized rigidity, confusion and unstable blood pressure. What concern requires immediate escalation?
options: Possible akathisia.
Possible infection-related delirium.
Possible neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Possible acute dystonia.
why: Akathisia causes inner restlessness and movement but does not explain severe generalized rigidity and high fever.
Infection remains a differential, but the recent dose increase and pronounced rigidity specifically raise concern for a medication emergency.
Fever, generalized rigidity, mental-status change and unstable blood pressure after antipsychotic escalation require emergency assessment for this syndrome.
Dystonia commonly causes focal sustained contractions; it does not adequately explain this systemic hyperthermic and autonomic pattern.
takeaway: Fever, generalized rigidity, mental-status change and unstable blood pressure after antipsychotic escalation require emergency assessment for this syndrome.
learningObjective: Differentiate a severe rigidity and hyperthermia syndrome from routine agitation after antipsychotic treatment.

title: Recognize acute dystonia
stem: Thirty minutes after receiving metoclopramide, a client develops painful neck twisting and difficulty opening the jaw. Breathing is currently unlaboured. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Request a physiotherapy review for neck stretching.
Report the movements as possible tardive dyskinesia.
Use the next prescribed metoclopramide dose for residual nausea.
Obtain urgent assessment and treatment for possible acute dystonia.
why: A new medication-related contraction requires acute treatment rather than a routine musculoskeletal plan.
The acute painful sustained contraction soon after exposure fits dystonia better than a chronic repetitive movement disorder.
Additional dopamine blockade may worsen the reaction; the medication plan needs urgent review.
The abrupt sustained contraction after dopamine blockade can extend to airway-related structures and needs prompt treatment.
takeaway: The abrupt sustained contraction after dopamine blockade can extend to airway-related structures and needs prompt treatment.
learningObjective: Respond to acute involuntary neck and jaw contraction after dopamine-blocking medication.

title: Distinguish akathisia from worsening psychosis
stem: After an antipsychotic dose increase, a client paces and says, “I cannot keep still inside.” Hallucinations have decreased, and the client asks for help to join activities. Which interpretation best fits?
options: Medication-related akathisia.
Worsening psychosis.
Anxiety about the environment.
Medication-related parkinsonism.
why: New distressing inner restlessness after dose escalation, despite improved psychotic symptoms, suggests akathisia.
Improved hallucinations and the dose-related onset of inner restlessness make a movement adverse effect more likely.
Environmental anxiety is possible, but the specific inner motor restlessness and medication timing favour akathisia.
Parkinsonism usually produces slowness, rigidity or tremor rather than a new distressing inner urge to keep moving after dose escalation.
takeaway: New distressing inner restlessness after dose escalation, despite improved psychotic symptoms, suggests akathisia.
learningObjective: Recognize medication-related inner restlessness before assuming a need for more antipsychotic.

title: Evaluate new repetitive movements
stem: A client who wears dentures and has taken an antipsychotic for years develops repetitive lip smacking and tongue movements. The dentures remain comfortable. What should the nurse do?
options: Track food intake to determine whether the movements need referral.
Document the movements and arrange timely medication review.
Arrange a routine dental review for denture adjustment.
Request an increase in the current antipsychotic dose.
why: Functional monitoring is useful, but reporting should not depend on eating becoming impaired.
The repetitive orofacial pattern after prolonged exposure may be tardive dyskinesia and warrants treatment reassessment.
An oral assessment may help exclude mechanical causes, but comfortable dentures do not explain away this medication-associated pattern.
Increasing exposure can temporarily obscure movements without addressing a potentially persistent adverse effect.
takeaway: The repetitive orofacial pattern after prolonged exposure may be tardive dyskinesia and warrants treatment reassessment.
learningObjective: Recognize possible tardive dyskinesia during prolonged antipsychotic exposure.

title: Respond to infection symptoms during clozapine therapy
stem: A client taking clozapine develops fever and a sore throat. Their last blood count was acceptable two weeks ago. What is appropriate?
options: Use the previous count to keep the next scheduled test date.
Give the prescribed antipyretic and reassess the fever response.
Arrange prompt clinical review and a current blood count.
Arrange a throat swab and routine follow-up.
why: Blood counts can change between scheduled tests, so new infection symptoms change the urgency.
Lowering the temperature does not exclude neutropenia or treat the underlying infection risk.
New fever and sore throat during clozapine use may indicate neutropenia even after an acceptable recent count.
A swab may be part of the assessment but does not promptly establish whether severe neutropenia is present.
takeaway: New fever and sore throat during clozapine use may indicate neutropenia even after an acceptable recent count.
learningObjective: Promptly assess possible neutropenia when infection symptoms develop during clozapine use.

title: Recognize severe clozapine-related constipation
stem: A client taking clozapine has no bowel movement for several days, increasing abdominal distension and vomiting. What should happen?
options: Offer the prescribed fibre supplement.
Encourage an oral fluid trial.
Arrange the next routine bowel-regimen review.
Obtain urgent abdominal assessment.
why: Routine fibre is not appropriate as the initial response when vomiting and distension suggest possible obstruction.
Fluids may help uncomplicated constipation but do not resolve the need to assess this more serious pattern.
The associated vomiting and progressive distension require a more urgent response than routine regimen adjustment.
Vomiting and distension with constipation during clozapine use raise concern for severe hypomotility, ileus or obstruction.
takeaway: Vomiting and distension with constipation during clozapine use raise concern for severe hypomotility, ileus or obstruction.
learningObjective: Escalate possible gastrointestinal hypomotility when constipation is accompanied by systemic abdominal symptoms.

title: Coordinate levodopa with meal effects
stem: A client taking levodopa reports worse mobility after large protein-rich meals but needs adequate nutrition. What is most useful?
options: Review dose timing and dietary protein distribution with the team.
Take each levodopa dose with a protein-rich snack.
Add a levodopa dose after a large meal.
Adjust activities to accommodate expected disease progression.
why: A coordinated plan can address meal-related response while preserving nutrition and the authorized regimen.
Protein can interfere with the response in some clients; adding it to every dose could worsen this reproducible pattern.
An unprescribed extra dose may cause adverse effects and does not establish a consistent long-term plan.
Progression should be considered, but the clear meal association suggests a modifiable treatment issue needing review.
takeaway: A coordinated plan can address meal-related response while preserving nutrition and the authorized regimen.
learningObjective: Address a reproducible meal-related levodopa response without unnecessary protein restriction.

title: Assess wearing-off symptoms
stem: A client moves well after levodopa but develops predictable stiffness shortly before each next dose. What information is most useful to record?
options: A daily stiffness score taken before the first morning dose
Dose times and the onset and duration of symptom changes
The total number of tablets taken during each week
The client’s best walking distance after the morning dose
why: One standardized morning score misses how symptoms recur across later dose intervals.
A timing diary helps identify wearing-off and guide regimen review.
A weekly adherence total does not show the relationship between individual dose times and symptom recurrence.
Peak postdose performance does not capture the timing and duration of end-of-dose stiffness.
takeaway: A timing diary helps identify wearing-off and guide regimen review.
learningObjective: Use the timing of symptom recurrence to support Parkinson medication review.

title: Teach phenytoin oral care
stem: A client starting long-term phenytoin asks about gum changes mentioned in teaching. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Use mouthwash alone instead of mechanical cleaning
Stop phenytoin independently if gums bleed during brushing
Regular gentle oral care and dental follow-up
Avoid brushing areas that begin to enlarge
why: Rinsing alone does not adequately remove plaque.
Seizure treatment changes require review rather than abrupt withdrawal.
Good hygiene and dental assessment help manage gingival overgrowth risk.
Avoidance can worsen plaque accumulation and inflammation.
takeaway: Good hygiene and dental assessment help manage gingival overgrowth risk.
learningObjective: Support prevention and early recognition of gingival complications during phenytoin therapy.

title: Assess possible benzodiazepine withdrawal
stem: A client who took a benzodiazepine regularly for months has missed it for several days and now has tremor, insomnia and marked anxiety. What is appropriate?
options: Schedule a routine anxiety-management review.
Recommend a structured sleep-hygiene routine.
Attribute the symptoms to recurrence of the original anxiety.
Obtain urgent withdrawal assessment and a medication plan.
why: The interruption history raises an acute withdrawal concern beyond routine management of baseline anxiety.
Sleep measures do not treat potentially dangerous physiological withdrawal.
The temporal link to missed doses requires consideration of withdrawal rather than assuming the original disorder has returned.
Abrupt interruption after months of regular use can cause significant withdrawal, including seizures.
takeaway: Abrupt interruption after months of regular use can cause significant withdrawal, including seizures.
learningObjective: Connect abrupt interruption of regular benzodiazepine use with withdrawal symptoms and seizure risk.

title: Monitor after naloxone response
stem: A client received naloxone for respiratory depression after an unintended extra dose of extended-release morphine. They are now awake with a respiratory rate of 16/minute. Which follow-up plan is most appropriate?
options: Continue protocol-based monitoring of ventilation and alertness.
Focus reassessment on the return of the original pain.
Prepare discharge after documenting the present normal findings.
Focus observation on nausea and withdrawal symptoms.
why: Extended-release opioid effects can recur after naloxone wears off, so one normal assessment does not establish sustained recovery.
Pain may recur after reversal, but pain scores do not reliably detect recurrent respiratory depression.
A single improved assessment is inadequate after this longer-acting exposure because respiratory depression may return.
These can occur after naloxone, but monitoring must prioritize sustained ventilation and consciousness.
takeaway: Extended-release opioid effects can recur after naloxone wears off, so one normal assessment does not establish sustained recovery.
learningObjective: Explain why improved ventilation after naloxone does not end monitoring requirements.

title: Prevent heat-related fentanyl exposure
stem: A client wearing a fentanyl patch plans to use a heating pad over the painful shoulder where the patch is placed. What should the nurse advise?
options: Remove the patch during heating sessions and reapply it afterward.
Avoid direct heat over the patch and discuss another comfort measure.
Cover the patch with another dressing during heat application.
Lower the pad temperature and inspect the skin regularly.
why: Intermittent removal and reapplication is not an authorized solution and disrupts prescribed patch use.
Heat can increase fentanyl absorption and overdose risk even when the skin does not look injured.
An added covering does not establish protection from heat-related increased absorption.
A lower setting and normal skin appearance do not reliably establish safe drug delivery.
takeaway: Heat can increase fentanyl absorption and overdose risk even when the skin does not look injured.
learningObjective: Recognize external heat as a factor that can increase transdermal fentanyl absorption.

title: Explain patient-only PCA activation
stem: A visitor presses a sleeping client's PCA button to prevent pain on waking. What is the best response?
options: Permit presses only near the end of the lockout interval
Ask the visitor to use the client's pain history to decide
Explain that only the client should activate this PCA button
Permit it if the visitor records each button press
why: Lockout timing does not make proxy dosing safe.
Predicted pain cannot replace current patient-controlled use and assessment.
The client's inability to self-activate while deeply sedated is a safety feature.
Documentation does not preserve the patient-controlled safety mechanism.
takeaway: The client's inability to self-activate while deeply sedated is a safety feature.
learningObjective: Preserve the patient-controlled analgesia safety mechanism by preventing family activation.

title: Plan for opioid-induced constipation
stem: A client starting regular opioid therapy has a history of constipation and a prescribed fluid restriction for heart failure. What should the nurse prioritize in the ongoing plan?
options: Begin a bowel regimen after the first missed bowel movement.
Increase dietary fibre as the main preventive measure.
Expect bowel effects to fade as opioid tolerance develops.
Review preventive bowel treatment and monitor bowel function.
why: Waiting for a change is less useful than planning prevention in a client with existing constipation risk.
Fibre requires an appropriate fluid and bowel plan and may be insufficient during opioid therapy with fluid restriction.
Tolerance to other opioid effects does not reliably eliminate constipation.
Constipation may persist during opioid use; a tailored preventive plan is useful, particularly when fluids cannot be freely increased.
takeaway: Constipation may persist during opioid use; a tailored preventive plan is useful, particularly when fluids cannot be freely increased.
learningObjective: Anticipate bowel effects when regular opioid treatment begins.

title: Detect duplicate acetaminophen products
stem: A client takes scheduled acetaminophen for arthritis and buys an acetaminophen-containing cold remedy for a new cough. Both labels provide adult dosing instructions. What should the nurse help the client do?
options: Review the combined daily amount and choose a suitable product plan.
Separate the two products by at least one hour.
Use the usual adult dose printed on each product label.
Track the cold-remedy dose separately from arthritis treatment.
why: Both products contribute to the same cumulative ingredient exposure, so their combined schedule must be reviewed.
Spacing doses does not remove the possibility of excessive total daily acetaminophen.
Each label cannot account for the client taking another product with the same ingredient.
Separate records do not replace adding the shared ingredient across both products.
takeaway: Both products contribute to the same cumulative ingredient exposure, so their combined schedule must be reviewed.
learningObjective: Identify overlapping active ingredients across prescription and nonprescription analgesic products.

title: Assess NSAID use during dehydration
stem: A client taking naproxen develops vomiting, low intake and markedly reduced urine output. What is appropriate?
options: Review urine colour for visible bleeding.
Assess hydration and renal function and review the naproxen plan.
Give the naproxen with food.
Ask about burning with urination.
why: Renal hypoperfusion or injury can occur without visible hematuria, so urine colour does not resolve the concern.
Vomiting and oliguria suggest volume depletion; NSAID effects on renal perfusion make continued therapy a concern.
Food can reduce gastrointestinal irritation but does not correct reduced renal perfusion.
Urinary infection symptoms may be relevant, but their absence would not exclude dehydration-related kidney injury.
takeaway: Vomiting and oliguria suggest volume depletion; NSAID effects on renal perfusion make continued therapy a concern.
learningObjective: Review renal risk before continuing an NSAID during acute volume depletion.

title: Clarify methotrexate frequency
stem: A client takes oral methotrexate once weekly for rheumatoid arthritis. New transfer orders list the same dose daily. What should happen before administration?
options: Assume the daily order replaces the home schedule
Divide the weekly dose into daily portions independently
Clarify the frequency discrepancy with the prescribing team
Give today's dose and clarify before tomorrow
why: A transfer discrepancy involving high-risk frequency needs verification.
An improvised schedule is not an authorized regimen.
Inadvertent daily low-dose methotrexate can cause severe toxicity.
The intended weekly day and last administration must be established first.
takeaway: Inadvertent daily low-dose methotrexate can cause severe toxicity.
learningObjective: Detect a dangerous daily-versus-weekly discrepancy in low-dose methotrexate treatment.

title: Distinguish urate control from acute analgesia
stem: A client newly prescribed allopurinol expects immediate relief of a painful gout flare. What is the best explanation?
options: It reduces the current joint inflammation as soon as the dose is absorbed.
It is taken when pain appears and stopped when the joint settles.
It prevents pain during each dose interval but does not change urate stores.
It lowers urate over time; the flare needs its separate treatment plan.
why: The medicine is not an acute analgesic or anti-inflammatory treatment for the existing flare.
Allopurinol is generally ongoing urate-lowering treatment according to the prescription, not an as-needed pain medicine.
The long-term reduction of urate burden is its therapeutic purpose, rather than short-lived pain masking.
Allopurinol is used for long-term urate control rather than immediate anti-inflammatory relief.
takeaway: Allopurinol is used for long-term urate control rather than immediate anti-inflammatory relief.
learningObjective: Explain the different purposes of long-term urate lowering and prescribed acute-flare treatment.

title: Review an opioid conversion
stem: A client's opioid order changes from morphine to hydromorphone, with the same route and dosing interval. A colleague suggests retaining the same milligram dose. What should the nurse do?
options: Verify the prescribed conversion and client-specific dose with the team.
Use the old milligram dose because the route is unchanged.
Assess how well the previous opioid controlled pain.
Use the dose listed in a published equianalgesic table.
why: Potency, previous exposure, incomplete cross-tolerance and individual risk must be considered before the new opioid is administered.
The same route does not make morphine and hydromorphone equivalent milligram for milligram.
That information supports review but cannot by itself establish a safe dose of a different-potency opioid.
A table supplies an estimate, not a complete client-specific order; cross-tolerance and risk can require adjustment.
takeaway: Potency, previous exposure, incomplete cross-tolerance and individual risk must be considered before the new opioid is administered.
learningObjective: Recognize that different opioids are not interchangeable milligram for milligram.

title: Evaluate analgesia with function and safety
stem: After an analgesic adjustment, which findings support an effective and tolerable plan? Select all that apply.
options: The client can cough and mobilize more comfortably
The client stays readily alert with stable breathing
The pain score is lower but the client is difficult to arouse
The client sleeps through all activities because of new drowsiness
The client avoids every movement despite an unchanged resting score
why: Improved useful function supports meaningful pain relief.
Analgesia should not require clinically important respiratory or sedation harm.
Reduced reported pain does not compensate for dangerous sedation.
Sedation-related inactivity is not the intended functional outcome.
A resting score alone misses inadequately controlled movement-related pain.
takeaway: Improved useful function supports meaningful pain relief.
learningObjective: Balance pain relief, function and adverse effects when evaluating an analgesic regimen.

title: Reduce inhaled-steroid oral effects
stem: A client starts an inhaled corticosteroid and asks how to reduce mouth irritation and thrush risk. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Reduce the prescribed frequency when the mouth feels irritated.
Attach a spacer to a dry-powder inhaler.
Rinse the mouth and spit after each prescribed dose.
Use a compatible spacer if prescribed for the device.
Rinse the mouth immediately before taking the dose.
why: Changing controller dosing may worsen asthma control; irritation requires a technique and treatment review.
Spacer use is device-specific and is not a solution for a dry-powder mechanism.
Removing oral residue limits local steroid exposure and helps reduce thrush risk.
A spacer can reduce oropharyngeal deposition with a suitable metered-dose inhaler.
A predose rinse does not remove steroid deposited during the subsequent inhalation.
takeaway: Removing oral residue limits local steroid exposure and helps reduce thrush risk.
learningObjective: Teach local adverse-effect prevention while preserving prescribed controller treatment.

title: Clarify an asthma controller gap
stem: A client's asthma list contains a long-acting beta agonist alone. No inhaled corticosteroid or combination controller is documented. What is appropriate?
options: Check recent pharmacy dispensing dates.
Review how often the reliever is used.
Arrange the next spirometry appointment.
Clarify the prescribed anti-inflammatory regimen.
why: Dispensing history may help reconciliation, but the key clinical issue is whether an anti-inflammatory component is actually prescribed.
Reliever frequency helps assess control but does not resolve the apparent controller omission.
Lung-function testing may help ongoing care, but it does not correct a potentially unsafe medication list.
The apparent LABA-only asthma regimen raises a safety gap that requires confirmation and an appropriate controller plan.
takeaway: The apparent LABA-only asthma regimen raises a safety gap that requires confirmation and an appropriate controller plan.
learningObjective: Recognize that an asthma LABA regimen needs an appropriate inhaled anti-inflammatory plan.

title: Prevent nebulized anticholinergic eye exposure
stem: A client receiving nebulized ipratropium reports mist blowing into the eyes from a loose mask. What is the most useful correction?
options: Adjust the interface to prevent eye exposure
Ask the client to keep the eyes closed throughout every treatment
Increase nebulizer flow to finish sooner
Apply lubricating drops while maintaining the same mask fit
why: Proper fit limits local anticholinergic exposure that can cause eye problems.
Eye closure alone does not correct the leaking interface.
Faster delivery does not resolve misdirected medication.
Lubrication does not eliminate the medication exposure.
takeaway: Proper fit limits local anticholinergic exposure that can cause eye problems.
learningObjective: Correct mask leakage that directs nebulized ipratropium toward the eyes.

title: Assess possible theophylline toxicity
stem: A client taking theophylline develops repeated nausea, tremor and a rapid irregular pulse after starting a new antibiotic. Which issue should the nurse raise most urgently with the treatment team?
options: Whether a prescribed antiemetic would improve oral intake.
Possible increased theophylline exposure from an interaction.
Whether taking theophylline with food would reduce nausea.
Whether the client has experienced similar palpitations before.
why: Symptom treatment does not resolve potentially excessive exposure associated with the irregular pulse and tremor.
This narrow-therapeutic-margin medicine can cause gastrointestinal, neurological and rhythm toxicity; the new drug and symptom cluster require prompt review.
Food may alter comfort but does not address the concurrent neurological and cardiac warning signs.
Prior symptoms are useful history, but they do not remove the current toxicity concern after a medication change.
takeaway: This narrow-therapeutic-margin medicine can cause gastrointestinal, neurological and rhythm toxicity; the new drug and symptom cluster require prompt review.
learningObjective: Recognize nausea with cardiac and neurological stimulation during theophylline exposure.

title: Interpret increasing reliever use
stem: A client is comfortable today but reports using the prescribed reliever much more often over the last week. What is the best next step?
options: Reassess the current breath sounds.
Recommend returning to the previous reliever schedule.
Review recent control, inhaler technique and the action plan.
Arrange a larger refill supply.
why: Today's findings are useful but cannot establish control across the reported week.
Restricting use to an earlier pattern does not treat the cause of increased symptoms or update the action plan.
Increased reliever use over a week can signal loss of control even when the client is comfortable at assessment.
Adequate supply matters, but it does not determine why use increased.
takeaway: Increased reliever use over a week can signal loss of control even when the client is comfortable at assessment.
learningObjective: Use an increasing reliever pattern as a cue to reassess asthma control and technique.

title: Protect dry-powder inhaler delivery
stem: During return demonstration with a dry-powder inhaler, which actions support delivery when consistent with that device's instructions? Select all that apply.
options: Rinse the powder chamber immediately before a dose.
Use a slow gentle inhalation as with a metered-dose inhaler.
Exhale away from the loaded device before inhaling.
Use the sufficiently forceful inhalation instructed for that device.
Attach a spacer to the powder mouthpiece.
why: Moisture can impair powder function; use the device's cleaning instructions.
A slow inhalation technique suitable for some aerosol devices may not provide the inspiratory effort needed for dry-powder delivery.
Exhaled moisture can affect the powder when blown into the device.
Dry-powder delivery depends on the user's inspiratory effort and the specific device mechanism.
Spacers are generally intended for suitable metered-dose devices, not this powder-delivery mechanism.
takeaway: Exhaled moisture can affect the powder when blown into the device.
learningObjective: Recognize technique errors that introduce moisture or impair a dry-powder inhalation.

title: Report neuropsychiatric changes during montelukast
stem: Two weeks after a child starts montelukast, which new changes need prompt medication-safety review? Select all that apply.
options: Agitation, depressed mood and statements about self-harm.
A mild headache that resolves after the usual fluids and rest.
Brief stomach discomfort after a dose, with normal eating afterward.
A mildly runny nose, with normal breathing and usual activity.
Distressing nightmares that repeatedly interrupt sleep.
why: New self-harm statements require immediate safety assessment and urgent help, alongside medication review; do not wait for a routine appointment.
A brief mild headache that resolves is not the same urgency as the significant new behavioural or sleep changes, though persistence or worsening should be reported.
Transient mild discomfort with preserved intake can be monitored and discussed in routine follow-up; severe or persistent symptoms require reassessment.
Mild isolated nasal symptoms with normal breathing and activity do not carry the same urgent warning as the new behavioural changes.
Marked new nightmares and sleep disruption are reported neuropsychiatric effects that warrant prompt communication and medication review.
takeaway: Significant new sleep disturbance is a reported neuropsychiatric effect that should be communicated promptly.
learningObjective: Include behavioural and mood warnings in teaching about montelukast.

title: Review an oral decongestant in hypertension
stem: A client whose recent home blood pressures average 172/98 mmHg asks whether oral pseudoephedrine is suitable for congestion. What should the nurse recommend about the requested medicine?
options: Take it at bedtime, separated from the blood-pressure medicine.
Review its cardiovascular suitability with the pharmacist or prescriber.
Try half the usual package dose for the first day.
Choose a longer-acting formulation to reduce the number of doses.
why: Timing separation does not reliably prevent the blood-pressure effect or establish suitability.
Systemic sympathomimetic effects can raise pressure or cause palpitations; uncontrolled readings make individual review important.
A self-directed lower dose does not establish safety with poorly controlled blood pressure.
Longer duration does not remove the systemic sympathomimetic effect.
takeaway: Systemic sympathomimetic effects can raise pressure or cause palpitations; uncontrolled readings make individual review important.
learningObjective: Assess sympathomimetic decongestant suitability in a client with uncontrolled blood pressure.

title: Recognize a first-generation antihistamine burden
stem: An older adult starts a first-generation sedating antihistamine. Which new findings fit its sedative or anticholinergic effects? Select all that apply.
options: Profuse watery diarrhea with increased bowel sounds.
Increasing sweating with excessive salivation.
New dependent ankle swelling with orthopnea.
Sleepiness and unsteadiness when walking.
Dry mouth, constipation and difficulty voiding.
why: This does not fit the expected anticholinergic bowel-slowing pattern and needs consideration of another cause.
Anticholinergic effects more often reduce secretions rather than increase them.
This pattern raises a different cardiopulmonary or fluid concern rather than the typical sedative-anticholinergic burden.
Central sedation can impair balance and increase fall risk.
These findings are consistent with reduced cholinergic activity.
takeaway: Central sedation can impair balance and increase fall risk.
learningObjective: Identify anticholinergic and sedative effects relevant to an older adult's medication review.

title: Evaluate prescribed lactulose treatment
stem: A client receives lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy. Which findings indicate a favourable response with acceptable tolerance? Select all that apply.
options: Mental status improves toward baseline.
Stool frequency meets the ordered target with stable hydration.
Profuse diarrhea develops with postural dizziness.
Cognition remains unchanged as the dose increases.
Appetite decreases during the treatment period.
why: Improved cognition supports a clinically meaningful response in encephalopathy.
The prescribed bowel effect is being achieved without signs of harmful fluid loss.
Excessive diarrhea and dizziness suggest fluid depletion, so this is not acceptable tolerance.
An absent clinical response warrants reassessment rather than being counted as a favourable outcome.
Reduced appetite does not demonstrate improved encephalopathy and may undermine nutrition.
takeaway: Improved cognition supports a clinically meaningful response in encephalopathy.
learningObjective: Balance encephalopathy improvement with bowel and hydration effects of lactulose.

title: Review bulk-forming fibre with swallowing limitations
stem: A client with significant dysphagia is prescribed a bulk-forming fibre product whose instructions require 240 mL of fluid with each dose. The swallowing plan does not permit that volume or consistency. What is appropriate?
options: Ask pharmacy and the prescriber to review a suitable bowel preparation.
Mix the prescribed powder into 30 mL to reduce swallowing effort.
Administer the usual dose mixed into a thickened preparation.
Divide the dose into several dry portions followed by sips.
why: The product's fluid requirement and swallowing limits must both be addressed before administration.
Concentrating the product does not satisfy its fluid requirement and can increase choking or obstruction risk.
Thickening alone may not meet the formulation's required fluid volume; pharmacy and swallowing-plan review are still needed.
Dividing dry material does not establish a safe preparation or resolve the overall fluid requirement.
takeaway: The product's fluid requirement and swallowing limits must both be addressed before administration.
learningObjective: Assess whether a bulk-forming preparation is suitable when safe fluid intake is restricted.

title: Match pancreatic enzymes to food intake
stem: A client with pancreatic insufficiency is learning to use prescribed enzymes. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Report continuing greasy stools or weight loss
Take the entire daily amount on waking before food
Chew enteric-coated enzyme beads for faster action
Skip enzymes when the meal contains protein but little fat
Coordinate doses with meals and snacks as prescribed
why: Persistent malabsorption can indicate a need to review the regimen.
A single fasting dose does not accompany later meals.
Chewing can damage the protective coating and irritate oral tissue.
The individualized enzyme prescription may support digestion of more than fat alone.
Enzymes need to accompany food to support digestion.
takeaway: Enzymes need to accompany food to support digestion.
learningObjective: Teach meal-associated pancreatic enzyme use for prescribed malabsorption treatment.

title: Administer liquid iron while limiting staining
stem: A school-age child who safely uses a drinking straw has tooth staining from liquid iron. Pharmacy confirms that each accurately measured dose may be mixed into a small amount of juice. Which instruction best limits tooth contact while preserving the dose?
options: Mix the measured dose into a full bottle of juice for use through the day.
Drink the measured juice mixture from a cup, then rinse the mouth.
Give the measured juice mixture through a straw, then rinse the mouth.
Rinse the mouth first, then drink the measured mixture from a cup.
why: The amount actually taken becomes uncertain if the bottle is not finished on schedule.
Measuring and rinsing preserve the dose and reduce residual iron, but a straw further limits contact during swallowing for this child.
The small completed mixture preserves the prescribed dose, while straw use and rinsing reduce tooth exposure.
A predose rinse does not remove iron left on teeth during administration.
takeaway: The small completed mixture preserves the prescribed dose, while straw use and rinsing reduce tooth exposure.
learningObjective: Teach a practical technique that preserves the prescribed iron dose and reduces tooth exposure.

title: Explain replacement in pernicious anemia
stem: A client with pernicious anemia feels better and has an improved blood count after B12 treatment. They ask whether replacement is now unnecessary. What is best?
options: A normal blood count means intrinsic factor has recovered.
Injected treatment can always be replaced by a standard multivitamin.
A higher dietary B12 intake removes the need for further treatment.
Improved stores do not necessarily correct the underlying absorption impairment.
why: Hematological improvement reflects replacement benefit, not restoration of the impaired absorption mechanism.
The route and dose must be individualized; ordinary multivitamin amounts may not meet replacement needs.
Better intake alone may not overcome the persistent absorption problem in pernicious anemia.
Pernicious anemia involves impaired intrinsic-factor-related absorption, so improvement often requires ongoing prescribed replacement to be sustained.
takeaway: Pernicious anemia involves impaired intrinsic-factor-related absorption, so improvement often requires ongoing prescribed replacement to be sustained.
learningObjective: Connect persistent intrinsic-factor deficiency with ongoing vitamin B12 replacement needs.

title: Distinguish folate correction from B12 evaluation
stem: A client with macrocytic anemia is being assessed before folate replacement is considered. Which additional finding should the nurse highlight to the prescriber?
options: Distal numbness with a new unsteady gait.
Fatigue with pallor during usual activities.
A sore tongue with reduced appetite.
Mild exertional breathlessness with tachycardia.
why: Neurological findings raise concern for B12 deficiency; folate can improve blood counts while unrecognized B12-related neurological injury continues.
These are general anemia features and do not specifically identify neurological involvement.
Oral and appetite symptoms can accompany several deficiencies and are less specific than the neurological cluster.
These may reflect anemia severity but do not distinguish B12-related nerve involvement.
takeaway: Neurological findings raise concern for B12 deficiency; folate can improve blood counts while unrecognized B12-related neurological injury continues.
learningObjective: Recognize why neurological symptoms with macrocytosis require consideration of vitamin B12 deficiency.

title: Monitor blood pressure during epoetin therapy
stem: A client receiving epoetin for renal anemia has a new headache. Repeated blood pressures are 186/106 and 184/104 mmHg. The client-specific order says to hold the dose and contact the prescriber if systolic pressure is 180 mmHg or higher. Which action follows the plan?
options: Repeat the pressure using a different cuff before deciding about epoetin.
Hold epoetin and obtain prompt assessment of the headache and pressure.
Give epoetin because the hemoglobin has improved on treatment.
Delay the dose until the client has rested, then give it if the headache eases.
why: Confirming technique can be useful, but two readings already exceed the prescribed threshold and headache adds urgency; another measurement should not postpone the ordered hold and clinical review.
Both readings exceed the supplied hold parameter, and symptoms add urgency to clinical review.
Hematological benefit does not override the explicit pressure parameter or establish safety.
Symptom relief alone does not establish that the pressure meets the prescribed conditions for dosing.
takeaway: Both readings exceed the supplied hold parameter, and symptoms add urgency to clinical review.
learningObjective: Recognize hypertension as a relevant safety concern during erythropoiesis-stimulating treatment.

title: Time phosphate binders with food
stem: A dialysis client takes all phosphate-binder tablets at bedtime because that is easiest to remember. What is the most useful teaching?
options: Take the whole daily amount before breakfast.
Use the usual bedtime dose whenever the daily total is unchanged.
Link prescribed doses to meals and relevant snacks.
Take each dose at a fixed two-hour interval after meals.
why: This would not appropriately accompany dietary phosphate in later meals and snacks.
The total amount alone does not ensure effective binding when it is separated from food.
The binder needs to be present with dietary phosphate in the gastrointestinal tract.
A delayed schedule can separate the medicine from the food it is intended to bind.
takeaway: The binder needs to be present with dietary phosphate in the gastrointestinal tract.
learningObjective: Explain how a prescribed phosphate binder's action determines administration timing.

title: Assess calcium during calcitriol therapy
stem: A client taking calcitriol develops constipation and weakness. Calcium is 2.95 mmol/L (reference 2.15–2.55). Which concern is most relevant to medication review?
options: Worsening hypocalcemia requiring more active vitamin D.
Gastrointestinal phosphate binding causing reduced calcium absorption.
A normal treatment effect indicating restored bone strength.
Calcitriol-associated hypercalcemia.
why: The supplied calcium is above range, so increasing treatment for low calcium is not supported.
Calcitriol is active vitamin D, not a phosphate binder, and the current value shows calcium excess.
Symptomatic above-range calcium is not an intended marker of successful bone treatment.
Active vitamin D can increase calcium absorption; the elevated value and compatible symptoms warrant treatment review.
takeaway: Active vitamin D can increase calcium absorption; the elevated value and compatible symptoms warrant treatment review.
learningObjective: Recognize symptoms and laboratory trends suggesting excessive calcium during active vitamin D therapy.

title: Evaluate prescribed bicarbonate in CKD
stem: A client with chronic kidney disease receives prescribed sodium bicarbonate for metabolic acidosis. Which follow-up cluster most directly assesses both the treatment goal and the sodium burden?
options: Serum bicarbonate, weight, edema and blood pressure.
Serum potassium, pulse rhythm and muscle strength.
Food intake, albumin and weekly appetite changes.
Creatinine, urine concentration and medication-clearance estimates.
why: Bicarbonate reflects the intended acid-base response, while volume and pressure findings assess tolerance of added sodium.
These are relevant renal safety measures but do not directly cover both bicarbonate correction and sodium-related fluid effects.
Nutrition assessment matters in CKD but does not directly evaluate this medicine's main acid-base goal and sodium burden.
Renal trends remain important, but this cluster is less specific for both bicarbonate response and fluid tolerance.
takeaway: Bicarbonate reflects the intended acid-base response, while volume and pressure findings assess tolerance of added sodium.
learningObjective: Assess correction of metabolic acidosis alongside sodium-related fluid tolerance.

title: Review magnesium antacids in advanced kidney disease
stem: A client with advanced kidney disease uses a magnesium antacid several times daily. What should the nurse do?
options: Use symptom relief to decide how often another dose is needed.
Review the product's renal safety with pharmacy or the treatment team.
Move the antacid to a different time from meals.
Change to another brand of magnesium antacid.
why: Heartburn relief does not establish safe magnesium exposure in advanced kidney disease.
Magnesium can accumulate when renal elimination is substantially reduced, especially with frequent use.
Changing timing does not remove the risk of magnesium accumulation.
A brand change does not remove the ingredient-specific renal concern.
takeaway: Magnesium can accumulate when renal elimination is substantially reduced, especially with frequent use.
learningObjective: Identify potential accumulation from a nonprescription magnesium-containing product during renal impairment.

title: Reduce systemic absorption of eye drops
stem: A client prescribed timolol eye drops is taught nasolacrimal occlusion. Which actions fit the instructed technique? Select all that apply.
options: Rub the eye firmly after placing the drop
Add a second drop whenever some fluid reaches the cheek
Close the eyelid gently after instillation
Apply gentle pressure near the inner canthus for the taught interval
Blink rapidly to spread the medicine into the tear duct
why: Rubbing risks irritation and does not provide controlled occlusion.
Routine extra dosing can increase exposure beyond the prescription.
Gentle closure helps limit immediate drainage without forceful blinking.
Occluding drainage can reduce systemic absorption through the nasolacrimal pathway.
Rapid blinking promotes drainage rather than reducing it.
takeaway: Gentle closure helps limit immediate drainage without forceful blinking.
learningObjective: Teach prescribed nasolacrimal occlusion to reduce systemic exposure to ophthalmic timolol.

title: Space separately prescribed eye products
stem: A client must use two different eye-drop medicines at the same administration time. Which teaching points are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Verify the prescribed order when an ointment is also used
Mix both solutions in one dropper bottle
Place both drops rapidly to shorten the procedure
Use extra drops to compensate for any expected overflow
Follow the recommended interval between products
why: Ointments and drops may need a specific sequence for effective delivery.
Mixing can create contamination, stability and identification problems.
Immediate sequential instillation can increase washout.
Unplanned extra dosing does not provide reliable compensation.
Spacing reduces the chance that the next drop washes out the first.
takeaway: Spacing reduces the chance that the next drop washes out the first.
learningObjective: Prevent immediate washout when more than one ophthalmic product is prescribed.

title: Measure and handle nitroglycerin ointment safely
stem: The order specifies a 2.5 cm strip of nitroglycerin ointment applied every 8 hours using the supplied calibrated paper. The nurse wears appropriate gloves. Which method gives the ordered amount?
options: Measure a 2.5 cm strip on the supplied dose paper.
Spread a thin film over 2.5 cm² of skin.
Cover the entire supplied paper with a thin ointment layer.
Use a 2.5 mL oral syringe to measure the ointment volume.
why: The order specifies strip length using the product measure; this provides the intended quantity while gloves limit unintended exposure.
Skin area is different from the prescribed strip length and cannot establish the same quantity.
The paper is a measuring aid, not an instruction to fill its whole area.
The ordered length cannot be replaced by the same numerical volume; the unit and measuring method matter.
takeaway: The order specifies strip length using the product measure; this provides the intended quantity while gloves limit unintended exposure.
learningObjective: Use the prescribed length measure rather than substituting skin area or volume for a topical ointment dose.

title: Check a medicated patch before MRI
stem: A client wearing a medicated patch is scheduled for MRI. The product's backing composition is unknown. What is appropriate?
options: Cover the patch with another dressing for the scan.
Verify product MRI compatibility and the replacement instructions.
Leave it in place because the active medicine is not magnetic.
Remove it and apply the next patch at the usual scheduled time.
why: An added covering does not establish protection from MRI-related heating.
Patch materials may heat during MRI, while removal affects medication delivery; both need product-specific planning.
The backing or other material, rather than the active drug alone, can create heating risk.
That interval may leave an unintended treatment gap or otherwise conflict with the specific replacement instructions.
takeaway: Patch materials may heat during MRI, while removal affects medication delivery; both need product-specific planning.
learningObjective: Use product and imaging guidance to manage a patch that may contain metal before MRI.

title: Evaluate epinephrine autoinjector readiness
stem: A client prescribed an epinephrine autoinjector practises with the correct trainer and its instructions. Which findings support readiness? Select all that apply.
options: The client identifies the needle end and targets the outer mid-thigh.
The client describes calling for emergency help after use.
The client places a thumb over the end from which the needle emerges.
The client selects the upper-arm muscle as the planned injection site.
The client removes the device as soon as it touches the skin, before completing its instructed sequence.
why: Correct end and site reduce delay and accidental injection risk during an emergency.
An initial response does not exclude persistent or recurrent anaphylaxis, so emergency follow-up remains necessary.
Covering the needle end risks an accidental finger injection and failed delivery to the intended site.
The standard autoinjector site is the outer mid-thigh; upper-arm selection is a technique error.
The demonstrated sequence must follow that device's instructions to activate and deliver its intended dose.
takeaway: Correct end and site reduce delay and accidental injection risk during an emergency.
learningObjective: Assess device-specific demonstration and the escalation plan after emergency epinephrine use.

title: Respond to a new transfusion reaction
stem: During red-cell transfusion, a client develops new chills, fever and back discomfort. Which actions belong in the immediate reaction response? Select all that apply.
options: Discard the bag and tubing immediately.
Give the prescribed antipyretic, then restart the unit once fever settles.
Stop the transfusion and promptly assess the client.
Notify the team and follow the reaction investigation protocol.
Slow the transfusion until the chills settle.
why: The component and set may be needed for investigation; follow the reaction protocol's handling instructions.
A lower temperature does not rule out a serious transfusion reaction or authorize restarting the implicated component; the reaction pathway must guide further decisions.
Further exposure should cease while the new systemic symptoms are assessed for a potentially serious reaction.
Coordinated assessment, samples and product handling help establish the cause and guide treatment.
Reducing the rate still continues exposure to a component that may be causing a serious reaction.
takeaway: Further exposure should cease while the new systemic symptoms are assessed for a potentially serious reaction.
learningObjective: Initiate the transfusion-reaction pathway when new systemic symptoms develop during blood administration.

title: Differentiate possible transfusion overload
stem: An older client with heart failure develops breathlessness during transfusion. Which findings particularly support circulatory overload in the differential? Select all that apply.
options: Rising blood pressure with venous congestion.
Isolated urticaria with unchanged breathing and pressure.
Severe back pain with hypotension and dark urine.
New fever and rigors with clear lungs and stable pressure.
New crackles with increasing oxygen requirement.
why: The pressure and venous findings support increased circulatory volume during transfusion.
This pattern more strongly supports an allergic skin reaction than circulatory overload.
This pattern raises concern for hemolysis rather than isolated volume overload.
A febrile or other reaction needs urgent evaluation, but this pattern does not specifically support congestion.
Pulmonary congestion can impair oxygenation and supports overload in the differential.
takeaway: Pulmonary congestion can impair oxygenation and supports overload in the differential.
learningObjective: Recognize a circulatory-overload pattern during transfusion while arranging urgent assessment.

title: Report delayed transfusion symptoms
stem: A client is discharged after an uncomplicated transfusion. Which new findings should be reported promptly with mention of the recent transfusion? Select all that apply.
options: A small venipuncture bruise becomes lighter over several days.
New jaundice or unusually dark urine.
Unexpected fever, worsening fatigue or breathlessness.
Mild resolving tenderness where the cannula was removed.
Gradually improving tolerance of usual activities.
why: A resolving localized bruise is not the same pattern as new jaundice, dark urine or systemic illness.
Delayed hemolysis can become apparent after discharge; recent transfusion is important assessment information.
New systemic symptoms require prompt assessment and the transfusion history can guide investigation.
A improving local insertion-site symptom is less concerning than new systemic deterioration.
Functional improvement may reflect the intended benefit of red-cell treatment.
takeaway: Delayed hemolysis can become apparent after discharge; recent transfusion is important assessment information.
learningObjective: Include delayed warning symptoms in post-transfusion discharge teaching.

title: Resolve a blood-unit identity discrepancy
stem: A blood unit's compatibility label has an identification number that differs from the client's wristband by one digit. The name matches. What is appropriate?
options: Ask the client to confirm their blood group
Correct the number on the label at the bedside
Stop the verification process and resolve the discrepancy
Use the matching name to approve the unit
why: A remembered blood group cannot replace compatibility and identity checks.
A handwritten correction does not establish the blood bank's intended compatibility.
All required identifiers must agree before exposing the client to the component.
A name match does not resolve a potentially serious identification error.
takeaway: All required identifiers must agree before exposing the client to the component.
learningObjective: Verify concordant client and component identifiers before transfusion.

title: Confirm compatible red-cell tubing fluid
stem: A red-cell unit is ready, but the intended line contains dextrose solution. What should the nurse do?
options: Connect the unit through the existing dextrose line.
Reduce the dextrose rate during transfusion.
Use the dextrose solution to prime the blood filter.
Establish an approved compatible blood-administration setup.
why: The dextrose solution's appearance does not establish compatibility with red cells.
A lower rate does not remove contact between the incompatible solution and blood.
Priming still leaves the solution in the pathway where it will contact the cells.
Red cells need a suitable fluid and tubing plan; normal saline is commonly used according to local policy.
takeaway: Red cells need a suitable fluid and tubing plan; normal saline is commonly used according to local policy.
learningObjective: Use approved compatibility guidance for fluids sharing red-cell administration tubing.

title: Assess a new fever before transfusion
stem: Immediately before a planned nonemergency transfusion, a client reports chills. Temperature is newly 38.4°C on two measurements; the nurse has assessed vital signs and current symptoms, and the unit is not connected. What is the best next action?
options: Report the changed baseline and clarify whether to start.
Obtain the routine pretransfusion premedication prescription.
Repeat the temperature once more after a rest period.
Collect cultures if they are part of the existing illness orders.
why: The new febrile illness needs review before transfusion and would complicate assessment of any subsequent reaction.
Premedication does not explain the current symptoms or establish that starting is appropriate.
The elevation has already been confirmed and assessed; further repetition should not replace communication of the change.
Cultures may be useful but do not resolve the decision about initiating the planned component in a changed clinical state.
takeaway: The new febrile illness needs review before transfusion and would complicate assessment of any subsequent reaction.
