learningObjective: Establish and communicate a changed baseline before initiating a prescribed blood component.

title: Evaluate a platelet transfusion response
stem: A client with thrombocytopenia receives prescribed platelets for mucosal bleeding. Which observations most directly assess the intended hemostatic response? Select all that apply.
options: Less mucosal oozing and no additional bleeding sites.
An increased hemoglobin with better exertional tolerance.
A normal temperature with no chills during administration.
A stable weight and blood pressure after the infusion.
The platelet count measured at the ordered post-transfusion time.
why: Clinical hemostasis shows whether the intended bleeding problem is improving.
This cluster more directly evaluates correction of red-cell anemia than platelet response.
These are important safety findings but do not demonstrate hemostatic effectiveness.
These help assess fluid tolerance rather than the intended platelet-count and bleeding response.
An appropriately timed result helps assess the platelet increment.
takeaway: An appropriately timed result helps assess the platelet increment.
learningObjective: Use platelet and bleeding findings to evaluate platelet-component therapy.

title: Explain a prescribed plasma component
stem: A client with a documented clotting-factor deficiency is prescribed plasma and asks why red cells are not being used instead. What explanation is most accurate?
options: Plasma directly increases the circulating platelet count.
Plasma stimulates the bone marrow to produce replacement red cells.
Plasma supplies clotting factors for the identified deficiency.
Plasma raises oxygen-carrying capacity in the same way as red cells.
why: A platelet component, rather than plasma, supplies platelets when that is the indicated need.
Plasma supplies proteins; it is not an erythropoiesis-stimulating treatment.
The component is selected to replace the deficient coagulation proteins.
Oxygen transport is primarily a red-cell function, not the principal purpose of plasma here.
takeaway: The component is selected to replace the deficient coagulation proteins.
learningObjective: Distinguish clotting-factor replacement from red-cell or platelet replacement.

title: Manage an unexpected PN interruption
stem: A client's continuous high-dextrose parenteral nutrition stops unexpectedly because the line fails. Alternative access and the prescribed interruption plan are being arranged. Why is an early glucose check particularly relevant?
options: Glucose must immediately rise when any PN infusion is interrupted.
The lost protein supply causes a glucose decline before carbohydrate changes matter.
A normal glucose before the interruption predicts stability until the next bag.
Glucose may fall after the abrupt reduction in carbohydrate delivery.
why: Stopping the carbohydrate supply does not predict an immediate rise; the actual response must be measured.
The immediate interruption concern is the change in dextrose delivery rather than rapid depletion of body protein.
A previous reading cannot establish the response to an abrupt change in substrate delivery.
The metabolic response to continuous glucose delivery may persist after it stops; assessment guides the ordered contingency treatment.
takeaway: The metabolic response to continuous glucose delivery may persist after it stops; assessment guides the ordered contingency treatment.
learningObjective: Explain glucose monitoring after an abrupt interruption of continuous high-dextrose parenteral nutrition.

title: Monitor a new PN regimen
stem: During the first two days of PN in a malnourished client, which trends require prompt review? Select all that apply.
options: Glucose increases to 19 mmol/L above the prescribed target of 6–10.
Phosphate falls to 0.45 mmol/L (reference 0.80–1.45).
New fever accompanies redness and tenderness at the catheter site.
Weight rises 0.1 kg while pressure, lung sounds and balance remain stable.
The client remains alert with glucose within the prescribed target.
why: Significant hyperglycemia indicates a need to review metabolic tolerance and the authorized regimen.
The decline during refeeding can be clinically important and requires electrolyte and nutrition-plan review.
The combination raises concern for a vascular-access infection and needs prompt assessment.
This small isolated change does not itself establish fluid intolerance, although trends remain necessary.
These observations are reassuring at that time and do not represent the new problems being sought.
takeaway: Significant hyperglycemia indicates a need to review metabolic tolerance and the authorized regimen.
learningObjective: Select metabolic, fluid and access assessments after parenteral nutrition is initiated.

title: Verify central PN access requirements
stem: A PN bag is labelled for central administration, but only a peripheral cannula is currently usable. What is appropriate?
options: Dilute the bag at the bedside to make it peripheral
Clarify access or an alternative formulation before infusion
Use the peripheral cannula because it flushes easily
Run the central formulation slowly through the peripheral line
why: Unapproved dilution compromises formulation and compounding safety.
A central formulation may be unsuitable for peripheral veins.
Patency does not establish that the formulation is suitable for that vessel.
A slower rate does not necessarily make its concentration appropriate.
takeaway: A central formulation may be unsuitable for peripheral veins.
learningObjective: Match a central PN formulation to a verified appropriate vascular-access route.

title: Protect a dedicated PN lumen
stem: A client has a designated central-lumen PN infusion and another usable lumen. Which practices support safe delivery? Select all that apply.
options: Verify a proposed co-infusion with an approved compatibility resource.
Add an ordered IV medicine into the hanging PN bag.
Use the PN lumen for the next antibiotic while the other lumen remains available.
Join a medicine to PN after checking that both fluids are clear.
Continue PN through its designated lumen.
why: PN contains multiple ingredients, so compatibility requires specific confirmation.
Bedside addition is not an approved compounding method and can affect stability and dose delivery.
A separate suitable lumen avoids unnecessary PN interruption and mixing; access choice should follow the dedicated-lumen plan.
Some incompatibilities are not visible, so clarity cannot replace a compatibility determination.
Dedicated use limits unnecessary interruption and reduces opportunities for incompatible mixing.
takeaway: Dedicated use limits unnecessary interruption and reduces opportunities for incompatible mixing.
learningObjective: Limit incompatibility and unnecessary manipulation of the parenteral-nutrition pathway.

title: Recognize refeeding-associated electrolyte decline
stem: Within a day of restarting nutrition, a severely malnourished client develops weakness and phosphate falls from 1.0 to 0.32 mmol/L (reference 0.80–1.45). Kidney function is unchanged and there are no new gastrointestinal losses. Which mechanism is most concerning?
options: Reduced kidney excretion causing phosphate retention.
A newly inadequate ongoing dietary phosphate intake.
Simple dilution from a large-volume fluid bolus.
An intracellular electrolyte shift associated with refeeding.
why: Retention would tend to increase phosphate and does not fit the marked fall with unchanged renal function.
The abrupt decline after feeding starts is more suggestive of redistribution than a new reduction in intake.
No such exposure is described; the severe malnutrition and timing after nutrition support refeeding physiology.
Renewed carbohydrate metabolism can drive phosphate into cells; the abrupt fall and weakness require urgent review of electrolytes and nutrition progression.
takeaway: Renewed carbohydrate metabolism can drive phosphate into cells; the abrupt fall and weakness require urgent review of electrolytes and nutrition progression.
learningObjective: Escalate new phosphate depletion and weakness after nutrition is restarted in severe malnutrition.

title: Explain prescribed isotonic volume replacement
stem: A client with vomiting and circulatory volume depletion is prescribed an isotonic crystalloid. What is the principal immediate treatment goal?
options: Support extracellular volume and circulating perfusion.
Replace intracellular free water as its main purpose.
Expand plasma oncotic pressure through added protein.
Supply the glucose needed for immediate caloric replacement.
why: An isotonic crystalloid can restore extracellular volume when vomiting has reduced intravascular filling.
This is more characteristic of a hypotonic free-water strategy than isotonic volume resuscitation.
A crystalloid does not provide colloid protein for that purpose.
The stated isotonic volume goal does not establish a glucose-containing nutritional prescription.
takeaway: An isotonic crystalloid can restore extracellular volume when vomiting has reduced intravascular filling.
learningObjective: Connect an isotonic crystalloid prescription with treatment of extracellular volume depletion.

title: Monitor prescribed hypertonic saline
stem: A client receives hypertonic saline under a protocol that limits the sodium rise to 8 mmol/L in any 24 hours and requires serial neurological and sodium checks. Which findings require prompt action under that protocol? Select all that apply.
options: Sodium rises from 112 to 123 mmol/L within 10 hours.
New headache and declining alertness develop during infusion.
Sodium rises 2 mmol/L in four hours while alertness improves.
Blood pressure remains close to its pretreatment value.
The verified pump rate matches the current authorized order.
why: The 11 mmol/L rise already exceeds the supplied 24-hour limit and requires urgent review of correction safety.
A neurological change during correction requires immediate assessment rather than being assumed to reflect recovery.
This finding alone does not exceed the stated limit, though the full ongoing 24-hour trend must still be monitored.
A stable pressure is not a new warning finding and does not replace sodium and neurological checks.
A correct setting is necessary but does not eliminate the need to act on adverse clinical or laboratory trends.
takeaway: The 11 mmol/L rise already exceeds the supplied 24-hour limit and requires urgent review of correction safety.
learningObjective: Apply controlled-rate and neurological monitoring during authorized hypertonic saline treatment.

title: Assess urine output before potassium replacement
stem: An IV potassium replacement order requires urine output of at least 30 mL/hour before infusion. Potassium from two hours ago is 3.3 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0). Output has fallen to 10 mL/hour with rising creatinine, and the infusion has not started. What is the best action?
options: Use a more dilute preparation for the same dose.
Request a new potassium level and proceed with the current order meanwhile.
Hold initiation and clarify the replacement order.
Start the dose because the recent potassium remains low.
why: Dilution changes concentration but not the total potassium load or unmet start criterion.
A repeat may be needed, but administering during clarification would disregard the specified output parameter.
The new renal findings violate the supplied condition and may reduce potassium elimination, so the plan needs review.
The low value does not override the explicit urine-output condition or the new renal change.
takeaway: The new renal findings violate the supplied condition and may reduce potassium elimination, so the plan needs review.
learningObjective: Recognize reduced potassium elimination as relevant before a replacement infusion.

title: Recognize magnesium toxicity
stem: A client receiving magnesium sulfate has a respiratory rate of 8/minute, absent deep-tendon reflexes and falling urine output. Another nurse is activating emergency help and supporting breathing. What medication-related action should occur first under the toxicity protocol?
options: Draw the ordered magnesium blood sample.
Review the total magnesium received during the shift.
Prepare the prescribed calcium rescue medicine.
Stop the magnesium infusion.
why: A sample supports assessment but should not delay stopping the suspected toxic infusion.
Exposure history is useful for the team, but the current clinical toxicity requires an immediate infusion action.
Rescue preparation may be urgent, but continued magnesium exposure should be stopped as that treatment is arranged.
Stopping further exposure addresses the suspected toxicity while respiratory support and the rest of the emergency protocol proceed.
takeaway: Stopping further exposure addresses the suspected toxicity while respiratory support and the rest of the emergency protocol proceed.
learningObjective: Escalate respiratory depression and loss of reflexes during magnesium sulfate infusion.

title: Distinguish seizure prophylaxis from pressure control
stem: A client with severe preeclampsia receives magnesium sulfate and a separate antihypertensive. They ask why both are needed. What is best?
options: Magnesium reduces seizure risk; the other medicine treats hypertension.
Magnesium treats hypertension; the other medicine prevents seizures.
Magnesium removes retained fluid; the other medicine treats hypertension.
Magnesium relaxes the uterus; the other medicine prevents seizures.
why: The two prescriptions address distinct complications of severe preeclampsia.
This reverses their principal intended roles in the stated plan.
Magnesium is not prescribed here primarily as a diuretic.
These purposes do not explain the prescribed seizure-prevention and pressure-control regimen.
takeaway: The two prescriptions address distinct complications of severe preeclampsia.
learningObjective: Explain why magnesium and a separate antihypertensive may both be prescribed in severe preeclampsia.

title: Review a possibly contaminated heparin sample
stem: A heparin-monitoring sample drawn through the infusing lumen is unexpectedly very high. The nurse has reported the critical result and sampling route; the client has no new bleeding. The local protocol requires team guidance for a possibly contaminated result. What should follow?
options: Repeat the sample through the same infusing lumen.
Obtain interim protocol guidance and a fresh appropriate-site sample.
Apply the routine dose-reduction table to this value.
Verify the infusion pump and use its setting to accept the result.
why: Repeating the same collection problem may produce another contaminated result unless an appropriate validated sampling method is used.
The value might be genuinely high or contaminated; immediate guidance plus valid repeat testing avoids both dismissal and unverified dose changes.
Possible contamination changes interpretation, and the supplied protocol requires guidance before using the routine table.
Checking programming is useful but does not establish that the sample reflects systemic anticoagulation.
takeaway: The value might be genuinely high or contaminated; immediate guidance plus valid repeat testing avoids both dismissal and unverified dose changes.
learningObjective: Consider sampling contamination before interpreting an unexpected anticoagulation result.

title: Recognize an unexpectedly high neuraxial block
stem: During epidural analgesia, an alert client develops numbness extending into both hands, increasing limb heaviness, low blood pressure and difficulty taking a deep breath. Which complication is most concerning?
options: A vasovagal episode.
Hypovolemia from earlier fasting.
An unexpectedly high neuraxial block.
Opioid-related sedation.
why: A vagal response can lower pressure but does not explain the ascending bilateral numbness and motor heaviness.
Low volume can contribute to hypotension but does not explain the new level of sensory and motor blockade.
Ascending sensory and motor changes with respiratory and circulatory effects require immediate epidural-protocol response and anesthesia review.
The client is alert and has a spreading sensory-motor block, which is more specific than isolated opioid sedation.
takeaway: Ascending sensory and motor changes with respiratory and circulatory effects require immediate epidural-protocol response and anesthesia review.
learningObjective: Escalate spreading weakness and breathing difficulty during epidural analgesia.

title: Recognize systemic local-anesthetic toxicity
stem: During a local-anesthetic procedure, a client develops ringing ears, metallic taste and slurred speech. Which priority actions address possible systemic local-anesthetic toxicity? Select all that apply.
options: Ask the client to practise slow breathing for procedural anxiety.
Offer a brief pause and then complete the remaining anesthetic dose.
Alert the procedural team and stop further anesthetic administration.
Prepare airway and circulatory support according to the emergency protocol.
Check capillary glucose as the initial response to the speech change.
why: Anxiety support may help distress but is not an adequate response to these drug-related neurological warning symptoms.
Resuming exposure before the team resolves the suspected toxicity could worsen the event.
Tinnitus, metallic taste and slurred speech can be early systemic toxicity; preventing further exposure is urgent.
Toxicity can progress to seizures and cardiac instability, so early resuscitation readiness matters.
Glucose may help evaluate altered neurological status, but the characteristic symptoms during anesthetic administration require stopping exposure and preparing emergency support first.
takeaway: Tinnitus, metallic taste and slurred speech can be early systemic toxicity; preventing further exposure is urgent.
learningObjective: Respond to early neurological warning symptoms during local-anesthetic administration.

title: Respond to an open central-line system
stem: A central-line connection opens and the client develops sudden dyspnea and chest discomfort. Which immediate physical action best interrupts the suspected mechanism while help is summoned?
options: Occlude the open central-line system.
Apply supplemental oxygen.
Measure blood pressure and oxygen saturation.
Reconnect the monitoring leads.
why: Sealing the open pathway prevents further air entry while emergency assessment and treatment proceed.
Oxygen is important supportive care but does not stop additional air entering through the open connection.
Measurements guide care but do not interrupt the source of possible air entry.
Monitoring may support assessment but does not stop the open-line mechanism.
takeaway: Sealing the open pathway prevents further air entry while emergency assessment and treatment proceed.
learningObjective: Stop further air entry and escalate sudden symptoms after central-line disconnection.

title: Account for medicine remaining in tubing
stem: A small-volume IV medicine has left the bag, but medication-containing fluid remains in the tubing. A compatible flush volume and rate are prescribed. What should the nurse do?
options: Increase the next dose to replace the estimated residual
Complete the prescribed flush at the specified rate
Disconnect immediately because the medication bag is empty
Flush rapidly to finish the medication round
why: Dose compensation is unprescribed and the residual should be managed now.
This delivers the residual medicine without an unintended rapid bolus.
An empty bag does not mean the full intended dose has reached the client.
Rapid flushing can deliver residual medicine faster than prescribed.
takeaway: This delivers the residual medicine without an unintended rapid bolus.
learningObjective: Use the prescribed compatible flush plan to deliver residual medicine safely after a small-volume infusion.

title: Maintain blood integrity when transfusion is delayed
stem: A nonemergency transfusion is postponed after the blood unit arrives on the unit. What should the nurse do?
options: Keep the unit at the bedside until the new start time is confirmed.
Put the unit in an ice-filled cooler from the ward.
Contact the blood bank and follow its return or storage instructions.
Place the unit in the ward medication refrigerator.
why: The period of uncontrolled storage matters even when the intended delay appears short.
Improvised cooling can expose the component to unvalidated temperatures and does not replace an approved storage process.
Blood integrity depends on validated time-temperature control; the service can guide safe handling of this delayed unit.
An ordinary medication refrigerator may not provide validated blood-storage conditions.
takeaway: Blood integrity depends on validated time-temperature control; the service can guide safe handling of this delayed unit.
learningObjective: Follow blood-bank time and storage requirements when an issued component cannot be started.

title: Limit injection-site bruising
stem: After a prescribed subcutaneous enoxaparin injection, the client sees a small drop of blood and begins rubbing the site. Which technique should the nurse reinforce?
options: Massage briefly to disperse the medicine under the skin.
Rub the site with an alcohol swab until the drop disappears.
Press and rub an adhesive dressing firmly over the site.
Hold gentle gauze pressure if needed and avoid rubbing.
why: Massage is not needed to disperse enoxaparin and can increase local trauma.
Repeated rubbing can worsen bruising and is not the appropriate way to control oozing.
A dressing may be used as indicated, but rubbing pressure is not the supported postinjection technique.
Gentle pressure can control minor oozing; rubbing adds tissue trauma and bruising risk.
takeaway: Gentle pressure can control minor oozing; rubbing adds tissue trauma and bruising risk.
learningObjective: Apply product-specific subcutaneous anticoagulant technique and avoid unnecessary tissue trauma.

title: Isotretinoin and missed menstrual period
stem: A 22-year-old taking oral isotretinoin reports a missed menstrual period and a condom break two weeks ago. A pregnancy test has not yet been performed. Which instruction is most appropriate now?
options: Stop isotretinoin and contact the prescriber today for pregnancy assessment.
Continue isotretinoin until a pregnancy test confirms the missed period's cause.
Take isotretinoin every other day while arranging the next clinic appointment.
Repeat a home pregnancy test in one week and discuss the result at follow-up.
why: Possible pregnancy during isotretinoin exposure requires immediate action because of serious fetal risk; testing and counselling must be arranged promptly.
Waiting for confirmation prolongs a potentially harmful exposure; a suspected pregnancy is sufficient reason to stop and seek advice.
An unprescribed dose reduction does not address the fetal risk or the need for prompt assessment.
Testing is necessary, but this delayed plan leaves immediate medication management and possible exposure unaddressed.
takeaway: Possible pregnancy during isotretinoin exposure requires immediate action because of serious fetal risk; testing and counselling must be arranged promptly.
learningObjective: Recognize a possible pregnancy during isotretinoin therapy as requiring immediate interruption and prescriber contact.

title: Pregnancy planning with epilepsy
stem: A client whose epilepsy has been controlled with valproate for three years wants to become pregnant in six months. They are using reliable contraception and have not changed treatment. Which counselling points should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Continue the current seizure medicine until an individualized change is prescribed.
Discuss contraception and folic acid with the prescribing team.
Reduce the valproate dose once the first menstrual period is missed.
Use a normal ultrasound result to decide whether medication review is needed.
Arrange a preconception medication review with the epilepsy specialist.
why: Abrupt withdrawal can precipitate seizures, so treatment changes require a supervised plan.
Pregnancy prevention during the review and an individualized supplementation plan are relevant parts of preconception counselling.
A self-directed reduction after possible conception is both late for prevention and potentially destabilizing for seizure control.
A later ultrasound cannot replace preconception risk assessment or exclude every medication-related developmental risk.
Valproate has substantial fetal risks; a planned review permits consideration of safer effective treatment before pregnancy.
takeaway: Valproate has substantial fetal risks; a planned review permits consideration of safer effective treatment before pregnancy.
learningObjective: Support specialist review of valproate before conception while protecting against abrupt loss of seizure control.

title: Breastfeeding medication assessment
stem: A breastfeeding parent asks whether a newly prescribed medicine is compatible with feeding. Their infant was born at 30 weeks and is now three weeks old. The parent has not yet taken the first dose. Which approach best supports a safe recommendation?
options: Recommend taking the dose immediately after a feed to minimize the next milk concentration.
Use the medicine's low adult dose as the main reason to continue breastfeeding.
Review the exact drug and dose with pharmacy using the infant's gestational and postnatal ages.
Base advice on whether the medicine was considered acceptable during pregnancy.
why: Dose timing can help for selected drugs but cannot establish compatibility, especially when feeding intervals and drug half-life vary.
An adult dose alone does not establish infant exposure, absorption or clearance; drug-specific review is required.
A premature infant may clear drugs less effectively; compatibility depends on the specific exposure and infant vulnerability.
Placental exposure and transfer through milk are different, and pregnancy advice does not establish safety for this premature infant.
takeaway: A premature infant may clear drugs less effectively; compatibility depends on the specific exposure and infant vulnerability.
learningObjective: Identify infant maturity and the actual medicine exposure as essential to individualized lactation advice.

title: Current weight and pediatric dose
stem: A child weighed 18 kg six months ago and weighs 23 kg on today's calibrated scale. A new weight-based antibiotic order was calculated using the older weight. The child is stable and the first dose is due in one hour. What should the nurse do?
options: Administer the ordered dose because the previous weight produces a smaller amount.
Recalculate and administer from today's weight using the old mg/kg instruction.
Repeat today's weight on a second scale to decide whether clarification is needed.
Ask the prescriber and pharmacist to verify the order using the current weight.
why: A smaller dose is not automatically appropriate and may undertreat infection.
The nurse should not independently replace a questioned prescription; the intended authorized dose needs clarification.
The current calibrated measurement already establishes a meaningful discrepancy; reweighing may verify it but does not resolve an order intentionally based on old data.
The confirmed weight discrepancy may affect safety and effectiveness, so the authorized dose should be resolved before the first administration.
takeaway: The confirmed weight discrepancy may affect safety and effectiveness, so the authorized dose should be resolved before the first administration.
learningObjective: Resolve a clinically important discrepancy in the weight used for a pediatric medication order.

title: Salicylate choice during viral illness
stem: A parent plans to give a 10-year-old with influenza an over-the-counter headache powder. The label lists acetylsalicylic acid. The child has no specialist-prescribed aspirin therapy. Which response is best?
options: Avoid this product and ask about a suitable non-salicylate fever medicine.
Use the children's dose printed on another acetylsalicylic acid product.
Give the powder with food to reduce the most relevant risk.
Choose an enteric-coated aspirin tablet instead of the powder.
why: Aspirin use during viral illness in children is associated with Reye syndrome; the ingredient, not the powder format, determines the concern.
Reducing the amount does not remove the viral-illness precaution for this child.
Food may reduce gastric discomfort but does not prevent Reye syndrome.
Changing the coating does not remove systemic salicylate exposure or its viral-illness risk.
takeaway: Aspirin use during viral illness in children is associated with Reye syndrome; the ingredient, not the powder format, determines the concern.
learningObjective: Recognize an aspirin-containing product as inappropriate self-treatment for a child's viral illness.

title: Oxytocin and uterine overstimulation
stem: A nurse with obstetric competence is monitoring oxytocin. The supplied local protocol says to reduce the rate for excessive contraction frequency with a reassuring fetal heart pattern, and stop oxytocin if excessive activity accompanies fetal deterioration. There are seven contractions per 10 minutes averaged over 30 minutes, little relaxation, and a new prolonged fetal deceleration. Which pump action is indicated while the team responds?
options: Pause during the next contraction and resume with relaxation.
Stop the oxytocin infusion.
Reduce the oxytocin infusion to half its current rate.
Maintain the current rate during a cervical examination.
why: Intermittent cycling is neither of the protocol's responses and does not reliably reverse overstimulation.
The excessive activity is accompanied by fetal deterioration, meeting the stopping branch of the supplied protocol.
Rate reduction corresponds to the protocol's reassuring-fetal-pattern branch, which does not describe this client.
The observations already meet the specified stopping criterion; a cervical examination should not postpone the pump action.
takeaway: The excessive activity is accompanied by fetal deterioration, meeting the stopping branch of the supplied protocol.
learningObjective: Interrupt oxytocin when excessive uterine activity accompanies fetal deterioration under the established response protocol.

title: Ergometrine and hypertension
stem: A postpartum client is bleeding from uterine atony despite first-line measures. The obstetric team is at the bedside. Blood pressure is 174/112 mmHg, and an order for ergometrine is received. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Request the same ergometrine dose by a slower route.
Request a reduced ergometrine dose because the pressure is high.
Raise the severe hypertension and request an alternative uterotonic.
Administer ergometrine and repeat pressure after bleeding slows.
why: Changing administration speed does not remove the systemic vasoconstrictive risk.
A dose-reduction proposal does not by itself resolve a severe-hypertension contraindication; an appropriate alternative is needed.
Ergometrine can worsen severe hypertension, so the team should urgently review the drug choice while haemorrhage treatment continues.
Monitoring after exposure does not address the severe hypertension already present.
takeaway: Ergometrine can worsen severe hypertension, so the team should urgently review the drug choice while haemorrhage treatment continues.
learningObjective: Use maternal blood pressure and medication properties to identify a uterotonic order requiring urgent clarification.

title: Carboprost and respiratory history
stem: A postpartum client has ongoing uterine atony, and carboprost is being considered. Which history should the nurse communicate most urgently before administration?
options: Gestational diabetes controlled with nutrition during pregnancy.
Iron-deficiency anemia treated with oral iron during pregnancy.
Gastroesophageal reflux managed with occasional antacid tablets.
Asthma requiring a rescue inhaler several times this month.
why: This matters to overall care but is not the major carboprost-related risk presented by these histories.
Anemia increases the consequence of blood loss but does not create the drug-specific bronchospasm risk.
Reflux may influence comfort and aspiration assessment but is less relevant to carboprost selection than asthma.
Carboprost may provoke bronchospasm; active asthma is important when the team chooses a uterotonic.
takeaway: Carboprost may provoke bronchospasm; active asthma is important when the team chooses a uterotonic.
learningObjective: Identify asthma as a clinically important precaution when selecting treatment for uterine atony.

title: Postpartum Rh immune globulin purpose
stem: An Rh-negative postpartum client has a negative antibody screen and an Rh-positive newborn. Rh immune globulin is prescribed. The client asks why they need it when this newborn is well. Which explanation is best?
options: It helps prevent you from forming anti-D after exposure to the baby's red cells.
It removes anti-D that your body has already formed.
It treats anemia that the newborn developed during pregnancy.
It prevents incompatibility from any future difference in blood group.
why: The aim is to prevent sensitization in an unsensitized Rh-negative parent, reducing risk to a future Rh-positive pregnancy.
Rh immune globulin does not reverse established sensitization; the negative antibody screen is relevant to prevention.
The postpartum maternal dose prevents sensitization rather than treating current newborn anemia.
Anti-D prophylaxis addresses RhD sensitization, not every possible maternal-fetal blood-group incompatibility.
takeaway: The aim is to prevent sensitization in an unsensitized Rh-negative parent, reducing risk to a future Rh-positive pregnancy.
learningObjective: Explain preventive Rh immune globulin to an unsensitized Rh-negative parent after an Rh-positive birth.

title: Tacrolimus and grapefruit routine
stem: A kidney-transplant recipient taking tacrolimus twice daily plans to drink grapefruit juice at lunch, six hours after the morning dose. Which instruction should the nurse give?
options: Choose whole grapefruit instead of juice to reduce the interaction.
Avoid grapefruit and check alternative juice choices with the transplant team.
Keep grapefruit at lunch and move the evening tacrolimus dose later.
Use the same amount of grapefruit each day so the prescribed dose remains effective.
why: The interacting substances can also be present in the fruit, so changing its form does not establish safety.
Grapefruit can increase tacrolimus exposure through effects that outlast a single meal, so separating the doses does not reliably prevent toxicity.
A longer gap does not reliably prevent the metabolic interaction.
Consistent intake is not a substitute for the transplant team's avoidance advice and therapeutic monitoring.
takeaway: Grapefruit can increase tacrolimus exposure through effects that outlast a single meal, so separating the doses does not reliably prevent toxicity.
learningObjective: Recognize that separating grapefruit and tacrolimus by a few hours does not reliably prevent the interaction.

title: Vaccination during immunosuppression
stem: A transplant recipient receiving tacrolimus and prednisone asks about measles-mumps-rubella vaccine and the inactivated influenza injection. Which responses are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Treat the live and inactivated vaccines as having the same infection risk.
Use a reduced live-vaccine dose to make routine administration safer.
Have the transplant team review the live MMR vaccine before it is given.
Discuss receiving the inactivated influenza vaccine according to the transplant schedule.
Explain that immunosuppression may reduce the vaccine's protective response.
why: The ability of a live vaccine to replicate is a meaningful distinction for this recipient.
Dose reduction is not a substitute for evaluating whether a live vaccine is appropriate during immunosuppression.
Live vaccines may cause disease during significant immunosuppression and require specialist assessment.
Inactivated vaccines cannot replicate, although timing and immune response require consideration.
Reduced immune response can occur even when an inactivated vaccine is appropriate, so additional prevention measures may remain important.
takeaway: Live vaccines may cause disease during significant immunosuppression and require specialist assessment.
learningObjective: Distinguish live-vaccine precautions from inactivated-vaccine planning for an immunocompromised client.

title: Latent tuberculosis before biologic therapy
stem: A client with rheumatoid arthritis feels well and is scheduled to start a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor. They ask why tuberculosis screening was ordered when they have no cough. Which explanation is best?
options: It creates a comparison result for any future TB exposure.
It predicts whether TB will be acquired during future treatment.
It measures how much protection remains from childhood BCG vaccination.
It identifies latent infection that the medicine could reactivate.
why: A baseline can be useful, but the immediate purpose is to address infection already present before immunosuppression.
Screening evaluates evidence of infection already present; it does not predict every future exposure or acquisition.
Latent-TB screening is not a measurement of remaining BCG protection; vaccination history and interpretation of specific test results are separate considerations.
TB may be present without cough or other symptoms; identifying it permits a prevention or treatment plan before TNF inhibition.
takeaway: TB may be present without cough or other symptoms; identifying it permits a prevention or treatment plan before TNF inhibition.
learningObjective: Explain why tuberculosis screening matters before tumour necrosis factor inhibitor therapy.

title: Interpret an early neutrophil rise during filgrastim
stem: On day 4 of a chemotherapy cycle, a client asks whether filgrastim can be stopped because the neutrophil count has risen from 2.4 to 5.2 × 10⁹/L (reference 1.5–7.5). For this cycle, the prescription is filgrastim 300 micrograms subcutaneously daily on days 2–8. The oncology team expects the lowest count around day 7 and has scheduled a blood count and treatment review on day 6. The client feels well. Which advice is best?
options: Continue the prescribed daily doses and scheduled blood tests; an early rise may be temporary.
Stop the remaining doses and keep the blood tests; a normal count indicates marrow recovery.
Give the remaining doses every other day; the rising count suggests the daily schedule is excessive.
Pause doses until the expected nadir; restart daily injections if the count then becomes low.
why: Filgrastim can produce an early transient neutrophil rise. This count precedes the expected nadir and does not establish recovery afterward; continue the current plan pending scheduled review.
A normal early count is not evidence that the later chemotherapy-related decline has passed. Stopping now could withdraw the prescribed support prematurely.
The count is within the supplied reference range and does not establish excessive dosing. Frequency changes require the oncology team to interpret the full treatment course.
This is prescribed preventive support, not a plan to wait for neutropenia. Delaying doses changes the regimen and could leave the anticipated decline unsupported.
takeaway: Evaluate filgrastim response in relation to the anticipated nadir and the individualized oncology plan, not one early normal neutrophil count.
learningObjective: Interpret an early normal neutrophil count during prescribed filgrastim without mistaking it for recovery after the chemotherapy nadir.

title: Rectal medication during marrow suppression
stem: A chemotherapy client has constipation, neutrophils 0.4 × 10⁹/L (reference 1.5–7.5) and platelets 22 × 10⁹/L (reference 150–400). A bisacodyl suppository is prescribed. The abdomen is soft, and there is no vomiting or severe pain. Which action is best?
options: Perform a digital rectal examination to guide the bowel treatment.
Request a suitable non-rectal bowel regimen.
Lubricate the suppository generously and insert it gently.
Substitute a small-volume enema for the suppository.
why: This introduces the same trauma and infection concern; an invasive rectal assessment is not the best initial response here.
Marked neutropenia and thrombocytopenia increase infection and bleeding risks from mucosal injury; the benign abdomen permits clarification of a safer route.
Gentler technique does not remove the concern about rectal mucosal trauma with these blood counts.
An enema still uses rectal instrumentation and may injure vulnerable mucosa.
takeaway: Marked neutropenia and thrombocytopenia increase infection and bleeding risks from mucosal injury; the benign abdomen permits clarification of a safer route.
learningObjective: Question a traumatic administration route when chemotherapy has caused neutropenia and thrombocytopenia.

title: Handling oral antineoplastic tablets
stem: A client's partner will help give an oral antineoplastic tablet. Pharmacy instructions for this product specify swallowing tablets whole and keeping them in the original container. Which directions should the nurse reinforce? Select all that apply.
options: Follow the pharmacy's glove instructions when another person handles tablets.
Contact the pharmacy about a broken tablet.
Wash hands after handling the container or removing gloves.
Crush a difficult-to-swallow tablet inside a sealed food container.
Transfer tablets into the shared weekly organizer with other medicines.
why: Caregiver handling precautions reduce unnecessary skin exposure to hazardous medicine.
A damaged tablet may release powder and cannot be assumed suitable for use or further division.
Hand hygiene reduces transfer of possible residues to other surfaces.
Crushing conflicts with the whole-tablet instruction and may release hazardous particles; swallowing problems need pharmacy review.
This conflicts with this product's original-container instructions and can increase exposure or mix-up risk.
takeaway: Caregiver handling precautions reduce unnecessary skin exposure to hazardous medicine.
learningObjective: Apply home handling precautions to intact oral cancer medication and damaged tablets.

title: Oral suspension volume
stem: This is a calculation-only task: the child's amoxicillin prescription has been clinically verified as 450 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days. The suspension contains 400 mg per 5 mL. What volume is needed for one dose, rounded to the nearest 0.1 mL?
options: 5.0 mL
0.9 mL
5.6 mL
why: 5 mL provides 400 mg, so it does not contain the prescribed 450 mg dose.
This approximates the combined volume for two doses, not one administration.
This result does not account correctly for the 5 mL concentration volume and would provide far less than 450 mg.
450 mg × 5 mL ÷ 400 mg = 5.625 mL, which rounds to 5.6 mL.
takeaway: 450 mg × 5 mL ÷ 400 mg = 5.625 mL, which rounds to 5.6 mL.
exhibit: Amoxicillin 450 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days
mL for one dose; nearest 0.1 mL
learningObjective: Convert a prescribed milligram dose into millilitres and round only the final volume.

title: Two-stage preparation and pump rate
stem: This is a calculation-only task with a verified order: cefazolin 1.2 g IV every 8 hours, each dose infused over 45 minutes. The reconstituted vial contains 100 mg/mL. Pharmacy instructions require dilution to a final total volume of 60 mL. Which withdrawal volume and pump rate are correct?
options: Withdraw 12 mL; set the pump to 80 mL/h.
Withdraw 12 mL; set the pump to 16 mL/h.
Withdraw 1.2 mL; set the pump to 80 mL/h.
Withdraw 12 mL; set the pump to 96 mL/h.
why: 1.2 g = 1200 mg; 1200 ÷ 100 = 12 mL. The final 60 mL divided by 0.75 hour gives 80 mL/h.
The withdrawal volume is correct, but 16 mL/h uses the 12 mL concentrate instead of the final 60 mL volume.
The rate matches the final volume, but the withdrawal misses the gram-to-milligram conversion and gives one tenth of the dose.
The final volume already includes the withdrawn drug; adding another 12 mL incorrectly produces a 72 mL calculation.
takeaway: 1.2 g = 1200 mg; 1200 ÷ 100 = 12 mL. The final 60 mL divided by 0.75 hour gives 80 mL/h.
learningObjective: Keep reconstituted withdrawal volume separate from final diluted infusion volume when calculating a pump rate.

title: Weight-based infusion conversion
stem: For this calculation-only task, a verified heparin protocol orders a continuous IV infusion of 18 units/kg/hour for a client weighing 75 kg. The bag contains 25,000 units in a final volume of 250 mL. No bolus is part of this calculation. What pump rate is required, rounded to the nearest 0.1 mL/hour?
options: 135.0 mL/hour
13.5 mL/hour
1.4 mL/hour
18.0 mL/hour
why: This rate is ten times the required volume and would deliver 13,500 units/hour from the stated bag.
18 × 75 = 1350 units/hour; the concentration is 100 units/mL, so 1350 ÷ 100 = 13.5 mL/hour.
This introduces a tenfold concentration error; at the actual concentration it would deliver about one tenth of the ordered amount.
18 is the weight-based units rate, not the volume rate; the client's weight and bag concentration must both be included.
takeaway: 18 × 75 = 1350 units/hour; the concentration is 100 units/mL, so 1350 ÷ 100 = 13.5 mL/hour.
exhibit: Heparin 18 units/kg/hour; no bolus in this task
learningObjective: Convert a verified units-per-kilogram-per-hour infusion order into millilitres per hour.

title: Gravity infusion rate
stem: For a calculation-only exercise, the verified order is 500 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride IV over 4 hours using gravity tubing labelled 15 drops/mL. What rate, rounded to the nearest whole drop per minute, corresponds to that order?
options: 21 drops/minute
63 drops/minute
31 drops/minute
125 drops/minute
why: This result does not use the stated 15 drops/mL factor correctly and would underdeliver the ordered volume.
This approximately doubles the correct rate, corresponding to about a two-hour delivery instead of four hours.
500 × 15 ÷ 240 minutes = 31.25 drops/minute, rounded to 31.
125 is the volume in mL/hour; it is not the drop rate for this tubing.
takeaway: 500 × 15 ÷ 240 minutes = 31.25 drops/minute, rounded to 31.
exhibit: 0.9% sodium chloride 500 mL IV over 4 hours
learningObjective: Convert a verified fluid volume and duration into whole drops per minute using the tubing factor.

title: Acetaminophen across two products
stem: A client has received four scheduled doses of acetaminophen 650 mg orally every 6 hours and one PRN combination tablet containing oxycodone 5 mg/acetaminophen 325 mg in the current rolling 24 hours. The combination is ordered one tablet orally every 4 hours PRN moderate pain. Another tablet is now requested and its interval is met, but the care plan limits total acetaminophen to 3000 mg in any 24 hours. Which calculation and action are correct?
options: The proposed total is 2925 mg; give the requested tablet within the interval.
The proposed total is 2600 mg; give the requested tablet within the interval.
The proposed total is 3900 mg; clarify the analgesia plan before giving the tablet.
The proposed total is 3250 mg; clarify the analgesia plan before giving the tablet.
why: 2925 mg is the amount already received; the requested tablet adds another 325 mg.
This counts only scheduled acetaminophen and omits the same ingredient in both combination tablets.
Clarification is warranted, but 3900 mg overcounts the actual listed doses and misrepresents the medication history.
Four doses give 2600 mg and two combination tablets give 650 mg; 3250 mg exceeds this client's explicit 3000 mg limit.
takeaway: Four doses give 2600 mg and two combination tablets give 650 mg; 3250 mg exceeds this client's explicit 3000 mg limit.
exhibit: One additional combination tablet containing acetaminophen 325 mg
learningObjective: Calculate the projected 24-hour acetaminophen total before giving a combination analgesic.

title: Accounting for ordered fluid volumes
stem: For this calculation-only exercise, a 24-hour plan limits total intake to 1200 mL. Parenteral nutrition is prescribed continuously at 40 mL/hour; two IV medication doses each have a final volume of 50 mL; six line flushes each contain 10 mL. These are the entire planned IV intake. How much remains for oral intake and other fluids during the same 24 hours?
options: 80 mL
140 mL
240 mL
180 mL
why: Parenteral nutrition supplies 960 mL, medications 100 mL and flushes 60 mL: 1120 mL total. The remaining allowance is 1200 − 1120 = 80 mL.
This subtracts nutrition and medication volumes but omits the 60 mL of flushes.
This subtracts nutrition alone and omits both medication carriers and line flushes.
This omits the two 50 mL medication doses from the total intake calculation.
takeaway: Parenteral nutrition supplies 960 mL, medications 100 mL and flushes 60 mL: 1120 mL total. The remaining allowance is 1200 − 1120 = 80 mL.
learningObjective: Include parenteral nutrition, medication carriers and flushes in a prescribed daily fluid allowance.

title: Two insulin formulations in one syringe
stem: A client has verified orders for insulin glargine subcutaneously once daily and insulin lispro subcutaneously with meals. At breakfast both are due. The client asks the nurse to combine them in one syringe to reduce injections. What is the best response?
options: Ask to move all of the lispro to the evening glargine administration time.
Give the two prescribed formulations as separate injections.
Draw lispro first and then add glargine to the same syringe.
Mix the two insulins immediately before administration and inject promptly.
why: Lispro is intended for mealtime coverage; changing its timing would not solve the mixing restriction and may leave breakfast uncovered.
Insulin glargine must not be mixed with other insulins; separate administration preserves the product's intended action.
Drawing short-acting insulin first is relevant to some compatible combinations, but it does not make glargine compatible for mixing.
Immediate use does not remove the formulation incompatibility.
takeaway: Insulin glargine must not be mixed with other insulins; separate administration preserves the product's intended action.
learningObjective: Distinguish a verified two-insulin regimen from permission to mix its formulations.

title: Jaw wound during bisphosphonate therapy
stem: An older adult taking alendronate weekly reports jaw pain and a nonhealing gum wound three weeks after a tooth extraction. They can swallow normally and have no heartburn. Which concern should the nurse communicate to the dental and prescribing teams?
options: A local dental infection considered unrelated to the medicine.
A calcium deficit suitable for increased home supplementation.
A possible medication-associated problem with jaw healing.
Esophageal irritation from the weekly alendronate tablet.
why: Local infection is a possible contributor, but the bisphosphonate exposure must be included rather than prematurely treated as irrelevant.
A supplement change does not evaluate the local wound or exclude a significant jaw complication.
Persistent jaw pain and a nonhealing extraction site warrant dental and prescribing-team assessment; the nurse should not claim osteonecrosis is established from this history alone.
Esophageal injury causes swallowing or retrosternal symptoms rather than a focal nonhealing gum wound.
takeaway: Persistent jaw pain and a nonhealing extraction site warrant dental and prescribing-team assessment; the nurse should not claim osteonecrosis is established from this history alone.
learningObjective: Recognize persistent jaw symptoms after dental work as a reportable bisphosphonate complication.

title: Opioid effect on breathlessness
stem: A client with advanced disease has a comfort-focused plan and prescribed low-dose oral morphine for refractory breathlessness after reversible contributors were assessed. Thirty minutes after a dose, the client says breathing feels easier and can speak with family; respiratory rate is 18/minute and they are readily alert. Which interpretation is best?
options: The dose has been ineffective because oxygen saturation has not increased.
The improvement mainly shows that morphine has corrected the underlying lung disease.
The respiratory rate must fall below the usual range before benefit is established.
The dose has reduced breathlessness with no current sign of excessive sedation.
why: Opioids may reduce the sensation of breathlessness without changing oxygen saturation; comfort and safety are key evaluation measures.
The medicine provides symptom relief; it does not reverse the underlying advanced disease.
A lower-than-normal respiratory rate is not a treatment target; excessive respiratory depression would be an adverse effect.
The client's reduced distress and preserved alertness support the intended symptom benefit; ongoing monitoring remains necessary.
takeaway: The client's reduced distress and preserved alertness support the intended symptom benefit; ongoing monitoring remains necessary.
learningObjective: Evaluate prescribed palliative opioid therapy using distress and function as well as respiratory safety.

title: Disintegrating tablet and aspiration risk
stem: A client with a new stroke is awaiting a swallowing assessment and has an order to remain NPO, including medicines. An orally disintegrating antiemetic has been prescribed. The product dissolves on the tongue and is then swallowed with saliva. The client is nauseated but has not vomited. What should the nurse do?
options: Clarify a suitable non-oral route while the swallowing restriction remains in effect.
Place the tablet on the tongue because no drinking water is required.
Crush the tablet into a small amount of thickened fluid.
Give the tablet during a period when the client is fully awake.
why: Dissolving in the mouth does not bypass swallowing or aspiration risk for this product; the route conflicts with the current restriction.
Water is not the deciding issue; the dissolved medicine and saliva still must be swallowed safely.
Changing texture does not replace the pending assessment or the explicit NPO order, and the formulation needs no crushing.
Alertness is helpful but does not by itself establish safe swallowing after a stroke.
takeaway: Dissolving in the mouth does not bypass swallowing or aspiration risk for this product; the route conflicts with the current restriction.
learningObjective: Recognize that an orally disintegrating formulation does not bypass the need for safe swallowing.

title: Recognize a silent chest during asthma
stem: A client with severe asthma was wheezing loudly. They now have barely audible breath sounds, exhaustion and difficulty speaking. What is the priority interpretation?
options: Mobilization of retained mucus.
Critically reduced airflow.
Resolving bronchospasm.
Reduced anxiety-related effort.
why: The overall deterioration does not support interpreting quieter sounds as successful secretion clearance.
Quieter breath sounds with exhaustion and limited speech suggest inadequate air movement and possible impending failure, requiring urgent support.
Improvement would include easier breathing and speech, not exhaustion and declining air entry.
The deteriorating ability to speak and marked exhaustion are physiological warning signs, not reassurance of calmer breathing.
takeaway: Quieter breath sounds with exhaustion and limited speech suggest inadequate air movement and possible impending failure, requiring urgent support.
learningObjective: Interpret quieter breath sounds with exhaustion as possible critical airflow reduction.

title: Evaluate a short-lived reliever response
stem: A client's prescribed asthma reliever briefly improves breathing, but severe dyspnea returns within minutes and they can speak only a few words. What should the nurse do?
options: Coach controlled breathing and relaxation.
Repeat peak-flow measurement to quantify the response.
Activate urgent support while continuing the authorized emergency plan.
Repeat treatment at the usual reliever schedule.
why: Coaching may assist comfort but is inadequate as the main response to severe airflow limitation.
Additional effort-dependent measurement must not postpone help when the client is struggling to speak.
Severe recurrent dyspnea and few-word speech indicate inadequate response and need emergency support.
The brief response and severe current symptoms require escalation beyond the routine schedule.
takeaway: Severe recurrent dyspnea and few-word speech indicate inadequate response and need emergency support.
learningObjective: Escalate severe asthma symptoms that recur after only transient reliever benefit.

title: Evaluate new drowsiness during COPD treatment
stem: During a COPD exacerbation, a client has an ordered oxygen saturation target of 88–92%. Oxygen was increased from 1 to 4 L/minute by nasal cannula, and saturation is now 98%. The client becomes drowsy and breathes shallowly. Which response is best?
options: Maintain 4 L/minute and request a routine blood gas.
Return to 1 L/minute and reassess at the next scheduled observation.
Request chest radiography to identify worsening lung disease.
Titrate oxygen to the target and obtain urgent ventilation review.
why: A blood gas is useful, but maintaining above-target oxygen and routine urgency do not address the current deterioration.
An earlier setting may not now achieve the target, and new altered consciousness requires urgent reassessment.
Imaging may assist later assessment but does not substitute for immediate oxygen titration and evaluation of ventilation.
The high saturation does not establish carbon dioxide clearance; new drowsiness and shallow breathing require urgent assessment while avoiding unnecessary oxygen excess.
takeaway: The high saturation does not establish carbon dioxide clearance; new drowsiness and shallow breathing require urgent assessment while avoiding unnecessary oxygen excess.
learningObjective: Assess ventilation and controlled oxygen needs when a client with COPD becomes drowsy.

title: Interpret oxygenation with worsening effort
stem: A client with pneumonia maintains saturation on increasing oxygen but becomes exhausted and uses accessory muscles. Which conclusion is best?
options: Worsening ventilatory reserve.
Adequate response to the current treatment.
Primarily anxiety-related respiratory effort.
Expected fatigue during respiratory recovery.
why: Increasing support, accessory-muscle use and exhaustion indicate deterioration despite a maintained saturation.
The same saturation achieved with increasing oxygen does not show stable or improving respiratory function.
Anxiety may coexist, but escalating support and exhaustion demand physiological assessment.
Fatigue accompanied by increased work of breathing is a warning of failure rather than an expected recovery milestone.
takeaway: Increasing support, accessory-muscle use and exhaustion indicate deterioration despite a maintained saturation.
learningObjective: Judge worsening respiratory effort despite saturation maintained by increasing support.

title: Recognize pneumonia deterioration in an older adult
stem: An older adult with pneumonia has a temperature of 37.4°C but is newly inattentive, breathing faster and eating little. What should guide the nurse's response?
options: Focus first on completing a nutrition supplement
Treat the change from baseline as possible acute deterioration
Wait for a fever above 38°C before reporting
Attribute inattention to the unfamiliar room alone
why: Immediate physiological assessment takes priority over supplement intake.
Older adults may deteriorate without a marked fever.
Absence of high fever does not exclude serious illness.
A new cognitive change with respiratory symptoms needs assessment.
takeaway: Older adults may deteriorate without a marked fever.
learningObjective: Recognize acute pneumonia deterioration without relying on a high fever.

title: Respond to vomiting during noninvasive ventilation
stem: A client wearing a tight noninvasive ventilation mask begins vomiting and cannot clear the contents. What should happen first?
options: Loosen the lower edge of the mask to allow drainage.
Administer the prescribed intravenous antiemetic.
Remove the mask and protect the airway while calling for help.
Turn the client laterally with the mask still fitted.
why: Partial loosening may leave contents within the mask and does not provide reliable access to clear the airway.
The medicine may help later nausea, but it does not promptly clear vomit already obstructing airway protection.
Removing the interface permits vomit clearance and immediate airway protection; trapped contents pose an aspiration threat.
Positioning may help clearance, but the sealed interface still traps vomit and needs immediate removal.
takeaway: Removing the interface permits vomit clearance and immediate airway protection; trapped contents pose an aspiration threat.
learningObjective: Prioritize airway protection when vomiting occurs inside a noninvasive ventilation mask.

title: Escalate an obstructed tracheostomy
stem: A tracheostomy-dependent client suddenly struggles to breathe. The trained nurse has removed the detachable inner cannula, but an appropriately sized suction catheter still cannot pass through the tube. What is appropriate next?
options: Try a smaller suction catheter to retrieve distal secretions.
Replace the humidification tubing attached to the tracheostomy.
Give the prescribed nebulized bronchodilator treatment.
Activate emergency airway support and use the tracheostomy algorithm.
why: Failure of an appropriate catheter to pass raises a tube-patency problem; a smaller catheter trial must not replace emergency oxygenation and airway management.
A circuit issue can affect delivery, but it does not explain persistent inability to pass the catheter through the tracheostomy tube.
A bronchodilator treats lower-airway constriction, not an obstructed or displaced artificial airway.
Persistent inability to pass the catheter after inner-cannula removal suggests obstruction or displacement requiring a structured emergency response.
takeaway: Persistent inability to pass the catheter after inner-cannula removal suggests obstruction or displacement requiring a structured emergency response.
learningObjective: Follow an emergency airway pathway when a tracheostomy suction catheter cannot pass.

title: Select a response to retained tracheal secretions
stem: A client with a tracheostomy has audible gurgling, visible secretions and an ineffective cough. Oxygen saturation has fallen from baseline. What is the most appropriate initial intervention by a competent nurse?
options: Perform protocol-based suctioning and reassess the response.
Increase supplemental oxygen.
Coach huff coughing.
Increase airway humidification.
why: Visible secretions, gurgling and ineffective cough indicate a clearance problem that suctioning can directly address.
Oxygen may be needed, but it does not remove the retained secretions causing airway compromise.
The cough is already ineffective, so coaching alone is unlikely to promptly clear the current secretion burden.
Humidification supports secretion management over time but does not rapidly remove material already obstructing airflow.
takeaway: Visible secretions, gurgling and ineffective cough indicate a clearance problem that suctioning can directly address.
learningObjective: Select protocol-based secretion removal for an ineffective cough and airway obstruction cues.

title: Respond to bradycardia during suctioning
stem: During tracheal suctioning, a client's pulse falls markedly and oxygen saturation drops. What should the nurse do first?
options: Shorten the next scheduled suction pass.
Withdraw the catheter and support oxygenation.
Pause suction while leaving the catheter in place.
Increase oxygen while completing the current suction pass.
why: Future technique changes may help, but the current instability requires immediate action.
Removing the provoking stimulus and restoring oxygenation address suction-associated vagal stimulation or hypoxemia; reassess and escalate if instability persists.
The catheter can continue to stimulate the airway even when suction is paused.
Continuing the stimulus may worsen bradycardia; the current pass should end rather than merely increasing oxygen.
takeaway: Removing the provoking stimulus and restoring oxygenation address suction-associated vagal stimulation or hypoxemia; reassess and escalate if instability persists.
learningObjective: Stop suctioning and support oxygenation when bradycardia and desaturation occur.

title: Evaluate expanding subcutaneous emphysema
stem: A client with a chest drain develops increasing neck and chest swelling that crackles on palpation, with new dyspnea. What is the priority?
options: Check and reinforce the dressing seal.
Temporarily clamp the drain.
Assess breathing and obtain urgent clinical review.
Record and mark the swelling border.
why: A dressing check can be part of assessment, but it does not adequately address possible intrathoracic air accumulation with dyspnea.
Clamping an air-leaking drain can trap air and increase intrathoracic pressure.
Expanding crepitus with dyspnea may indicate a significant air leak or drainage problem and requires prompt respiratory assessment.
Tracking spread is useful but does not address the associated acute respiratory change.
takeaway: Expanding crepitus with dyspnea may indicate a significant air leak or drainage problem and requires prompt respiratory assessment.
learningObjective: Escalate expanding subcutaneous emphysema with respiratory compromise during chest drainage.

title: Manage an accidental chest-drain disconnection
stem: A pleural drain that was bubbling in its water-seal chamber disconnects at the drainage-unit connector. The client is alert and oxygen saturation is unchanged. A sterile replacement water-seal unit and connector are ready at the bedside. The supplied unit protocol states: “For this device, promptly replace the disconnected unit using sterile connections; avoid routine clamping when an air leak is present.” Which action best follows this protocol?
options: Clamp the patient tubing while observing whether bubbling would have continued.
Wipe the detached connector and reconnect the original drainage unit.
Attach the patient tubing directly to the available wall suction tubing.
Connect the patient tubing to the prepared sterile replacement unit.
why: The prior bubbling indicates an air leak; a clamping trial is not the restoration process specified by this protocol.
Surface wiping is not the sterile replacement process required by the supplied protocol.
Direct suction bypasses the prepared water-seal system and does not follow this device protocol.
The available equipment permits prompt restoration using the stated device-specific process, while avoiding trapping an active air leak.
takeaway: The available equipment permits prompt restoration using the stated device-specific process, while avoiding trapping an active air leak.
exhibit: Water-seal unit disconnected at its connector; active air leak before separation
Sterile replacement water-seal unit and connector at bedside
Promptly replace the disconnected unit using sterile connections; avoid routine clamping when an air leak is present
learningObjective: Restore chest-drain system integrity using the local emergency protocol.

title: Recognize an acute post-procedure pneumothorax
stem: Soon after central venous catheter placement, a client has sudden dyspnea, falling blood pressure and markedly reduced breath sounds on one side. Which complication is most concerning?
options: Tension pneumothorax.
Pulmonary edema.
Vasovagal episode.
Mucus plugging.
why: Sudden unilateral loss of air entry with circulatory compromise after this procedure requires emergency assessment for pressurized pleural air.
Edema can cause dyspnea but more often produces bilateral findings rather than a sudden unilateral reduction after line insertion.
A vagal episode may lower blood pressure but does not explain the marked unilateral breath-sound change.
A plug can reduce regional ventilation, but the procedural timing and shock pattern make tension pneumothorax the more urgent concern.
takeaway: Sudden unilateral loss of air entry with circulatory compromise after this procedure requires emergency assessment for pressurized pleural air.
learningObjective: Recognize a possible tension pneumothorax after central venous catheter placement.

title: Prioritize active hemoptysis
stem: A client coughs up increasing amounts of bright blood and struggles to clear the airway. The bleeding source is not known. What takes priority?
options: Prepare a sputum specimen for laboratory examination.
Obtain help and support airway clearance and oxygenation.
Obtain additional large-bore intravenous access.
Measure and document the total visible blood loss.
why: Diagnostic sampling may be useful after stabilization but does not address current airway compromise.
Active blood in the airway threatens ventilation; oxygenation and clearance take priority while the team manages the bleeding.
Access is important for resuscitation, but the stated inability to clear the airway requires immediate respiratory support.
Quantification supports management but should not delay action for airway flooding.
takeaway: Active blood in the airway threatens ventilation; oxygenation and clearance take priority while the team manages the bleeding.
learningObjective: Prioritize airway clearance and respiratory support during active major hemoptysis.

title: Support a symptomatic pleural effusion
stem: A client with a large pleural effusion becomes more breathless when the bed is lowered. They are alert, blood pressure is stable and there is no spinal precaution. Painful wrist arthritis prevents bearing body weight through the hands or forearms. Prescribed drainage is being arranged. Which position should the nurse try first and then evaluate?
options: Sit leaning forward with the forearms bearing weight on the knees.
Remain recumbent with the knees supported.
Raise the head and support the client upright.
Use supported side-lying with the head near bed level.
why: This posture depends on the upper-limb weight bearing that the client cannot tolerate.
Knee support may improve comfort but does not address the respiratory effect of lowering the trunk.
Back-supported upright positioning addresses recumbent breathlessness without requiring painful arm weight bearing.
The low head position does not best address the observed worsening when the trunk is lowered.
takeaway: The observed intolerance of recumbency supports an upright trial to ease expansion while definitive treatment is prepared.
learningObjective: Use tolerated positioning while definitive treatment of a symptomatic pleural effusion is arranged.

title: Respond to postoperative thoracic bleeding
stem: After lung surgery, chest drainage increases from 25 mL of serosanguineous fluid in the previous hour to 180 mL of bright-red fluid in 20 minutes. Pulse rises from 84 to 118/minute, blood pressure falls from 126/74 to 92/58 mmHg, and the client is pale. What is the priority?
options: Obtain the next complete blood count.
Reinforce the insertion-site dressing.
Confirm the chamber markings and recalculate the output.
Assess circulation urgently and activate surgical review.
why: A count is useful, but an early result may not reflect acute loss and collection must not delay the urgent response.
A local dressing action does not explain or control rapidly increasing blood within the drainage chamber.
Measurement accuracy matters, but the concurrent physiological deterioration already demands urgent action.
Rapid fresh drainage accompanied by tachycardia and hypotension indicates possible significant bleeding; response should not wait for further confirmation.
takeaway: Rapid fresh drainage accompanied by tachycardia and hypotension indicates possible significant bleeding; response should not wait for further confirmation.
learningObjective: Recognize postoperative thoracic bleeding from drainage changes and systemic signs.

title: Deliver oxygen after total laryngectomy
stem: A client with a total laryngectomy becomes hypoxemic. A colleague places oxygen at the nose, but saturation does not improve. What change is needed?
options: Apply oxygen through the neck stoma.
Increase the nasal oxygen flow.
Apply an oxygen mask over the nose and mouth.
Use a bag-mask ventilation seal over the face.
why: After total laryngectomy, the stoma is the connection to the lungs, so oxygen equipment must deliver there.
The nose is surgically separated from the lower airway after total laryngectomy.
A face mask cannot deliver oxygen to the lungs through the separated upper airway.
A face seal does not ventilate the lower airway in a total laryngectomy; rescue ventilation equipment must connect appropriately to the stoma.
takeaway: After total laryngectomy, the stoma is the connection to the lungs, so oxygen equipment must deliver there.
learningObjective: Deliver oxygen through the only functional airway after total laryngectomy.

title: Manage ineffective clearance in cystic fibrosis
stem: A client with cystic fibrosis completes their prescribed airway-clearance session. Before treatment they had audible coarse secretions and difficulty coughing up sputum. Which finding best supports that the session was effective?
options: A smaller sputum amount while chest congestion increases.
Less coarse airway noise with easier expectoration.
Less coughing because the client is too tired to continue.
An unchanged saturation while oxygen needs increase.
why: Less expectorated sputum with increasing congestion suggests retained material rather than better clearance.
Easier removal of sputum together with reduced retained-secretions sounds supports improved clearance.
Fatigue can suppress an effective cough and should not be mistaken for successful clearance.
Maintained saturation with greater support does not demonstrate improved airway clearance.
takeaway: Easier removal of sputum together with reduced retained-secretions sounds supports improved clearance.
learningObjective: Evaluate airway-clearance effectiveness using expectoration and retained-secretion findings.

title: Evaluate a bronchiectasis exacerbation
stem: A client with bronchiectasis reports increased purulent sputum, worsening breathlessness and less ability to perform usual activities. What is most appropriate?
options: Schedule a physiotherapy review of clearance technique.
Maintain the established regimen and symptom record.
Arrange prompt assessment for a possible exacerbation.
Increase routine hydration within the prescribed plan.
why: Technique review may help ongoing care, but the acute symptom change warrants clinical assessment now.
Recording trends is useful, but continuing unchanged care does not address the new deterioration.
New purulence, dyspnea and loss of usual function represent a clinically significant change from baseline.
Hydration can support secretion clearance but does not replace assessment of possible infection or exacerbation.
takeaway: New purulence, dyspnea and loss of usual function represent a clinically significant change from baseline.
learningObjective: Recognize a bronchiectasis exacerbation from changes in sputum and function.

title: Respond to aspiration during feeding
stem: During tube feeding, a client develops sudden coughing, wet respirations and falling saturation. What should the nurse do first?
options: Check the tube insertion marking against the recorded length.
Measure gastric residual if included in local protocol.
Reposition the feeding pump and tubing.
Stop the feed and assess airway and breathing.
why: Tube displacement is relevant, but the immediate priority is the client’s airway and breathing rather than equipment verification.
Residual assessment does not promptly treat respiratory compromise and should not delay the initial response.
Equipment arrangement may need later review, but it does not address suspected aspiration and falling saturation.
Interrupting further feed delivery and supporting breathing address possible aspiration during acute respiratory deterioration.
takeaway: Interrupting further feed delivery and supporting breathing address possible aspiration during acute respiratory deterioration.
learningObjective: Stop feed delivery and prioritize breathing when aspiration is suspected.

title: Recognize airway risk after a burn
stem: A client rescued from an enclosed fire has facial burns, soot around the mouth and a newly hoarse voice. Saturation is initially 97%. What is the priority?
options: Arrange urgent airway assessment.
Estimate the total burned body-surface area.
Apply the appropriate dressings to visible burns.
Obtain a detailed exposure and medical history.
why: Soot, hoarseness and enclosed-fire exposure suggest potentially progressive inhalation injury even with an initially normal saturation.
Burn size guides later care but does not take priority over signs of a threatened airway.
Wound care is important after immediate airway and respiratory threats are addressed.
A focused history can be gathered during care, but it must not delay urgent airway assessment.
takeaway: Soot, hoarseness and enclosed-fire exposure suggest potentially progressive inhalation injury even with an initially normal saturation.
learningObjective: Escalate a potentially progressive airway injury despite initially normal saturation.

title: Interpret oximetry after smoke exposure
stem: A client from an enclosed garage is confused and has a headache after engine exhaust exposure. Routine pulse oximetry reads 99%. What should the nurse do?
options: Assess fluid intake and dehydration from work in the garage.
Arrange urgent toxic-exposure assessment and protocol-based oxygen.
Repeat conventional pulse oximetry at another finger.
Reassess after a period of fresh air and quiet rest.
why: Dehydration could contribute to headache, but the exposure history and confusion make toxic hypoxia the priority concern.
Carbon monoxide poisoning may coexist with a normal conventional oximeter reading; neurological symptoms after exhaust exposure warrant urgent treatment and testing.
A different site does not correct the device limitation in distinguishing carboxyhemoglobin.
Removing exposure matters, but confusion and headache warrant assessment rather than relying on spontaneous symptom resolution.
takeaway: Carbon monoxide poisoning may coexist with a normal conventional oximeter reading; neurological symptoms after exhaust exposure warrant urgent treatment and testing.
learningObjective: Recognize the limitation of conventional pulse oximetry after carbon monoxide exposure.

title: Recognize worsening ventilation after chest trauma
stem: After blunt chest trauma, a client has painful shallow breaths, a segment of chest moving abnormally and increasing fatigue. What is most urgent?
options: Coach repeated coughing and deep breathing.
Position the client on the injured side.
Obtain respiratory support and give ordered analgesia.
Arrange chest imaging to define the injury.
why: These may be useful after pain and ventilation are addressed; a fatigued client may not be able to perform them effectively now.
