stem: A client receiving a prescribed six-week oral antimicrobial course for osteomyelitis reports improved bone pain at week three but has missed the last two doses because of persistent nausea. There is no rash, breathing difficulty or vomiting. What should the nurse do next?
options: Assess nausea and intake, and arrange review of the antimicrobial plan
Reinforce the planned course length and review the medication teaching sheet
Review meal and beverage choices as the main approach to dose tolerance
Use the improved pain score to request a shorter treatment course
why: Persistent nausea and missed doses need a practical tolerability review; the team can address the barrier while maintaining effective bone-infection treatment.
The client has identified a tolerability barrier, so repeating course-completion teaching does not by itself resolve the missed doses.
Food-related strategies may help with some medicines, but are drug specific and do not replace review of persistent nausea and missed doses.
Pain can improve before bone infection is eradicated; that symptom alone is not a sound basis for shortening the prescribed course.
takeaway: Improvement and adverse effects both need assessment during a prolonged antimicrobial course.
learningObjective: Address an adherence barrier during prolonged bone-infection treatment without independently changing the regimen.

title: Assess an acutely painful paediatric joint
stem: A previously well 6-year-old has a temperature of 39.2°C, a visibly swollen warm knee, marked pain with gentle passive movement and refusal to bear weight. There is no injury history. Which concern most urgently needs to be excluded?
options: Septic arthritis affecting the knee
Transient synovitis following a viral illness
A minor soft-tissue sprain
Activity-related growing pains
why: A hot swollen joint, fever and severe movement limitation require urgent assessment for joint infection.
Transient synovitis more commonly affects the hip and usually has a less toxic presentation; it cannot safely explain this pattern without excluding infection.
Absent trauma and prominent fever with a hot swollen joint argue against assuming a sprain.
Growing pains do not explain an acutely hot swollen joint, high fever or refusal to bear weight.
takeaway: A febrile child who will not bear weight needs timely evaluation of an acute joint problem.
learningObjective: A febrile child who will not bear weight needs timely evaluation of an acute joint problem.

title: Investigate new foot drop after surgery
stem: Following lower-leg surgery, a client who could dorsiflex the ankle at handover can no longer lift the front of the foot. There is new numbness on its upper surface; surgical pain is unchanged. Which interpretation best guides the focused assessment?
options: Generalized muscle deconditioning from bed rest
Pain-limited effort during an otherwise unchanged examination
New focal motor and sensory compromise requiring assessment for compression or injury
Expected stiffness from keeping the ankle still
why: Deconditioning develops more broadly and does not explain a new focal sensory deficit over one shift.
Unchanged pain with a new sensory change makes pain-limited effort an inadequate explanation.
Compare neurovascular findings with baseline and report the acute focal change promptly; examine potential compression within the authorized care plan.
Stiffness may reduce range, but does not account for new numbness and loss of active dorsiflexion.
takeaway: Compare postoperative motor and sensory function with the documented baseline.
learningObjective: Compare postoperative motor and sensory function with the documented baseline.

title: Evaluate an established phantom-pain plan
stem: A client after below-knee amputation has an established multimodal plan for phantom pain. The agreed goals are tolerable episodes, improved sleep and participation in transfers. At review, which finding best demonstrates a useful response?
options: The incision is closed and appetite improves, but painful episodes still interrupt sleep and transfers
Episodes are shorter, sleep rises from three to six hours, and planned transfers are completed
The plan is followed, but sleep remains three hours and transfers require extra rests because of pain
The pain rating falls briefly after doses, but sleep and transfer tolerance remain unchanged
why: Wound and appetite improvements are useful, but the agreed pain-related sleep and transfer goals remain unmet.
Shorter episodes with improved sleep and completed transfers directly support useful benefit against the agreed goals.
Following the plan is important, but the persistent sleep and transfer limitations indicate that its effect needs review.
A short-lived rating change is insufficient when pain continues to prevent the agreed functional outcomes.
takeaway: Assess how pain treatment changes daily function as well as the pain rating.
learningObjective: Evaluate pain treatment against agreed sleep and functional goals.

title: Separate residual-limb deterioration from phantom pain
stem: A client with a history of phantom sensations reports new severe pain in the residual limb. The skin is now pale and cool compared with the previous assessment. What is the priority response?
options: Review the timing and duration of the usual phantom sensations
Assess whether the current prosthesis schedule is increasing skin friction
Review adherence to the established neuropathic-pain regimen
Obtain urgent neurovascular assessment of the new pale, cool tissue
why: Pain history is useful but does not account for the new perfusion findings.
Friction generally causes local pressure or skin injury; pallor and coolness require urgent perfusion assessment.
Medication review may help chronic pain but cannot explain away objective tissue deterioration.
New severe pain with pallor and coolness raises a perfusion concern requiring prompt assessment.
takeaway: A familiar pain history should not obscure new objective tissue changes.
learningObjective: A familiar pain history should not obscure new objective tissue changes.

title: Evaluate neurovascular status around splinting
stem: A forearm splint has just been applied. Before application, the fingers were warm and pink with normal movement and sensation. Which new findings suggest distal neurovascular compromise and require prompt reassessment? Select all that apply.
options: Tingling and reduced ability to move the fingers
Bruising remains localized over the original injury
Fingers become cool and pale compared with the opposite hand
Tenderness at the fracture is unchanged from the baseline
why: New sensory and motor changes after splinting may indicate pressure or another neurovascular problem.
Unchanged local bruising does not by itself demonstrate a new distal deficit.
New distal pallor and coolness are concerning perfusion changes.
Persistent expected local tenderness needs management, but is not the same as a new neurovascular change.
takeaway: Document a baseline so changes after immobilization can be recognized.
learningObjective: Document a baseline so changes after immobilization can be recognized.

title: Evaluate a functional rehabilitation goal
stem: After ankle-fracture treatment, a client may bear weight as tolerated using a walker. The agreed goal is a bathroom transfer with one assistant, stable balance and pain no greater than 4/10 during and after the task. Which findings meet these criteria? Select all that apply.
options: The client completes the transfer with one assistant and maintains balance
The transfer is faster, but two assistants must prevent a fall
Pain is 3/10 during the transfer and 4/10 afterward
Walking distance increases, but transfer pain rises to 7/10
why: The observed assistance level and balance meet the stated functional criteria.
Greater speed does not compensate for failing the balance and assistance criteria.
Both pain ratings remain within the agreed limit.
Distance is useful information, but the pain response does not meet this goal.
takeaway: Evaluate rehabilitation using observed function and the physiological response to the task.
learningObjective: Evaluate rehabilitation using observed function and the physiological response to the task.

title: Recognize heat illness with cognitive change
stem: At an outdoor event, an adult who has been working in intense heat becomes confused and unsteady. The skin is hot, and the client cannot reliably follow swallowing instructions. Which action is best?
options: Move to shade and reassess cognition after a period of quiet rest
Activate emergency help and begin rapid active cooling in a safe cool area
Apply a cool cloth to the forehead and reassess after it warms
Support seated rest in shade while preparing oral rehydration
why: Shade reduces further exposure, but altered cognition requires immediate emergency assessment and active cooling.
Neurological change during heat exposure suggests severe heat illness; start cooling promptly while emergency care is activated.
A small local cloth is insufficient cooling for suspected heat stroke and should not replace emergency care.
The impaired ability to follow swallowing instructions makes oral intake unsafe; rest and hydration planning do not address the urgent cooling need.
takeaway: Heat exposure with altered cognition requires immediate cooling and emergency assessment.
learningObjective: Heat exposure with altered cognition requires immediate cooling and emergency assessment.

title: Interpret cessation of shivering
stem: A cold-exposed adult remains wet and cold. Earlier the person shivered vigorously; now shivering has stopped and speech is slurred. Which interpretation is safest?
options: Stopping shivering means enough heat has been generated
The main remaining problem is local frostbite in the hands
Reduced shivering with cognitive change may indicate worsening hypothermia
The person is ready to walk briskly to complete rewarming
why: Cessation without actual rewarming can indicate deterioration.
Systemic cognitive change requires attention beyond local skin injury.
Reduced heat-generating response and neurological impairment are concerning; arrange emergency care and handle gently while preventing further heat loss.
Exertion is not the safe response to significant hypothermia and impaired coordination.
takeaway: Interpret shivering in relation to temperature recovery and neurological status.
learningObjective: Interpret shivering in relation to temperature recovery and neurological status.

title: Protect frostbitten fingers
stem: A client with frostbitten fingers has reached a heated clinic where refreezing can be prevented. The treatment team is arranging controlled rewarming. Which actions should the nurse avoid? Select all that apply.
options: Rubbing the numb fingers briskly to restore circulation
Removing rings carefully before swelling increases
Applying direct dry heat from a heating pad to numb skin
Protecting the affected hand from additional trauma
why: Rubbing can further damage injured tissue.
Removing constricting jewellery, when possible without trauma, is appropriate.
Numb tissue can be burned by poorly controlled direct heat.
Protection from trauma is part of appropriate care.
takeaway: Prevent mechanical and thermal injury while following a controlled rewarming plan.
learningObjective: Prevent mechanical and thermal injury while following a controlled rewarming plan.

title: Assess symptoms after a water rescue
stem: A child is awake after rescue from brief submersion. Over the next ten minutes, coughing persists, respiratory rate rises from 26 to 38/min and SpO2 falls from 97% to 92% in room air. Which interpretation should guide urgent assessment?
options: Respiratory impairment may be evolving despite preserved consciousness
Anxiety is the most likely explanation because the child remains awake
Coughing indicates effective clearance and therefore improving lung function
The falling saturation is an expected consequence of brief exertion during rescue
why: Worsening respiratory rate and oxygenation after submersion warrant urgent evaluation and breathing support.
Consciousness does not exclude pulmonary impairment; the objective trend cannot be attributed to anxiety.
Cough can persist with lung injury, and the oxygenation trend contradicts recovery.
A persistent downward oxygenation trend with tachypnoea is not a reassuring post-exertion finding.
takeaway: Persistent respiratory symptoms after submersion require assessment, not reassurance based on consciousness alone.
learningObjective: Persistent respiratory symptoms after submersion require assessment, not reassurance based on consciousness alone.

title: Evaluate initial cooling after heat exposure
stem: A client arrived confused after severe heat exposure, with core temperature 40.4°C and pulse 132/min. Active cooling and monitoring are underway. Which subsequent finding most strongly supports physiological improvement?
options: Core temperature is 40.1°C and pulse 128/min; skin feels cool but confusion persists
Core temperature is 39.5°C and pulse 134/min; discomfort improves but disorientation persists
Core temperature is 39.0°C and pulse 126/min; the client becomes harder to arouse
Core temperature reaches the team’s target and pulse is 98/min; orientation is restored
why: Surface cooling with persistent marked core elevation and confusion does not establish adequate recovery.
Partial temperature and comfort improvement must be weighed against persistent tachycardia and disorientation.
A falling temperature does not make decreasing responsiveness reassuring; this neurological change needs prompt reassessment.
Improvement across core temperature, orientation and circulation supports a favourable response; continue monitoring and follow the clinical cooling plan.
takeaway: Evaluate heat-illness treatment using neurological and physiological recovery, not skin feel alone.
learningObjective: Evaluate heat-illness treatment using neurological and physiological recovery, not skin feel alone.

title: Respond to a boggy postpartum uterus
stem: Twenty minutes after vaginal birth, a client's bleeding increases and the uterus feels boggy. The nurse calls for assistance and begins the facility's postpartum-haemorrhage response. Which immediate action directly addresses the identified uterine finding?
options: Perform fundal massage using the approved technique
Assess the bladder for distension
Quantify the ongoing blood loss
Prepare for assessment of genital-tract trauma
why: Massage directly stimulates contraction of the boggy uterus while the broader haemorrhage response proceeds.
Bladder distension can contribute to atony and needs assessment, but this does not directly stimulate the poorly contracted uterus.
Measuring loss guides treatment but is not the intervention directed at uterine tone.
Trauma is another possible bleeding source, but the identified boggy uterus calls for an immediate intervention for atony.
takeaway: Match the immediate intervention to the assessed cause while activating the broader haemorrhage response.
learningObjective: Match the immediate intervention to the assessed cause while activating the broader haemorrhage response.

title: Reassess continued bleeding with a firm uterus
stem: A postpartum client continues to lose bright red blood, but the uterus is firm and midline after initial assessment. Which interpretation should guide the nurse's urgent handover?
options: A firm uterus means the measured blood loss is no longer clinically important
Bleeding from a genital-tract injury or another source still needs assessment
More fundal massage is the definitive treatment for this pattern
The bleeding can be categorized as normal lochia based on uterine tone
why: Tone does not determine whether ongoing blood loss is safe.
Persistent bleeding despite a firm uterus requires evaluation for trauma and other causes while monitoring circulation.
Massage targets atony and does not resolve every source of postpartum bleeding.
Bleeding amount, trajectory and physiological effect must be assessed, not tone alone.
takeaway: Do not assume that correcting uterine tone has corrected every source of postpartum haemorrhage.
learningObjective: Do not assume that correcting uterine tone has corrected every source of postpartum haemorrhage.

title: Protect a pregnant client during a seizure
stem: A client admitted with severe pre-eclampsia begins a generalized seizure in bed. Which actions should the nurse take immediately? Select all that apply.
options: Call for emergency assistance and protect the head from injury
Insert a padded object between the teeth to preserve the airway
Position laterally when feasible and prepare airway support
Hold the arms and legs against the mattress during the jerking movements
why: Emergency support and protection from injury are immediate priorities.
Objects in the mouth can injure the client and obstruct the airway.
Lateral positioning when feasible and airway readiness help manage secretions and breathing; follow the emergency plan.
Forceful restraint can cause injury and does not terminate the seizure.
takeaway: Protect from injury and support airway/breathing during an obstetric seizure.
learningObjective: Protect from injury and support airway/breathing during an obstetric seizure.

title: Evaluate treatment of hyperemesis
stem: A pregnant client receiving treatment for persistent vomiting has improved nausea after medication. Which additional findings best support meaningful recovery from the episode? Select all that apply.
options: The client can retain the prescribed oral-fluid trial
The client reports less nausea but still becomes faint on sitting
Urine output improves and postural symptoms settle
Urine remains concentrated and output stays below the treatment target
why: Demonstrated intake tolerance is a functional outcome of treatment.
Persistent postural symptoms suggest recovery is incomplete despite less nausea.
Improved output and circulation-related symptoms support better hydration.
Persistently low concentrated urine does not support adequate hydration recovery; reassess the whole response.
takeaway: Evaluate vomiting treatment using intake and hydration, not symptom relief or task completion alone.
learningObjective: Evaluate vomiting treatment using intake and hydration, not symptom relief or task completion alone.

title: Avoid an unsafe examination during pregnancy bleeding
stem: A client at 32 weeks has painless vaginal bleeding. Placental location has not yet been confirmed. While urgent obstetric assessment is arranged, which proposed action requires clarification before proceeding?
options: Record maternal vital signs and quantify visible blood loss
Prepare for the ordered ultrasound assessment
Perform a digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilation
Assess the fetal heart rate using the available protocol
why: These observations help assess severity and are appropriate while care is coordinated.
Imaging can establish placental location and guide the plan.
A digital examination may provoke severe bleeding if placenta previa is present; obtain the obstetric plan first.
Fetal assessment is relevant and does not create the examination-related bleeding risk.
takeaway: Establish the safety of an invasive examination when placental location is unknown in late-pregnancy bleeding.
learningObjective: Establish the safety of an invasive examination when placental location is unknown in late-pregnancy bleeding.

title: Interpret limited visible bleeding in abruption
stem: A client at 35 weeks develops severe constant abdominal pain, a tense tender uterus and dizziness. There is a small amount of vaginal blood. Pulse is 128/min and BP is 86/50 mmHg. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: The loss is mainly external because vaginal blood is visible
The findings fit uncomplicated labour with a pain-related pulse increase
Painless low-lying placental bleeding best accounts for the uterine findings
A concealed placental bleed may explain the shock signs and tense tender uterus
why: Visible blood does not establish where most of the loss is occurring.
A persistently tense tender uterus with marked hypotension does not fit uncomplicated labour.
Placenta previa classically produces painless bleeding; the painful tense uterus points to a different urgent concern.
Possible abruption can involve substantial concealed loss; the pulse and BP require immediate obstetric and circulatory assessment.
takeaway: Visible blood may underestimate the severity of an obstetric haemorrhage.
learningObjective: Visible blood may underestimate the severity of an obstetric haemorrhage.

title: Escalate possible ectopic rupture
stem: A person with a positive pregnancy test and no confirmed intrauterine pregnancy develops one-sided pelvic pain, shoulder-tip pain and near-syncope. Emergency assessment is being arranged. Which concern best explains the combination and must urgently be excluded?
options: Ectopic pregnancy with intra-abdominal bleeding
An uncomplicated early-pregnancy miscarriage
A lower urinary-tract infection
Expected stretching discomfort in early pregnancy
why: One-sided pain with referred shoulder pain and circulatory symptoms raises concern for internal bleeding from an ectopic pregnancy.
Miscarriage may cause pain and vaginal bleeding, but this pattern requires exclusion of ectopic bleeding rather than assuming an uncomplicated loss.
A lower urinary infection does not adequately explain referred shoulder pain and near-syncope.
Expected discomfort does not explain signs of possible circulatory compromise.
takeaway: Early-pregnancy pain with referred shoulder pain or circulatory symptoms needs emergency assessment.
learningObjective: Early-pregnancy pain with referred shoulder pain or circulatory symptoms needs emergency assessment.

title: Recognize a prolapsed cord emergency
stem: Following rupture of membranes, a cord loop is visible and the fetal heart rate falls. The obstetric emergency response is activated. A qualified clinician is preparing manual elevation of the presenting part. The nurse is trained and authorized to provide emergency positioning. Which position should the nurse assist the client into to reduce pressure on the cord?
options: High Fowler’s position with the knees gently flexed
Knee-chest position with the client supported safely
Flat supine position with both legs supported
Lithotomy position to provide access to the perineum
why: An upright position can increase downward pressure and is not the appropriate pressure-relief position in this situation.
Knee-chest positioning can reduce pressure from the presenting part while the obstetric team provides definitive care.
Flat supine positioning does not use gravity to relieve the cord compression described.
Access for examination is different from relieving cord pressure; follow the emergency positioning and obstetric plan.
takeaway: Apply the supplied emergency protocol promptly while the obstetric team prepares definitive treatment.
learningObjective: Prompt recognition and a trained response are essential when cord prolapse compromises fetal circulation.

title: Look beyond visible postpartum loss
stem: Two hours after an assisted vaginal birth, a client reports increasing deep perineal pressure and severe pain. Lochia is scant, the uterus is firm and midline, pulse rises to 118/min and one side of the perineum is increasingly swollen. Which concern should be highlighted during urgent assessment?
options: Expected symmetrical postpartum tissue oedema
Bladder distension displacing the uterus
An expanding perineal haematoma
Uterine atony causing free vaginal blood loss
why: Progressive unilateral swelling with severe pressure and tachycardia is not a reassuring expected pattern.
The uterus is midline and the dominant change is a unilateral perineal swelling, not a displaced fundus.
A concealed collection can produce pressure, swelling and circulatory change despite scant lochia.
Atony usually involves a poorly contracted uterus; the firm fundus and local swelling suggest another source.
takeaway: A concealed postpartum bleed may present with pressure and swelling rather than heavy lochia.
learningObjective: A concealed postpartum bleed may present with pressure and swelling rather than heavy lochia.

title: Treat symptomatic neonatal hypoglycaemia urgently
stem: A 6-hour-old newborn is lethargic and feeding poorly, with bedside glucose 1.7 mmol/L. The unit protocol requires immediate neonatal review and IV glucose for symptomatic hypoglycaemia; a confirmatory sample is collected without delaying treatment. What is the best next action?
options: Obtain a laboratory result before requesting the IV treatment
Offer an oral feed and use the post-feed result to decide on review
Repeat the bedside reading at the next scheduled glucose check
Activate the protocol and prepare the prescribed treatment while a confirmatory sample is obtained
why: Confirmation is important, but symptomatic treatment must not wait for the result.
A feed-first reassessment approach does not follow this symptomatic-infant protocol; poor feeding also limits reliability.
The symptoms and low value already meet the supplied action criteria.
Proceed with urgent protocol-based treatment and confirmation in parallel. Any interim measure, including dextrose gel while IV access is established, follows the neonatal team plan.
takeaway: Symptoms plus low newborn glucose require prompt treatment, not routine surveillance alone.
learningObjective: Symptoms plus low newborn glucose require prompt treatment, not routine surveillance alone.

title: Reassess oral feeding during neonatal distress
stem: A newborn awaiting assessment is breathing 78/min with grunting and chest recession. A bottle feed is due. What is the safest nursing approach?
options: Pause the oral feed and obtain an immediate respiratory and feeding-plan review
Offer a smaller paced feed with closer observation
Review the infant's weight trend and previous feed volumes
Discuss the longer-term feeding schedule with the parent
why: Marked respiratory distress can impair suck-swallow-breathe coordination; address breathing and determine a safe feeding route before proceeding.
Smaller paced feeds can help some stable infants, but grunting, recession and a rate of 78/min require respiratory assessment first.
Weight and intake history are relevant but do not resolve the immediate safety of this feed.
Education is useful after the immediate respiratory and feeding-safety issue is addressed.
takeaway: Significant respiratory distress changes the safety of a routine oral feed.
learningObjective: Significant respiratory distress changes the safety of a routine oral feed.

title: Recognize concerning newborn colour and effort
stem: A term newborn is 36 hours old. Which findings need prompt assessment rather than reassurance about normal peripheral colour change? Select all that apply.
options: Blue discoloration of the tongue during quiet breathing
Briefly cool hands with a pink tongue and comfortable breathing
Recurrent sweating and marked breathlessness during feeds
Pink central colour after warming the feet with normal feeding tolerance
why: Central cyanosis is concerning and requires assessment of oxygenation and circulation.
Isolated peripheral colour change can occur with cooling; assess the whole infant and response rather than equating it with central cyanosis.
Repeated feeding-related distress can indicate a cardiopulmonary problem.
This is a reassuring pattern if the overall assessment remains normal.
takeaway: Distinguish central and functional cardiopulmonary signs from transient peripheral colour changes.
learningObjective: Distinguish central and functional cardiopulmonary signs from transient peripheral colour changes.

title: Prepare an infant with pyloric stenosis safely
stem: An infant with confirmed pyloric stenosis has repeated vomiting, reduced urine and dehydration. Surgery is planned after stabilization. The parent asks why the operation is not starting immediately. Which explanation is best?
options: The team is completing the required fasting interval to reduce aspiration risk
Fluid and electrolyte abnormalities need correction to reduce anaesthetic risk
A sustained improvement in body weight is needed before the operative repair
Routine surgical and anaesthetic preparations need to be completed before repair
why: Fasting precautions are relevant, but they do not correct the dehydration and vomiting-related abnormalities that require stabilization.
Dehydration and electrolyte or acid-base disturbances must be corrected before surgery because they affect perioperative safety.
Nutrition matters, but restoring body weight is not the immediate stabilization endpoint for this dehydrated infant.
Preparation is necessary, but the stated clinical reason for delaying anaesthesia is physiological correction rather than routine arrangements.
takeaway: Urgent surgical conditions may require physiological stabilization before anaesthesia.
learningObjective: Urgent surgical conditions may require physiological stabilization before anaesthesia.

title: Interpret well intervals between abdominal episodes
stem: A 9-month-old has repeated brief episodes of intense crying with knees drawn up, pallor and vomiting. Between episodes the infant becomes quiet and sometimes appears comfortable. Which interpretation should guide urgent assessment?
options: The comfortable intervals favour ordinary infant colic
The vomiting is most consistent with uncomplicated reflux
An intermittent bowel obstruction such as intussusception remains a concern
A diffuse gastroenteritis pattern best explains the discrete severe episodes
why: Temporary well intervals do not exclude intussusception; pallor and severe episodic pain are concerning.
Reflux does not adequately explain repeated severe colicky episodes with pallor.
Intermittent pain, pallor and vomiting can occur with intussusception; urgent assessment should not wait for bloody stool.
Gastroenteritis is possible in a vomiting child, but the discrete painful episodes with pallor favour an intermittent obstructive concern.
takeaway: Intermittent symptoms can still represent an urgent bowel problem.
learningObjective: Intermittent symptoms can still represent an urgent bowel problem.

title: Evaluate hydration support in bronchiolitis
stem: An infant with bronchiolitis has a prescribed nasogastric hydration plan because oral intake was inadequate. Before treatment, urine output averaged 0.4 mL/kg/hour. Six hours later breathing effort is stable. Which finding best supports an effective, tolerated hydration response?
options: The prescribed volume was delivered, but urine output remains 0.3 mL/kg/hour
Urine output rises to 1.3 mL/kg/hour, the mouth is moist and no new oedema appears
Body mass rises quickly while eyelid swelling and increasing recession develop
The infant takes one good oral feed, but subsequent intake and urine remain low
why: Completion of the prescribed intake does not by itself demonstrate a physiological response.
Improved urine and mucosal hydration without new fluid-intolerance signs supports a favourable response; continue the full clinical assessment.
Rapid gain with swelling and worsening breathing suggests a need to reassess tolerance rather than assume successful rehydration.
An isolated feed does not establish sustained hydration when the subsequent trend remains poor.
takeaway: Check the physiological response to a hydration plan, not just the volume delivered.
learningObjective: Evaluate intake support using urine, hydration and tolerance trends.

title: Evaluate gentle nasal clearance
stem: A congested infant with bronchiolitis receives gentle nasal suction according to the care plan before a supervised feed. Which observation best indicates a useful response?
options: Nasal noise is reduced, but chest recession and oxygen need increase
The infant finishes the feed faster, but has repeated coughing and desaturation
Nasal airflow improves and the infant feeds with fewer respiratory pauses
More mucus is collected, but feeding volume and respiratory effort are unchanged
why: Less nasal noise does not outweigh worsening respiratory indicators.
Speed is not a favourable endpoint when feeding causes respiratory instability.
Improved airflow and safer feeding directly demonstrate the intended functional benefit.
Recovered mucus is a process observation; unchanged function does not demonstrate the desired benefit.
takeaway: Evaluate secretion clearance by breathing and feeding function rather than procedure completion.
learningObjective: Evaluate secretion clearance by breathing and feeding function rather than procedure completion.

title: Assess bronchiolitis discharge readiness
stem: A hospitalized infant with bronchiolitis is being assessed for discharge under the local plan. Which findings support readiness? Select all that apply.
options: Work of breathing has improved and oxygenation meets the discharge target on room air
The infant has adequate oral intake and the caregiver knows when to seek help
Wheezing is quieter, but the infant is increasingly lethargic
Oxygen saturation meets the target during supplemental oxygen, then falls below it in room air
why: Improved effort with satisfactory room-air oxygenation supports readiness under the stated plan.
Adequate intake and a workable caregiver plan are also necessary.
Quieter sounds with increasing lethargy can indicate deterioration.
A continuing oxygen requirement does not meet this routine discharge plan; a separately authorized home-oxygen pathway would require its own criteria.
takeaway: Use respiratory recovery, feeding and a workable home plan together when assessing discharge.
learningObjective: Use respiratory recovery, feeding and a workable home plan together when assessing discharge.

title: Minimize distress during croup care
stem: A toddler with croup has stridor at rest and becomes more distressed when separated from the parent. Treatment is being prepared. Which approach best supports breathing during assessment?
options: Observe breathing with the child upright on the parent's lap
Separate the child briefly to obtain an accurate weight before treatment
Begin a supine chest examination on the assessment trolley
Complete temperature and blood-pressure measurements before observing breathing
why: Parent-held positioning reduces agitation and permits respiratory assessment while necessary treatment is prepared.
Weight may be needed for treatment, but unnecessary separation can worsen distress; use the least disruptive feasible approach.
Forced supine positioning may worsen distress and is not required to begin assessment.
Start with observation of the airway and breathing in the least distressing way; stage other measurements according to urgency.
takeaway: Adapt assessment to minimize agitation when upper-airway obstruction is present.
learningObjective: Adapt assessment to minimize agitation when upper-airway obstruction is present.

title: Interpret quieter stridor with fatigue
stem: A child with severe croup previously had loud stridor and vigorous chest recession. Stridor becomes quieter, but air entry is now poor and the child is drowsy. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: The quieter sound indicates that the airway inflammation is resolving
Reduced airflow and fatigue may signal impending respiratory failure
Drowsiness is an expected benefit of reduced coughing
The child can now tolerate an oral-fluid challenge
why: A quieter sound is not reassuring when air movement and alertness worsen.
This combination requires immediate emergency reassessment and airway support.
New drowsiness in severe respiratory illness is a danger sign, not a treatment endpoint.
Feeding should not distract from a possible failing airway.
takeaway: Interpret respiratory sounds together with air entry, effort and consciousness.
learningObjective: Interpret respiratory sounds together with air entry, effort and consciousness.

title: Maintain observation after rapid croup relief
stem: A child's stridor improves shortly after prescribed nebulized epinephrine. The local plan requires observation for recurrence before discharge. The parent asks to leave immediately. Which explanation is best?
options: Observation tracks the response as the prescribed corticosteroid begins to act
Observation checks whether swallowing and oral intake have returned to the usual level
Epinephrine relief can fade, so breathing must remain improved as its effect wears off
Observation checks for persistent medicine-related tachycardia or tremor
why: Corticosteroid response contributes to care, but the specific reason immediate relief is insufficient is the short-lived effect of epinephrine.
Intake matters for discharge readiness, but adequate swallowing alone does not establish sustained airway improvement after this drug.
Nebulized epinephrine can provide temporary improvement; reassess for recurrence as its effect fades under the observation plan.
Adverse-effect assessment is relevant, but it does not replace the main need to confirm sustained respiratory improvement.
takeaway: Rapid symptom relief after a short-acting treatment needs reassessment for recurrence.
learningObjective: Rapid symptom relief after a short-acting treatment needs reassessment for recurrence.

title: Recognize a dangerous drooling presentation
stem: A child has high fever, drooling, a muffled voice and difficulty breathing, and sits leaning forward on the parent's lap. The nurse can keep the child comfortable while another team member acts. Which request should take priority?
options: Arrange the equipment for a routine throat culture
Obtain the immunization record from the family
Prepare transport for the requested neck radiograph
Activate immediate expert airway assessment at the bedside
why: Microbiological testing may be considered later, but throat procedures can agitate a threatened airway.
Immunization history helps assessment but does not address the immediate airway risk.
Investigations should be coordinated after airway safety is assessed; transport can separate the child from needed support.
The pattern suggests a potentially serious upper-airway process. Obtain skilled airway support promptly while avoiding unnecessary agitation.
takeaway: Drooling with respiratory distress requires airway-focused care and cautious handling.
learningObjective: Drooling with respiratory distress requires airway-focused care and cautious handling.

title: Adapt oral rehydration after vomiting
stem: A child with mild dehydration is alert, has no shock signs and is on an oral rehydration plan. A large cup of solution triggers vomiting. Which adjustment is most appropriate initially?
options: Restart with small frequent measured amounts under the existing plan
Pause for a longer interval, then retry the same large cup
Change to a different solution flavour while keeping the large portions
Reduce the total prescribed replacement target to avoid further vomiting
why: Small frequent volumes may improve tolerance; reassess intake, losses and hydration and escalate if the trial fails.
A brief pause may be appropriate after vomiting, but repeating the same large portion does not address the delivery problem.
A flavour change may improve acceptance, but it does not correct the volume-related intolerance described.
The replacement target should not be independently reduced simply because the delivery method needs adjustment.
takeaway: Adjust the delivery of a safe oral rehydration trial and evaluate tolerance.
learningObjective: Adjust the delivery of a safe oral rehydration trial and evaluate tolerance.

title: Reassess a sudden change in appendicitis pain
stem: A child awaiting treatment for appendicitis briefly reports less pain, then develops widespread abdominal tenderness, fever and a faster pulse. Which interpretation should guide immediate reporting?
options: Resolving appendiceal inflammation explains the temporary pain relief
Possible perforation is causing more widespread peritoneal inflammation
Normal fluctuation of localized appendicitis pain explains the pattern
Reduced muscle guarding indicates recovery despite the higher temperature
why: The later objective deterioration contradicts uncomplicated improvement.
Transient relief followed by diffuse tenderness and systemic change requires urgent reassessment for a complication; it is not a definitive diagnosis from symptoms alone.
Loss of localization with worsening systemic signs should not be normalized as simple fluctuation.
A possible change in guarding must be interpreted with the entire worsening pattern.
takeaway: Evaluate a change in pain together with the subsequent abdominal and systemic findings.
learningObjective: Evaluate a change in pain together with the subsequent abdominal and systemic findings.

title: Recognize urgent referred abdominal symptoms
stem: A 14-year-old reports sudden lower abdominal pain and vomiting. During private assessment, he describes abrupt severe pain in one testicle. There was no trauma or preceding urinary discomfort. Which concern needs time-critical exclusion?
options: Testicular torsion
Epididymitis associated with urinary infection
A scrotal contusion
Referred discomfort from constipation
why: Sudden unilateral testicular pain with vomiting may represent torsion; urgent assessment is needed to protect perfusion.
Infection is a differential, but the abrupt onset without urinary symptoms requires urgent exclusion of torsion.
There is no trauma history, so assuming a contusion would not explain the presentation.
Constipation does not adequately account for the new severe unilateral testicular pain.
takeaway: Clarify associated symptoms that can reveal a time-critical cause of abdominal pain.
learningObjective: Clarify associated symptoms that can reveal a time-critical cause of abdominal pain.

title: Recognize neurological deterioration during paediatric DKA care
stem: A child being treated for diabetic ketoacidosis initially becomes more alert. Two hours later, headache worsens, vomiting recurs and responsiveness decreases. Bedside glucose is 12 mmol/L; pulse has fallen from 118 to 76/min while BP rises. Which complication is most concerning and requires immediate protocol-based assessment?
options: Hypoglycaemia from the insulin infusion
Uncomplicated resolution of dehydration
Gastrointestinal intolerance of oral intake
Cerebral injury associated with diabetic ketoacidosis
why: The measured glucose does not support hypoglycaemia as the explanation, although glucose remains part of the urgent assessment.
Worsening consciousness and headache are not expected signs of uncomplicated recovery.
Gastrointestinal intolerance does not account for the neurological and circulatory changes.
New neurological deterioration with relative bradycardia and rising BP is concerning for cerebral injury; immediate expert assessment and the emergency protocol are required.
takeaway: Follow neurological status during paediatric DKA treatment even when metabolic measures improve.
learningObjective: Follow neurological status during paediatric DKA treatment even when metabolic measures improve.
